votes:
confirmed: The defect is real in lib/server/export.ts, in loadTargetProfiles (lines 324-334). The query has no .range() and no paging. It orders effective_from and rev ascending, and supabase/config.toml sets max_rows = 1000. Past 1000 rows PostgREST drops the newest revisions. profileForDate (line ~336) walks that truncated ascending list and returns the last row it has, so later dates resolve to the 1000th revision. The page is read at line 416, and no error is raised.

I found no guard upstream and no owner ruling that accepts this. Nothing in docs/decisions or docs/audit mentions the export's target read or a cap on it. The sibling reader in lib/server/target-recompute.ts (futureRevisions, line 166) pages the same table with fetchAllRows, so the repo treats this table as exceeding 1000 rows.

The trigger is narrow. An account needs more than 1000 target_profiles rows. lib/targets/revision.ts (line 152) describes the phone cache as about six months (180 dates) of daily weigh-in revisions, so a long-lived account would pass 1000 after roughly three years. The failure is silent, and the progress export then returns stale kcal_target, day_type and target_revision for recent dates.

I ran no test; this rests on reading the code.

confirmed: The code defect is real, but it only bites an account with more than 1000 target_profiles rows, which is rare. I traced the path and did not run a repro.

- `loadTargetProfiles` (lib/server/export.ts:324-335) selects `*` from `target_profiles` with `.lte("effective_from", through)`, ordered ascending by `effective_from` then `rev`. It has no `.range()` and no paging helper.
- `supabase/config.toml:10` sets `max_rows = 1000`. A silent cut at 1000 rows keeps the OLDEST rows and drops the newest.
- `profileForDate` (line 337) walks that ascending list and keeps the last row whose `effective_from` is on or before the date. After truncation, every date past the 1000th row's `effective_from` resolves to that stale row.
- The result feeds `targetFor` (line 428), so `kcal_target`, `day_type`, `target_revision` and `targets` come out stale. No error is raised, because `rows.error` is empty on a capped result.
- `lib/server/target-recompute.ts:166` reads the same table through `fetchAllRows`. The progress export is the only unpaged read of this table I found.

I rate it low rather than medium because it needs more than 1000 revisions on one account. Revisions are written on a profile change, a weigh-in-driven recompute, or an adaptive or proposal row, not once a day. A typical account is far below 1000 rows. The same cap would also hit an account whose rows are all backdated.

The fix is to page this query with `fetchAllRows` and keep the existing order.

confirmed.title: Conflict rebase deletes the old op before enqueueing its replacement (three non-atomic steps)
confirmed.defect: The generic onConflict does putRow(merged), then deleteOp(old), then enqueue(rebased), in three separate transactions. The op's payload is the only surviving record of the user's edit. If the page dies, the account switches (AccountChanged), or enqueue throws between deleteOp and enqueue, the edit is gone while the mirror already shows it as saved. assertKeyMatchesPayload in enqueue can also throw a TypeError after the old op was deleted.
confirmed.failureScenario: The app is backgrounded or killed right after the conflict response is processed. The old op is deleted and the rebased op was never written. The row holds the merged values locally, the server never receives the user's change, the outbox is empty, and SyncStatus reports everything as sent.
confirmed.evidence: outbox.ts:185-188 `await putRow(...); await deleteOp(h, op.op_id); await enqueue(h, rebased, now());`.
confirmed.fix: Do the delete, mirror write and enqueue in a single readwrite transaction (like settleUserSettings), or enqueue the rebased op first and delete the old op afterwards.
votes: confirmed: The finding is accurate. In onConflict (lib/sync/outbox.ts:185-188), the generic path runs putRow(merged), then deleteOp(old), then enqueue(rebased) as three separate IndexedDB transactions. Between the last two, the old op is already deleted and the rebased op is not yet written. If the page is killed, the account switches, or enqueue throws in that gap, the edit is lost. The mirror already holds the merged row, so nothing is left to re-send it, and the outbox count reads empty. I found no recovery path and no guard that makes the sequence atomic. The SETTINGS path is atomic (settleUserSettings), but the generic path is not. No ruling in docs/audit or docs/decisions accepts this. The only hit, R24 in the 2026-09-13 report, is about a different issue (delete/restore ops being rebased). I downgrade to low because the window is a few milliseconds between IDB transactions. The assertKeyMatchesPayload throw is also unlikely, because the rebased payload comes from a merge that keeps the key columns and entity_id is unchanged. A fix is to swap the old op for the rebased one in one transaction, as appendOpWithRow does for op plus row. Files: /Users/zero-suminc./projects/clients/Sasha/wt/audit-2026-10-10/lib/sync/outbox.ts, lib/sync/idb.ts.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run a crash repro. In lib/sync/outbox.ts, onConflict (lines 185-188) ends with `putRow(merged, rev: current_rev)`, `deleteOp(old)`, `enqueue(rebased)`. These are three separate IndexedDB writes. putRow goes through writeEntity, and deleteOp goes through `write`, which opens its own transaction (idb.ts:116-119 and 481). enqueue is a third transaction through appendOp. If the page is killed, or the account switches, or enqueue throws after deleteOp, the edit is lost. The account switch is caught by assertCurrent throwing AccountChanged. The mirror row already holds the merged values at the server's rev, so a later pull would not restore the server value. pendingCount then reads 0 and SyncStatus says "Everything is sent". The old op's payload was the only record of the edit. The settings path avoids this with an atomic settleUserSettings, and the NEVER_MERGED path has no payload to lose, so only the generic path is exposed. The window is only the gap between awaited writes, so it is narrow. The assertKeyMatchesPayload TypeError is unlikely, because rebaseOp's payload comes from merged, which keeps the key columns. The fix is one transaction that does putRow, deletes the old op and appends the rebased op. I found no audit or owner ruling accepting this behaviour. The earlier 2026-09-13 audit finding on onConflict (R24) is about delete/restore kinds, not this window. I rate it low because the window is narrow.

So the date is 7 to 13 days before a Monday-UTC fire, and further back by the time the user approves. The picker in lib/server/targets.ts activeProfile orders by effective_from desc, then rev desc, and the SQL picker does the same. A revision dated after the proposal's Monday, such as a recompute or manual pin dated on the account day, therefore outranks the newly approved row, and the approval has no effect. With no later revision, the approval backdates targets onto days already lived. decideProposal calls accountDay for the eligibility check only and does not pass the date to the RPC. Nothing supersedes or invalidates a pending proposal when a newer revision lands, so the approval still returns 'approved'. Neither docs/decisions nor docs/audit accepts this; the only mention of week_start is the unique index in the phase-6 spec. The 2026-09-13 audit dealt with the stale-grams angle only. Medium severity fits: it is a silent failure and it needs a revision to land inside the window, but no data is lost.

  - Nothing supersedes or expires pending proposals when a newer revision is written. `target-recompute.ts` only writes newer revisions.
  - I found no `docs/decisions` ruling that accepts this.

confirmed.title: A whole-batch 4xx (including 401) charges every op in the batch an error attempt, so valid ops get parked for a year
confirmed.defect: isClientFault treats every 4xx except 408 and 429 as the op's own fault. When /api/sync/ops rejects the whole request, parkOrRetry runs on every op in `due`. A single schema-invalid op in the first 200 (zod rejects the entire body), an expired or lapsed session (401), or a 403 or 404 all park the entire batch after 3 passes.
confirmed.failureScenario: The session cookie lapses after the phone was offline. Three back-to-back passes (online event, visibility change, debounce) get 401. All up to 200 queued ops, valid ones included, reach error_attempts=3 and next_attempt_at = now + 1 year. They stay unsent until the user finds and taps 'Sync now' (the only caller of retryParked, SyncStatus.tsx:161). The same happens to every valid op sharing a batch with one malformed op.
confirmed.evidence: outbox.ts:235-238 isClientFault; outbox.ts:374-377 `for (const op of due) await parkOrRetry(...)`; app/api/sync/ops/route.ts uses OpsRequestSchema over the whole body; lib/server/auth.ts returns 401 for a missing session.
confirmed.fix: Treat 401/403 as transport-like (back off without spending the error budget). For other 4xx, bisect the batch or retry the ops singly so only the offending op is charged.

If isClientFault is true, it calls parkOrRetry on every op in `due`. isClientFault (outbox.ts:235) is true for any SyncHttpError with status 400-499 except 408 and 429. pushOutbox (client.ts:345-347) throws SyncHttpError for any `!res.ok`. accountFetch only special-cases 409 account-mismatch, so a 401, 403 or 404 reaches the outbox as a client fault. parkOrRetry adds one error_attempt per pass. At MAX_ERROR_ATTEMPTS=3 it sets next_attempt_at to now + PARK_MS (365 days, settings.ts:37). Only retryParked releases parked ops, and the finding names SyncStatus "Sync now" as its only caller. The existing test "parks a 4xx push" (outbox.test.ts:403) covers a single op; the code does not tell a whole-request rejection from one op's fault. OpsRequestSchema validates the whole body (types.ts:67), so one schema-invalid op yields a 400 for the batch. No guard upstream stops this, and no ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts it. Limits on severity: the ops are parked, not lost, and one tap of "Sync now" restores them. Middleware normally refreshes the session, so a 401 needs a truly dead refresh token. One malformed op is the more likely trigger. Medium is a fair rating; low is arguable.

confirmed: Traced the real path. lib/sync/client.ts pushOutbox throws SyncHttpError(res.status) for any non-ok /api/sync/ops response. accountFetch (lib/device/account.ts) only special-cases 409 account mismatch, so a 401 is thrown as-is. In drainOutbox (lib/sync/outbox.ts ~373), isClientFault is true for every 4xx except 408 and 429, and it runs parkOrRetry on EVERY op in `due`. Each pass adds one error_attempt. Backoff is 1s then 2s (backoff.ts FIRST_RETRY_MS=1000), so three passes (online event, visibility change, debounce) reach MAX_ERROR_ATTEMPTS=3 within seconds. The third pass sets next_attempt_at = now + PARK_MS (365 days). Only retryParked releases them, and the finding says it is wired to SyncStatus 'Sync now' only. The route validates the whole body with OpsRequestSchema via readJson, so one schema-invalid op yields a 400 for the whole batch and parks all of its siblings. The existing test 'parks a 4xx push instead of retrying it forever' (outbox.test.ts:404) shows the park happens for a 400 with no per-op attribution. confirmed.title: A rebased log-entry note is joined with the server note unconditionally, duplicating or resurrecting text
confirmed.defect: The note op's payload carries the user's full replacement note, not a delta. rebaseLogNote runs joinNotes(server.note, mine.note) whenever the entry conflicts for any reason (another device changed items or rev), without checking whether the server's note differs from the note the edit was based on.
confirmed.failureScenario: The server holds note 'felt fine'. The user edits it to 'felt fine, then good'. The entry's rev was bumped by another device, so the update conflicts. The rebased note becomes 'felt fine\nfelt fine, then good', which duplicates the old text. If the user cleared the note, the join returns the server's old note and the deletion is reverted.
confirmed.evidence: log-entry-ops.ts:116 `const note = joinNotes(server.note, mine.note, ...)`; log-note-client.ts:49 builds `note: note || null` as the whole note; joinNotes returns `${first}\n${second}` for two differing non-empty strings.
confirmed.fix: Record the note the edit was based on (or the server's rev/note at queue time) and join only when the server note differs from that base. Otherwise use the user's note.
votes:
confirmed: I could not refute it. rebaseLogNote (lib/sync/log-entry-ops.ts:116) runs joinNotes(server.note, mine.note, ...) on every conflict. It never compares the server note with the note the edit was based on. No guard upstream stops this. save() in lib/log-note-client.ts queues the whole replacement note (`note: note || null`) with base_rev only, and handleLogEntryResult sends every update conflict to rebaseLogNote. joinNotes (lib/sync/merge.ts:45) returns the first string when the other is empty and "first\nsecond" when the two differ. Tracing the two scenarios gives:
- Server note 'felt fine', user edits it to 'felt fine, then good', and the rev was bumped by another device. The re-aimed payload note becomes 'felt fine\nfelt fine, then good', which duplicates the old text.
- The user clears the note while the server still holds 'felt fine'. The join returns 'felt fine', so the deletion is reverted.
No owner ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts this. The code comment says "a note is evidence — neither side's is dropped", which is a design intent to avoid losing a note when two sides write different notes. It is not a ruling on a note that was edited from the server's own base. The existing tests in lib/sync/log-entry-ops.test.ts only cover a server note of null, so they miss both scenarios. The impact is limited to a conflict on a note edit, and the cause is a deliberate lossless bias. Neither case loses data, so severity stays low.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run a repro. rebaseLogNote (lib/sync/log-entry-ops.ts:116) calls joinNotes(server.note, mine.note, ...) on every conflict. It never compares the server note with the note the edit was based on. joinNotes (lib/sync/merge.ts:45-52) trims both strings and returns the other one if one is empty. It returns a single copy if they are equal. In every other case it returns `${first}\n${second}`, with no substring or prefix check. Two cases fail as described. (1) The server holds 'felt fine', the user saved 'felt fine, then good', and another device bumped rev. The rebased note is 'felt fine\nfelt fine, then good', which duplicates the old text. (2) The user cleared the note, so mine.note is null and `second` is empty. joinNotes returns the server's old note and the deletion is reverted. log-note-client.ts builds `note: note || null` as a whole replacement note, so the payload is not a delta. That design never considered the case where the server's note is unchanged from the edit's base. I found no owner ruling that accepts the duplication or the resurrected note. The impact is limited to cosmetic text duplication and a rare reverted clear that needs a rev conflict, so the severity stays low.

confirmed.title: Re-starring a favorite after it was unstarred and synced is silently dropped
confirmed.defect: A server delete writes change_log.current = null, so the next pull does deleteRow on the local tombstone (client.ts:278). Starring the same food again then takes the create path (favorites-client.ts toggleAs: row missing -> create, base_rev null). The server answers 'conflict' because the tombstoned row still exists. onConflict merges with settle(), where a tombstone on either side always dominates (merge.ts:59), and the rebased op is an 'update'. apply_sync_op answers 'deleted' for any non-restore op on a tombstoned row, and the client then deleteRow's the entry. The user's new star is discarded without any signal.
confirmed.failureScenario: Star a food and sync. Unstar it and sync (pass N pushes the delete, pass N+1's pull removes the local tombstone). Star the same food again. The create op conflicts and is merged into a tombstoned update, the server returns 'deleted', and the mirror row is removed. The food shows as unstarred on every device, and the second tap is lost. I ran mergeEntity('favorites_foods', local{deleted_at:null, sort:2}, server{deleted_at:'...'}) and it returned deleted_at set (the server's tombstone). The _sync_upsert favorites branches never clear deleted_at, so no update could revive it either. No test covers re-star after a pull (tests/favorites/favorites-client.test.ts).
confirmed.evidence: merge.ts:59 `const tomb = server.deleted_at ?? local.deleted_at; ... out.deleted_at = tomb`; client.ts:278 `else await deleteRow(h, change.entity, change.entity_key)` for current===null; supabase/migrations/20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:460-463 returns 'deleted' for a non-restore op on a tombstoned row; the same file's favorites_* _sync_upsert branches do not set deleted_at = null in DO UPDATE.
confirmed.fix: In onConflict, when the op is a create/update and the server row is tombstoned, rebase it as a 'restore' (or have the client always use restore after a conflict on a tombstoned favorite). Alternatively keep the tombstone in the mirror on pull instead of deleting it, so toggleAs uses the restore path.
votes:
confirmed: I traced every step of the claimed chain in the code and found no guard or ruling that stops it. Nothing in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts this behaviour. I did not run the failing scenario end to end.

1. Unstar is a soft delete on the server. `_sync_tombstone` for the favorites tables sets `deleted_at` and keeps the row. `apply_sync_op` writes `change_log.current = null` for `kind = 'delete'`.

2. The next pull removes the local tombstone. `lib/sync/client.ts` (~278) calls `deleteRow` when `change.current === null`. The changes route does not exclude the caller's own ops.

3. Starring again takes the create path. In `toggleAs` (`lib/favorites-client.ts`) the row is missing, so it writes a `create` op with `base_rev: null`.

4. The server answers `conflict`. `apply_sync_op` returns `conflict` for any `create` when `_sync_current` is non-null, and `_sync_current` returns tombstoned rows too. The returned `current` carries `deleted_at`.

5. The client turns the create into a tombstoned update. `onConflict` (`lib/sync/outbox.ts`) calls `mergeEntity`, which runs `newerWinsFields` and then `settle`. `settle` (`lib/sync/merge.ts:59`) copies the server's `deleted_at` into the merged row. `rebaseOp` changes `create` to `update`, so the rebased update payload carries `deleted_at`.

6. The server rejects the update. `apply_sync_op` returns `deleted` for any non-restore op on a tombstoned row. `applyResult` then calls `deleteRow` and drops the op.

7. Retrying does not help. The local row is gone, so every later star repeats steps 3 to 6.

8. No server-side revival exists. The favorites branches of `_sync_upsert` write `deleted_at = null` only in the insert values, not in the `DO UPDATE` set. The same holds in later migrations of `_sync_upsert` (20261022090000 and 20261025090100). An update would not clear the tombstone even if it were accepted.

The only working path is a `restore` op, and that exists only while the local tombstone row is still present. That row is lost once the pull has removed it.

Severity stays high. A user cannot re-star a food they previously unstarred and synced, and the failure is silent.

confirmed.title: Per-entity ordering is not enforced: a delete can run before a backed-off create, which then resurrects the deleted row
confirmed.defect: drainOutbox selects due ops with only `next_attempt_at <= at` and has no per-entity barrier. If a create or update got an 'error' result and is backing off, a later delete of the same entity_id is due and is sent alone. The server answers 'gone' because the row was never created. onGone then deleteRow's the mirror and deleteOp's the delete (outbox.ts:329-334). When the backed-off create is retried it applies, and applyApplied writes the row back.
confirmed.failureScenario: Create op for a user_food or favorite gets an error result (transient RPC exception, backoff 1-2 s). The user deletes the item in that window. The delete drains alone and returns 'gone', so the op is dropped. The create then lands: the item the user deleted exists on the server, on every device, and in the local mirror again.
confirmed.evidence: outbox.ts:360 `all.filter((o) => o.next_attempt_at <= at ...)`; onGone lines 329-334 for delete/restore; apply_sync_op returns 'gone' for non-create on a missing row.
confirmed.fix: When selecting ops, skip any op whose entity_id has an earlier-seq op that is not being sent in this batch (backoff, parked or in flight). Alternatively coalesce a delete into a pending create by cancelling both.
votes: confirmed: I found no guard. drainOutbox (lib/sync/outbox.ts:360) filters only on next_attempt_at and entity, and drainable() only skips log_entries that are mid-commit. appendOp/writeOp does no coalescing or cancelling of a pending create when a delete is queued for the same entity_id, and no ruling or test covers this ordering. apply_sync_op (20260911000600_rpc.sql:347-351) answers 'gone' for a non-create op on a missing row. app/api/sync/ops/route.ts:35 turns a per-op exception into status 'error', which parkOrRetry backs off, and after repeated errors it parks the op for PARK_MS. onGone (outbox.ts:329-334) then calls deleteRow on the mirror and deleteOp on the delete, so the delete is dropped. The backed-off or parked create is retried later and lands. The deleted item reappears on the server and on other devices. The window is narrow for a one-off transient error, but parking widens it a lot. Delete-op writers exist for recipes, favorite meals and log entries (log entries have their own handler, log-entry-ops). I did not run the failing scenario in a test.

confirmed: I confirmed this by tracing the code. I did not run a vitest or tsx repro.

- **No ordering barrier.** `drainOutbox` (lib/sync/outbox.ts:360) selects ops with only `next_attempt_at <= at && entity !== SETTINGS`. Nothing holds a later op for an entity while an earlier op for the same `entity_id` is backing off.
- **The create backs off.** A per-op `error` result goes through `parkOrRetry`, which writes `next_attempt_at = now + backoffMs(...)`. The create then waits 1-2 s or longer.
- **Deletes are queued blind.** `removeFavoriteMeal` (lib/favorite-meals-client.ts:~585) and `deleteRecipe` (lib/recipes-client.ts:~131) tombstone the local row and enqueue a delete with a fresh `next_attempt_at`. Neither checks for a pending create or cancels it. Both can run while the create is waiting out its backoff.
- **The delete goes out alone.** It is the only due op, so it is pushed by itself.
- **The server drops it.** `apply_sync_op` (supabase/migrations/20260911000600_rpc.sql:~349) returns `gone` for any non-create op on a missing row.
- **The client erases the delete.** `onGone` for `delete` or `restore` (outbox.ts:329-334) calls `deleteRow`, removing the local tombstone, then `deleteOp`.
- **The create then lands.** Its backoff expires and the create is retried. The server has no row, so it applies the create (rev 1).
- **The row comes back locally.** `applyApplied` does `putRow({...({}), ...payload, rev})`, which writes the row back with no `deleted_at`.

So the deleted item exists on the server, on every device, and in the local mirror, and no op remains to correct it. The case where the create op is still queued but not backing off is not affected. It gets sent in the same batch, ordered by `seq`.

A transient per-op `error` on the create is the trigger. app/api/sync/ops/route.ts:35 can emit it.

I found no owner ruling that accepts this behaviour.

confirmed.title: Any pull-side failure, including the unrelated post-pull food and target projection, blocks the push entirely
confirmed.defect: runPass awaits pullChanges and rethrows its failure before pushOutbox is attempted. pullChanges ends with refreshFoodProjection and refreshTargetHistory. These make direct browser Supabase reads (loadAccountFoodSnapshot, paging, the food_refs join) that have nothing to do with the outbox.
confirmed.failureScenario: The direct PostgREST reads fail (a transient error, a paging check, a permission fault) while /api/sync works. Every pass throws after the cursor was already saved, so the push never runs and queued user edits are never sent. This persists as long as the read fails.
confirmed.evidence: client.ts:484-489 `pull = await pullChanges(...)` in try/catch that rethrows; client.ts ~line 320 `await refreshFoodProjection(h); await refreshTargetHistory(h);` inside pullChanges.

votes: confirmed: I read the code and the claim holds. In lib/sync/client.ts, runPass wraps pullChanges in a try/catch that records the failure and rethrows. pushOutbox sits after that block, so a pull failure means the push never runs. pullChanges (lines 307-308) ends with `await refreshFoodProjection(h); await refreshTargetHistory(h);` with no guard. refreshFoodProjection calls loadAccountFoodSnapshot, a direct browser Supabase read, and a failure there rejects the whole pull. By then the cursor has already been saved by setCursor, so the next pass repeats the same failure. Every flush path (syncOnce, flushOutboxNow, flushOnboardingWritesNow) goes through syncOnce, so none of them bypasses it. I found no guard upstream, no test covering this path, and no owner ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts it. The "pull before push" ordering is intentional: the file comments say it lets a conflict merge against the freshest row, and a settings op with no baseline waits for the pull. That justifies ordering the two steps. It does not justify letting the unrelated post-pull projection refresh block the push. A persistent failure of those direct reads, for example a paging-check error from inconsistent data, would stall all queued edits while /api/sync still works. That trigger is narrow, and most pull failures (network down) would fail the push anyway. So I rate it low, as the finding says. It is a real availability weakness, not a design the owner has accepted. I did not run a vitest or tsx reproduction. The verdict rests on reading the code.

In lib/sync/client.ts, runPass (about lines 483-489) awaits pullChanges in a try/catch that records the failure and rethrows. pushOutbox sits after that block, so a pull throw means it never runs. pushOutbox is called from nowhere else in app code. flushOutboxNow and syncOnce both go through runPass, so no other path sends queued ops. pullChanges ends (about lines 305-307) with `await refreshFoodProjection(h); await refreshTargetHistory(h);`, which run after the cursor is saved. refreshFoodProjection calls loadAccountFoodSnapshot (lib/sync/food-refs.ts), which makes direct browser Supabase reads: paged user_foods and user_food_prefs selects plus loadOwnedFoodRefs. confirmed.title: Health ingest records its dedupe event before applying samples, so a failed apply makes the retry a silent no-op and the samples are lost
confirmed.defect: applyIngest calls the health_ingest_event RPC first, which inserts an ingest_events row keyed (source_id, payload_hash) in its own transaction. It then calls health_ingest_apply as a separate RPC. If the apply fails, the route answers 500 but the event row stays. The retry carries the same payload and hash, so health_ingest_event hits ON CONFLICT and returns is_new=false. applyIngest returns status 'duplicate' with accepted 0 and never applies the samples. Nothing deletes or marks the event on failure. The Oura pull in lib/server/oura.ts avoids this by applying regardless of is_new. Only the HTTP ingest path has the bug.
confirmed.failureScenario: A Health Auto Export or Shortcut client posts a payload. health_ingest_apply fails with a transient DB error or a timeout, and the client gets 500. The client retries the identical body, which is the normal behaviour for HAE. The server answers 200 {status:'duplicate', accepted:0}. The client treats the data as delivered, and the weight, HRV and other samples never reach health_samples. The loss is silent and permanent. For HAE the sample window is only 8 days, so the data is gone once it ages out.
confirmed.evidence: lib/server/health-ingest.ts:97-109: `const event = await admin.rpc("health_ingest_event", ...); ... if (!row.is_new) { return { ... status: "duplicate", accepted: 0 ...}; } const applied = await admin.rpc("health_ingest_apply", ...); if (applied.error) throw new HttpError(500, ...)`. supabase/migrations/20260925000000_phase5_health_ingest.sql:43-61: `insert into ingest_events ... on conflict (source_id, payload_hash) do update set status = 'duplicate' returning id, (xmax = 0)`. There is no compensating delete and no status check on a failed apply.
confirmed.fix: Make recording the event and applying the samples one transaction, for example by doing both inside a single RPC. Or, when the apply fails, delete the event row or mark it 'failed'. Or, on is_new=false, still call health_ingest_apply, which is idempotent because it upserts, as the Oura pull does.
confirmed.knownBefore: Raised as a spec-review note in docs/audit/specs/2026-09-22-phase-10-r1-gpt6-sol.md item 8, with no ruling or fix.
votes: confirmed: The defect is real in the code. applyIngest (lib/server/health-ingest.ts:97-109) calls health_ingest_event as its own RPC, so the ingest_events row commits at once. Only after that does it call health_ingest_apply, and a failure there throws a 500. A retry with the identical body gives the same payload_hash, so the migration's ON CONFLICT (source_id, payload_hash) branch returns is_new=false. The code then returns status 'duplicate' with accepted 0 and never applies the samples. Nothing deletes the event or marks it failed, and no code reads the event's status. The existing unit test "returns duplicate and applies nothing on a repeated payload" encodes this skip but never covers a failed apply. The Oura pull in lib/server/oura.ts calls apply regardless of is_new, which confirms the HTTP path is the odd one out. No ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts this. The only failure is that the apply RPC errors, for example on a transient DB error or timeout. The retry window is bounded by the sent_at replay check (409 'replayed') and, for HAE, the 8-day freshness window, so the loss is permanent once those pass. Because the trigger needs a failed apply, I rate it medium rather than high.

The two calls are separate PostgREST requests, so they are separate transactions. health_ingest_event inserts the ingest_events row with on conflict (source_id, payload_hash) and returns (xmax = 0) as is_new (migration 20260925000000_phase5_health_ingest.sql:43-61). If the apply RPC errors, the code throws HttpError 500, but the committed event row stays. No delete, status check or compensation exists. A retry with the identical body gives the same payload hash, so the insert conflicts and is_new is false. applyIngest then returns {status:'duplicate', accepted:0} without calling apply, and the samples are never written. The 8-day freshness filter (MAX_SAMPLE_AGE_MS) makes the loss permanent once the data ages out. A prior spec review, docs/audit/specs/2026-09-22-phase-10-r1-gpt6-sol.md item 8, flagged the same pattern, but only as a spec note with no owner ruling accepting it. The finding is not an accepted behaviour.

In lib/sync/client.ts, pullChanges sets cursor = 0 whenever settingsAwaitingBaseline is true (line 243). The baseline is applied only when `recoveringSettings && !hasMore`. The pull is capped at 50 pages of 500 changes, so it covers 25,000 changes at most. setCursor saves progress, but the next pass resets to 0 again as long as the baseline is unconfirmed (stored null or rev null). The server feed (sync_changes RPC, change_log) is not compacted or deduplicated, and the route returns raw seq order with no snapshot shortcut. The trigger is realistic. AuthGate calls captureTimeZone on the first online open when the local user_settings row has no time_zone, which is the case on a new device. That queues a settings op with no baseline, and it runs alongside the first pull. Impact is limited. Only the time_zone settings op stays parked, and for accounts with more than 25k change rows. confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run a repro.

- `settingsAwaitingBaseline` (lib/sync/settings.ts:215) returns true whenever a settings op is queued and the stored baseline is null or has `rev === null`.
- `pullChanges` (lib/sync/client.ts:243) then sets `cursor = 0` on every call, ignoring the saved cursor. It does this on each pass, because `syncOnce` -> `runPass` calls `pullChanges(h, undefined, options)` (client.ts:485).
- While recovering, `user_settings` rows are only recorded in `recoveredSettings`. The baseline is applied or established only under `if (recoveringSettings && !hasMore)`.
- The loop stops at `maxPages` = 50 pages of `PAGE_LIMIT` = 500, which is 25,000 changes. So a feed longer than that leaves `hasMore` true and the baseline is never confirmed.
- `setCursor` still saves the advanced cursor after each page, but the next pass overwrites it with 0.
- The feed is not compacted. `sync_changes` (supabase/migrations/20260911000600_rpc.sql) returns raw `change_log` rows ordered by seq, so a feed over 25k rows is real.
- Trigger path: `captureTimeZone` (settings.ts:114) runs from AuthGate's `whenReady` and queues a time_zone op when the local row has no zone. On a fresh device that op can be queued before any pull has confirmed a baseline.
- Effect: the settings op stays parked, and each pass costs 50 GETs. The route allows 60 requests per minute per user, so the passes also crowd out other sync traffic.

Severity stays low. It needs a feed over 25k rows, and the baseline can still be confirmed when an ordinary pull applies a settings row before the op is queued. Recovery has no per-pass progress that survives to the next pass.

confirmed.title: Meal, recipe and water exports silently truncate at PostgREST max_rows (1000) while the default limit is 5000, and no next cursor or truncation notice is emitted
confirmed.defect: streamMeals, streamRecipes and streamWater fetch `.limit(opts.limit + 1)` and compute `hasMore = rows.length > opts.limit`. limitParam defaults to MAX_LIMIT (5000). supabase/config.toml sets max_rows = 1000, and PostgREST caps the response at 1000 rows whatever .limit() asks for. With limit >= 1000, `rows.length > limit` can never be true, so hasMore is false and next_cursor is null. The CSV 'Export truncated' notice is keyed off next_cursor, so it never appears. The body-profile export and the backup already page around this cap. These three do not.
confirmed.failureScenario: A user who has logged a year or more of meals (over 1000 log_entries) requests GET /api/export?kind=meals, with the default limit or any limit of 1000 or more. They get the first 1000 entries as a complete-looking file. There is no next_cursor and no truncation line, so the rest of their history is silently missing from their data export. Water is affected after more than 1000 logged days. Recipes are affected after more than 1000 recipes.
confirmed.evidence: lib/server/export.ts:198 `.limit(opts.limit + 1)` and :202 `const hasMore = entries.length > opts.limit;`. Same pattern at export.ts:487/494 (recipes) and lib/server/export-water.ts:98/109. app/api/export/route.ts:29 `const MAX_LIMIT = 5000;` and :70 `if (raw === null) return MAX_LIMIT;`. supabase/config.toml:10 `max_rows = 1000`. tests/export/body-profile.test.ts:307 models 'PostgREST stops a response at max_rows ... silently', but there is no equivalent for meals.

No decision or audit doc accepts it for re-edits. The consequence is the target revision derived at the stale weight, plus a bogus history point. Impact is bounded: the next real weigh-in corrects it, and the fake point is a one-day value. So I rate it medium rather than high.

confirmed.title: get_or_create_food_ref and favor_food_families take the two clock rows in opposite order, so same-user concurrency can deadlock
confirmed.defect: favor_food_families locks the account's account_rules_clock row FOR UPDATE and then evidence_clock FOR SHARE (lines 136-137). get_or_create_food_ref inserts a food_refs row first. The statement-level trigger evidence_clock_food_refs_ins updates the global evidence_clock row and holds that row lock until commit. It then inserts a user_food_prefs backfill row. The row trigger rules_clock_user_food_prefs updates that user's account_rules_clock row. The order is evidence then rules, the reverse of Favor's rules then evidence.
confirmed.failureScenario: The same user taps Favor on a family while another request (a log commit or the sync of a first-use food) mints a new catalog food_ref for that account. Favor holds rules_clock and waits for the evidence share lock. The mint transaction holds the evidence row and waits for rules_clock. Postgres reports 40P01 after the deadlock timeout. If Favor is the victim, the user sees a 500 on Favor. If the mint is the victim, get_or_create_food_ref's 'exception when others' block (line 258) swallows the deadlock and the new ref is left without its inherited family mark.
confirmed.evidence: favor_food_families: 'select rules_rev ... from account_rules_clock ... for update' then 'select evidence_rev from evidence_clock where id = 1 for share'. 20261213091100_evidence_clock_food_refs.sql installs the food_refs insert trigger. 20261213090500_rules_clock_user_food_prefs.sql installs the user_food_prefs trigger. get_or_create_food_ref inserts food_refs and then user_food_prefs inside one transaction.
confirmed.fix: Take the clocks in one global order. In favor_food_families, read evidence_clock FOR SHARE before the account_rules_clock FOR UPDATE. Alternatively make the backfill in get_or_create_food_ref run its inserts before the food_refs insert, or narrow its exception handler to catch only unique_violation.
votes:
confirmed: I could not refute it. I read the migrations but did not run a concurrent test.

- **Favor's order:** favor_food_families (20261215090000, lines 135-137) locks the user's account_rules_clock row FOR UPDATE, then takes evidence_clock id=1 FOR SHARE.
- **Mint's order:** get_or_create_food_ref inserts into food_refs. The statement-level trigger evidence_clock_food_refs_ins (20261213091100) calls evidence_clock_bump, which UPDATEs the evidence_clock row. That update takes the row lock and holds it until commit. The same function then inserts a user_food_prefs backfill row. The row trigger rules_clock_user_food_prefs calls _bump_rules_clock for that user, which needs the same account_rules_clock row Favor holds. So the mint locks evidence first and rules second, the reverse of Favor.
- **Deadlock:** with both transactions in flight, Favor holds the rules row and waits on evidence. The mint holds evidence and waits on rules. Postgres raises 40P01 for one of them.
- **Swallowed error:** the evidence bump happens outside the mint's inner begin/exception block, so only the backfill insert can be caught there. If the mint is the victim, the 'exception when others' handler turns the deadlock into a warning and the new ref misses its inherited mark. If Favor is the victim, the user gets an error.
- **No guard or ruling:** the advisory locks Favor takes cover only per-family note locks, not the clock rows. grep found no owner ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts this lock order.
- **Why it stays low:** the deadlock needs a same-user mint of a new catalog ref at the same moment as a Favor tap. The mint must also reach the backfill insert, which happens only when the family already has an avoid or ordinary eats membership. The window is narrow. The mint-victim case loses nothing permanent, because the ref still exists and a later membership write restores the mark.

In get_or_create_food_ref (same file, ~lines 194-262): when no food_refs row exists, it inserts one. The statement-level trigger evidence_clock_food_refs_ins (20261213091100) runs evidence_clock_bump (20261213090200), which updates evidence_clock row id=1. That row lock is held until commit. The function then inserts a user_food_prefs backfill row, but only if a membership row exists and is not a Favor (status eats with favor_rev = rev). The row trigger rules_clock_user_food_prefs (20261213090500) calls _bump_rules_clock(p_user_id), which upserts that user's account_rules_clock row. So the mint takes evidence then rules, the reverse of Favor, and a deadlock cycle is possible. Narrowing conditions: the mint must create a new catalog or user food_ref for the same account at the moment Favor runs. A membership status that carries over (avoid, or a non-Favor eats) must exist for the family name. The evidence_clock update is skipped if last_xact already equals the current xact. If the mint is the victim, the inner EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS block catches 40P01. It rolls back only the subtransaction, so the backfill is lost silently. The evidence lock from the food_refs insert stays, and the ref is returned without its inherited mark. If Favor is the victim, the route gets an error. Both outcomes are narrow and low impact, so the severity stays low.

confirmed.title: approve_target_proposal picks the active revision with the database's UTC current_date, not the account's day
confirmed.defect: The floors, goal rate and step cap carried into an approved proposal come from the revision selected by 'effective_from <= current_date'. current_date is the UTC date of the Postgres session. It is also the fallback for effective_from when week_start is null (line 37). The repo rule (lib/server/account-day.ts, t24b) says the server's 'today' for target revisions must be the account's own day, never a deployment-wide default.
confirmed.failureScenario: A US-evening user (for example 20:00 PDT, already the next day in UTC) has a revision scheduled for 'tomorrow' in their zone. The approval selects that future revision as v_active, so its kcal_min, protein_g_min, fat_g_min and goal rate become the carried-over floors. The correct in-force revision, today's, is ignored. An approved proposal can then be written with floors from a revision that is not yet in force.
confirmed.evidence: 20261023090500_approve_proposal_via_revision.sql:25-27 'select * into v_active from target_profiles where user_id = p_user_id and effective_from <= current_date order by effective_from desc, rev desc limit 1'. Line 37 is 'coalesce(v_prop.week_start, current_date)'. The write path in lib/server/targets.ts uses account-day.
confirmed.fix: Have the service pass the account-day date as a parameter, or compute it in SQL from user_settings.time_zone with a pg_timezone_names check, and use that in both places.
votes:
confirmed: The core defect is real. The live body of approve_target_proposal is in 20261023090500 (no later migration redefines it; the others only re-grant or revoke). It selects v_active with `effective_from <= current_date`, which is the Postgres session's UTC date. lib/server/proposals.ts runs assertApprovalEligible with accountDay, but then calls the RPC, which passes no day and uses UTC. So in the UTC-ahead window (US evening), a revision scheduled for the account's "tomorrow" is picked as v_active. Its kcal_min, protein_g_min, fat_g_min, carb_g_min, goal_rate_bp_week and max_weekly_kcal_step then carry into the approved proposal. The assertApprovalEligible pace check uses the account day, so the two can disagree. No owner ruling or audit accepts this (nothing in docs/decisions or docs/audit mentions it).

Part of the claim is wrong. Line 37's `coalesce(v_prop.week_start, current_date)` is dead code, because target_proposals.week_start is NOT NULL (20261006090100). The new revision's effective_from is always the proposal's week_start, which the weekly-proposal job computes from the account's local date.

Impact is small. It needs a future-dated revision to exist, which is rare (pins, a scheduled change, or hold re-derivations), and an approval inside the few hours when UTC is a day ahead of the account. The harm is limited to the carried floors and goal rate. The fix is to pass the account day, or the proposal's week_start, into the RPC and use that in place of current_date. Severity stays low.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run it, because Bash was denied partway through, so the failing case is traced rather than executed.

The latest `approve_target_proposal` definition still selects `v_active` with `effective_from <= current_date`. Migration 20261209090000_target_seed_freeze.sql patches that same body and keeps the line. Supabase Postgres runs in UTC, so `current_date` is the UTC date. `lib/server/proposals.ts` `assertApprovalEligible` does use `accountDay` for the pace-hold check, but the RPC takes no date argument. The SQL therefore always uses UTC to choose the revision whose floors and goal rate carry over, and as the `effective_from` fallback when `week_start` is null.

A US-evening account (for example 20:00 PDT, already the next day in UTC) with a revision scheduled for its tomorrow would hit the failure. The function selects that not-yet-in-force revision as `v_active` and copies its `kcal_min`, `protein_g_min`, `fat_g_min`, goal rate, step cap and seed fields into the approved revision. The eligibility check, which uses the account's real day, looks at the correct revision, so the two can disagree.

The impact is narrow. It needs a future-dated revision and an approval during the zone-versus-UTC gap. `week_start` is normally set, so the `effective_from` fallback rarely applies. Severity stays low. A fix would pass the account day in as a parameter.

confirmed.title: pantry/photo accepts an unvalidated mediaPath, so the owner check passes a path-traversal key
confirmed.defect: POST /api/pantry/photo validates mediaPath only as z.string().min(1).max(200). Every other media entry point (capture, plan/inspire, plan/document, coach attachments) applies the MEDIA_PATH regex 'media/<uuid>/<uuid>.<ext>'. fetchOwnedObject then checks only objectKey(path).split('/')[0] === userId before downloading with the service-role client. Unlike capture, the pantry path also skips the media_objects liveness and owner check (assertLiveMediaObject).
confirmed.failureScenario: Account A sends mediaPath = '<A-uid>/../<B-uid>/<B-object-uuid>.jpg'. The first segment equals A's id, so the ownership check passes. The service-role download then asks Storage for that key. If the Storage layer resolves '..', or any future path-handling change does, A's pantry photo draft reads B's private image. Exploitation also needs B's random object uuid and depends on Storage key normalisation, so this is defence in depth, not a demonstrated leak.

A path like "<A>/../<B>/<uuid>.jpg" therefore passes the ownership check, and the service-role admin client downloads that key. Nothing upstream rejects it. requireRecipeUser is only an auth and pilot gate, and the 2 KB limit is a body-size cap. I found no media_objects owner or liveness check in pantry-photo.ts, which capture does have (lib/server/capture.ts). I did not run the traversal against Storage. The finding is real as a missing-validation and defence-in-depth gap, and low severity is right. The fix is to apply the MEDIA_PATH regex and assertLiveMediaObject, as the other entry points do.

confirmed: The code matches the finding. app/api/pantry/photo/route.ts:24 validates mediaPath only as z.string().min(1).max(200). fetchOwnedObject (lib/server/media.ts:71-80) checks only key.split("/")[0] === userId. It then calls admin.storage.download(key) with the service-role client. lib/server/pantry-photo.ts does no media_objects lookup. objectKey() only strips a leading "media/", so "<A>/../<B>/<obj>.jpg" passes the owner check.

confirmed.title: Calendar (.ics) meal times ignore the app's clamped slot resolution and can end before they start
confirmed.defect: effectiveMinutes returns base + shiftMinutes unclamped, and formatTime wraps modulo 1440 while the date stays the fixed anchor date. The app's resolveSlotTimes/shiftTime (lib/plan.ts) clamps each time to 00:00-23:59. DTEND = start + 15 min is wrapped separately, so a start near midnight gets a DTEND earlier on the same anchor date.
confirmed.failureScenario: With a +240 min whole-day shift and meal-1 set to 23:50, Today shows meal-1 at 23:59 but the exported calendar puts it at 03:50. A slot at 23:55 gets DTEND 00:10 on the same date, which is before DTSTART, an invalid VEVENT. A negative shift is wrong the same way: 07:00 minus 8 h exports as 23:00 instead of 00:00. Night-shift users get reminders at the wrong hours. I ran generateMealPlanIcs with shift 240 and meal-1 23:50 and got DTSTART 20260101T035000 while resolveSlotTimes gave 23:59.
confirmed.evidence: lib/ics.ts:78-86 `parseTime(base) + shiftMinutes`; lib/ics.ts:66-71 `((totalMinutes % 1440) + 1440) % 1440`; lib/ics.ts:198-199 `endMinutes = startMinutes + EVENT_DURATION_MINUTES`; lib/plan.ts shiftTime clamps to [0, 23*60+59].
confirmed.fix: Resolve each slot with resolveSlotTimes using the real slotTimes and shiftMinutes (so the clamp applies), and compute DTEND from the clamped start, capped to the same day or rolled to the next day's date.
votes: confirmed: The code matches the finding. In lib/ics.ts, effectiveMinutes returns parseTime(base) + shiftMinutes with no clamp. formatTime then wraps modulo 1440, and the date stays fixed at the anchor. The app's shiftTime in lib/plan.ts clamps to [0, 23:59]. DTEND is computed separately as start + 15 min and wrapped separately. A slot at 23:55 therefore gets DTEND 00:10 on the same anchor date, before DTSTART. A +240 shift on 23:50 exports as 03:50 where the app shows 23:59. Only the export path is affected, and I found no ruling that accepts the behaviour. generateMealPlanIcs is used by components/settings/ScheduleSection.tsx, so the bug is reachable by users. I rate it low rather than medium because it only bites when a slot time plus a shift crosses midnight or lands near 23:45 or later, and it affects only the calendar export.

confirmed: Reproduced with generateMealPlanIcs and resolveSlotTimes. A +240 shift with meal-1 at 23:50 gives DTSTART 20260101T035000, while resolveSlotTimes gives 23:59. A slot at 23:55 with no shift gives DTSTART 235500 and DTEND 001000 on the same date, so the end is before the start. A -480 shift on 07:00 exports 23:00, while resolveSlotTimes gives 00:00. Cause: effectiveMinutes in lib/ics.ts adds the shift with no clamp, and formatTime wraps modulo 1440. The only caller is components/settings/ScheduleSection.tsx. I found no owner ruling that accepts this. I rate it low rather than medium because the failing cases need a time at or after about 23:45 or a large shift, and the export is a manual calendar file. The DTEND-before-DTSTART case is an invalid VEVENT, but it needs a slot in the last 15 minutes of the day.

confirmed.title: Pre-auth body parsing can throw on non-object JSON batch elements and returns 500
confirmed.defect: toolNamesInBody reads candidate.method on each batch element with no null check. scopesForBody runs before withTokenUser, so this happens before authentication. TOOL_SCOPES[name] is also a plain object lookup, so a name such as "constructor" or "toString" returns an inherited function that is truthy and not "read".
confirmed.failureScenario: An unauthenticated POST with body [null] throws a TypeError at line 67, which becomes a 500 from jsonError instead of a 400 or 401. An authenticated read-only token calling tools/call with name "constructor" is added as a required scope and gets 403 "Token lacks the [function] scope" instead of an unknown-tool error. Both are harmless but wrong.
confirmed.evidence: app/api/mcp/route.ts:66-72 casts call to an object and reads candidate.method; app/api/mcp/route.ts:78 `const scope = TOOL_SCOPES[name]` has no own-property check.

votes: confirmed: Confirmed by reading the code. I did not run a test. In app/api/mcp/route.ts, toolNamesInBody (lines 66-72) reads candidate.method on each element of a JSON array with no null check. A body of [null] makes it read a property of null, which throws a TypeError. That call happens inside guarded's try block, via scopeForBody before withTokenUser, so no authentication has run yet. jsonError treats the TypeError as non-HttpError, logs it, and returns 500 "internal". Only the pre-identity rate limits run first (30/min per token and per IP). I found no upstream guard and no owner ruling accepting this. The second claim also holds. TOOL_SCOPES is a plain object, so TOOL_SCOPES["constructor"] returns the inherited Object function. The function is truthy and not "read", so it is added to the required scopes. withTokenUser and the later hasScope check then treat it as a missing scope, so the caller gets a 403 "Token lacks the [function] scope" message (the finding quotes this text). A "constructor" tool name is the wrong error, but it is only a mislabelled rejection and grants nothing. confirmed: Both claims hold in app/api/mcp/route.ts. (1) toolNamesInBody reads candidate.method with no null check. A body of [null] or the bare JSON null throws "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'method')". guarded() calls scopeForBody(raw) as an argument to withTokenUser, so the throw happens before any auth check. An unauthenticated caller would hit that scope in withTokenUser first, which most likely gives a 401. Impact is low: a wrong status code and error message, with no data exposure or auth bypass. confirmed.evidence: lib/mcp/health-tools.ts:20 and :32 use the regex and a NaN-blind comparison `span < 0 || span + 1 > MAX`; lib/server/health-daily.ts:68 calls new Date(NaN).toISOString(). Date.parse("2026-02-30T00:00:00Z") returns 1772409600000.
