votes: confirmed: The code and the failure behaviour match the finding. In lib/mcp/health-tools.ts, isoDate is only the regex /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/. The span guard is `span < 0 || span + 1 > MAX`, which never rejects NaN. I ran Date.parse in node on both inputs. "2026-02-30T00:00:00Z" returns 1772409600000, which is 2026-03-02, so the window shifts silently. "2026-13-01T00:00:00Z" returns NaN, which passes the guard. mergedDays then calls rawSamples, whose `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` throws RangeError. mergedDays does no date validation of its own, and I found no upstream guard or owner ruling that accepts this. Impact is low. The tool is read-only and scoped to the caller's own data. A bad date gives a wrong window or an unfriendly error, not a security or data-integrity failure.

confirmed: Reproduced with node. The regex /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/ accepts 2026-02-30 and 2026-13-01. Date.parse("2026-02-30T00:00:00Z") returns 1772409600000, which is 2026-03-02, so the window silently shifts. Date.parse("2026-13-01T00:00:00Z") is NaN, so span is NaN and `span < 0 || span + 1 > 90` is false. The guard passes and mergedDays calls rawSamples (lib/server/health-daily.ts:68), where new Date(NaN).toISOString() throws "RangeError: Invalid time value". That error replaces the intended validation message. Impact is low: it affects only agent input handling, and no data is exposed.

confirmed.title: Non-UUID ids reach Postgres and come back as 500 instead of 400 or 404
confirmed.defect: Several id-param routes do not validate the id as a UUID before using it in a uuid-typed query: DELETE /api/health/tokens/[id], POST /api/proposals/[id]/decide, DELETE and PATCH /api/coach/threads/[id], DELETE /api/coach/threads/[id]/messages. Recipes [id] and favorite use `/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/i`, which accepts a string such as 36 dashes. Postgres raises 22P02 (invalid input syntax for type uuid). The code either rethrows the raw error (health tokens and proposals, which reach jsonError's generic 500 with an 'Unhandled error' log) or wraps it as HttpError 500 (coach thread delete and rename). Scoping by user_id is correct everywhere, so this is not a leak.
confirmed.failureScenario: DELETE /api/health/tokens/not-a-uuid returns 500 'Something went wrong' and logs an unhandled error, where the contract says 404 for an unknown source. POST /api/proposals/abc/decide with decision 'reject' likewise returns 500 instead of 400 or 404. DELETE /api/coach/threads/abc returns 500 'Could not delete the thread.' while GET on the same id returns 404. Clients that retry on 5xx will retry forever, and the noisy 5xx can trip error alerts.
confirmed.evidence: health/tokens/[id]/route.ts:20-24 `.eq("id", id)` with no check; proposals/[id]/decide/route.ts:33-34 passes id straight to decideProposal, whose update at lib/server/proposals.ts:98-102 throws the raw error; lib/server/coach-threads.ts:334 and :373 map any error to 500; recipes/[id]/route.ts:14 loose regex.
confirmed.fix: Validate `z.uuid().safeParse(id)` and return 400 or 404 before querying, as the shopping, care-messages and coach/undo routes already do.
votes: confirmed: I read the code but did not run it. Nothing validates the id as a UUID in the health tokens route, the proposals decide route (decideProposal, lib/server/proposals.ts), or the coach thread delete, rename and clear paths. The id goes straight into a uuid-typed `.eq("id", ...)`, so Postgres would reject a non-UUID with 22P02. Health tokens and proposals throw the raw error, and jsonError (lib/server/http.ts:45-46) returns a generic 500 with an "Unhandled error" log. The coach thread helpers in lib/server/coach-threads.ts (lines 334 and 373, plus the clear path) wrap any error as HttpError 500. The middleware matcher excludes /api, so nothing upstream filters ids. The only code that handles 22P02 is lib/server/recipe-plan.ts:40, which does not cover these routes. Every query is scoped by user_id, so there is no data leak. This is a real but low-severity validation defect: a bad id gives 500 where 400 or 404 is expected.

confirmed: Confirmed by code trace; no live Postgres call was run. Health tokens DELETE (route.ts:20-24) puts the raw id in `.eq("id", id)` and does `if (error) throw error`. Postgres rejects a non-UUID with 22P02, and jsonError turns that non-HttpError into a generic 500 with an "Unhandled error in route" log. Proposals decide only validates the body, not the id. It passes the id to decideProposal, whose reject path runs `.eq("id", proposalId)` and `if (error) throw error` (proposals.ts:~98-102), so the same raw error becomes a 500. The approve path goes through the RPC and probably fails the same way, though I did not trace it. deleteChatThread, clearChatThread and renameChatThread map any query error to HttpError(500, "internal"). The coach thread GET uses `if (thread.error || !thread.data) throw 404`, so the same bad id gives 404 there, as the finding says. Every query is scoped by user_id, so nothing leaks. Impact is limited to wrong status codes (500 instead of 400/404) and noisy error logs.

confirmed.title: Seeds balance silently truncated at the 1,000-row API cap
confirmed.defect: readCarePoints and readCareShop compute `balance` (and `pending`) by selecting every settled/pending ledger row with a plain `.select()` and summing in JS. No `.order()`, no paging. PostgREST caps the response at max_rows=1000 and gives no sign of truncation. The repo's own `fetchAllRows` helper exists for exactly this case and is not used.
confirmed.failureScenario: An account passes 1,000 settled/pending ledger rows. Up to about 6 rows a day can be awarded, plus purchases, so a daily user gets there in under a year. GET /api/care/points and GET /api/care/shop then sum an arbitrary 1,000 rows and show a balance lower than the real one. `care_purchase` checks the full ledger in SQL. The phone's shop state uses the truncated balance, so the UI can show 'insufficient' for items the user can really afford. The number can also change between calls because the order is undefined.
confirmed.evidence: care-points.ts:36-37 `client.from("care_points_ledger").select("delta, status").eq("user_id", userId).in("status", ["settled","pending"])`. care-shop.ts:17 `...select("delta, status").eq("user_id", userId).eq("status","settled")`. supabase/config.toml:10 `max_rows = 1000`. lib/server/paged-read.ts documents the silent-truncation hazard.
confirmed.fix: Page the read with `fetchAllRows` ordered by `id`, or have the server sum the balance. For example, add a `care_balance(p_user_id)` RPC and use it in both places.
votes: confirmed: readCarePoints (care-points.ts:36) and readCareShop (care-shop.ts:17) sum balance and pending in JS from a plain unpaged, unordered select on care_points_ledger. supabase/config.toml sets max_rows = 1000, and neither file uses fetchAllRows. The migration awards day_recorded, day_complete, protein_goal and water_goal each day, plus weekly rows, purchases and reversals. That is roughly 4 or more ledger rows a day, so an active account passes 1,000 rows in under a year. The migration's care_points_sync and care_purchase sum the full ledger in SQL (line 412 onward), so the API balance would disagree with the server's own check. I found no owner ruling or upstream guard that accepts this. I did not run a test. The code comment only mentions the old 200-row concern. Medium severity fits because the display is wrong and the shop can show 'insufficient' wrongly, but no money or data is lost.

confirmed: I traced the code but did not run a repro. Both reads are plain `.select()` calls with no `.order()` and no paging. `readCarePoints` (care-points.ts:36-37) selects every settled or pending ledger row and sums in JS. `readCareShop` (care-shop.ts:17) selects every settled row and sums the same way. `supabase/config.toml:10` sets `max_rows = 1000`, so PostgREST returns at most 1000 rows with no truncation signal. `lib/server/paged-read.ts` documents this hazard and provides `fetchAllRows`, which neither file uses. Once an account has more than 1000 matching ledger rows, `balance` and `pending` are sums over an arbitrary subset, because the order is undefined. The migration's ledger kinds (`day_recorded`, `day_complete`, `protein_goal`, `water_goal`, `five_day_week`, `weigh_in_week`, plus purchases and reversals) can award several rows a day, so a daily user plausibly passes 1000 rows within a year. `care_purchase` checks the full ledger in SQL, so the phone's shop state can disagree with it, and the displayed balance can change between calls. No owner ruling or prior audit mentions it. Medium is the right severity. It is a display and gating inconsistency, not a safety or data-loss bug, and it only appears after about 1000 ledger rows.

confirmed.title: full-week accolade can only be granted by a sync call made on the Sunday itself
confirmed.defect: The rule is defined as 'a retained meal on all seven dates of a completed local week'. The grant is only evaluated when `p_local_date = v_today` and `isodow(p_local_date) = 7`. Once Sunday has passed, no later sync can ever grant it.
confirmed.failureScenario: A user logs Monday to Sunday but does not open the care or accolades endpoint until Monday. `care_accolades_sync` runs with a Monday date, the Sunday branch is skipped, and the full-week accolade is never granted. The same happens if they only open the app Sunday before logging that day's meal.
confirmed.evidence: care_accolades.sql:172-181 `if p_local_date = v_today and extract(isodow from p_local_date)::int = 7 then ... v_week_dates = 7`. There is no look-back to the previous completed week.
confirmed.fix: Evaluate the previous completed Monday to Sunday week, and the current week once it has closed, on any sync. Grant it with idempotent evidence keyed to the week.
votes: confirmed: The code matches the finding. In care_accolades_sync (supabase/migrations/20261225090300_care_accolades.sql, lines 172-181), full-week is evaluated only when p_local_date = v_today and isodow(p_local_date) = 7. It then counts distinct log dates from Monday to that Sunday. Nothing looks back at the previous completed week, and nothing else grants the key. The spec trigger in components/today/care/awards.ts says 'a retained meal on all seven dates of a completed local week'. That wording does not limit the grant to a sync made on Sunday itself. If the user first syncs on Monday or later, or logs Sunday's meal only after their last Sunday sync, the week is never granted. The Sunday-only gate was added deliberately, to stop a caller naming a future Sunday from granting early. A look-back over past weeks would have closed that hole without this side effect, so the miss is a real spec mismatch, not an accepted behaviour. I found no ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts it. Impact is low: it is a cosmetic accolade, and a user who opens the app on the Sunday after logging still gets it.

confirmed: I read the SQL and did not run it. In `supabase/migrations/20261225090300_care_accolades.sql` (lines 172-181), the `full-week` grant sits inside `if p_local_date = v_today and isodow(p_local_date) = 7`. `v_today` is the account's current day, computed from `now()`. That branch is the only place `full-week` is granted anywhere in the repo (grep found no other grant). So a sync that runs on Monday or later takes the `else` path. It never looks back at the previous Monday–Sunday window, and the user never earns the accolade. The same happens if the first sync of Sunday comes before that day's meal is logged and no later sync happens that day. The rule text at line 70 says "a retained meal on all seven dates of a completed local week", which the code does not honour once Sunday has passed. The Sunday-only gate looks deliberate. Its comment says the Sol review closed a hole where a caller named a future Sunday and so could forge `full-week` and `welcome-back`. The effect is an accolade that is missed, not data corruption or a safety problem. Severity stays low. A fix would let the grant also look back at the most recent completed week, with the week bounded by the account's real today.

confirmed.title: Care points and accolades sync fail when the phone's day differs from the stored zone's today
confirmed.defect: The phone always sends `?date=<its local day>`, and `resolveCareDay` forwards it as `p_local_date`. `care_points_sync` raises 22023 'future_date' when that date is later than today in the account's stored zone (`_care_effective_zone`). The route maps 22023 to HTTP 400. `readCareShop` on the phone calls points first and returns 'failed' on any non-2xx, so the whole shop and Seeds view fail. `care_accolades_sync` has no 22023 mapping, so the same condition on a later zone-derived path would surface as 502. When the phone's day is behind the stored zone's today, `p_local_date <> v_today` and nothing is minted.
confirmed.failureScenario: The stored zone was captured on first sync as America/Los_Angeles. The user travels to Auckland or Tokyo, and the phone's date is a day ahead of the stored zone's today. Every GET /api/care/points returns 400, the shop reads 'failed', and no Seeds can be viewed or spent. In the other direction, with phone-day behind stored-zone, `p_local_date <> v_today` skips every award for that day. The skipped award is never backfilled, because only today's date can mint.
confirmed.evidence: care-points sync migration line 306-310 (`v_today := (now() at time zone v_zone)::date; if p_local_date > v_today then raise exception 'future_date' using errcode='22023'`), line 322 (`if p_local_date = v_today then` gates every award). lib/server/care-points.ts:21 maps 22023 to 400. components/today/care/care-api.ts:101-104 treats a non-ok points response as 'failed' for the whole shop read. lib/server/care-zone.ts forwards the client day unchanged.
confirmed.fix: In `care_points_sync`, ignore a `p_local_date` that is not today in the effective zone and use `v_today` instead of raising. Alternatively, have resolveCareDay derive the date from the stored zone for the sync call, and use the client day only for display or purchase dating.
votes: confirmed: The mechanism holds. The phone sends its own day, and plausibleClientDay accepts any date within one UTC day, so resolveCareDay forwards it unchanged. care_points_sync (migration line 306-310) then raises 22023 'future_date' when that date is later than today in _care_effective_zone, and lib/server/care-points.ts:18 maps that to a 400. readCareShop returns "failed" on any non-2xx points call, so the whole shop and Seeds view fail. When the phone day is behind the stored zone's today, the `p_local_date = v_today` gate mints nothing, and a past date is never backfilled. captureTimeZone (lib/sync/settings.ts:106-120) writes the zone once and never rewrites it, so it goes stale after the user changes zone. No test, owner ruling or audit accepts this; the future_date grep hit only the weigh-in tests. It needs the user to be in a zone whose day differs from the stored zone's day, which means travel or a relocation. For ordinary users the phone day equals the stored-zone day, so most users never see it. I rate it low to medium rather than a broad regression. I did not run the SQL or the route, so the 502 claim for care_accolades_sync is unverified. I confirmed only that care_accolades_sync derives its date from _care_effective_zone (migration 20261225090300 line 121-123).

confirmed: I confirmed this by tracing the code. I did not run a snippet. The phone sends `?date=<its local day>` (`today()` in `care-api.ts`). `resolveCareDay` calls `accountDay`. `accountDay` honours a plausible client day (within one day of UTC) and returns `zone: null`. `resolveCareDay` then fills the zone from the stored `user_settings.time_zone`. `care_points_sync` (migration 20261225090100, lines 306-310) overrides that zone with `_care_effective_zone`, so the stored zone wins. It computes `v_today` in that zone and raises 22023 `future_date` when `p_local_date > v_today`. `syncCarePoints` maps 22023 to HTTP 400. `readCareShop` calls points first and returns "failed" on any non-2xx, so the shop read fails.

Two things make travel trigger it. `captureTimeZone` never rewrites a stored zone, so travel does not update it. The 'plausible' client-day check allows UTC-12 to UTC+14, which covers the traveller case. A phone one day ahead of the stored zone (for example Auckland or Tokyo against a Los Angeles zone) therefore gets 400 on every GET.

In the other direction, a phone day behind the stored zone gives `p_local_date <> v_today`. The `if p_local_date = v_today` gate then skips every award, and the migration comment says backfill never mints, so that day's award is lost.

I found no owner ruling that accepts this. The failure only affects an account that has travelled to a different date than its stored zone, and the main path is unaffected. That is why I corrected the severity to low. The accolades claim ('would surface as 502') is speculative, because the sync RPC `care_accolades_sync` is not shown in this finding. Only the points path is demonstrated.

confirmed.title: Coach recentGut lookback window computed from the UTC date
confirmed.defect: recentGut computes `from` as the UTC date of (now minus days) and filters gut_log.local_date >= from. local_date is a user-local date.
confirmed.failureScenario: For a user west of UTC in the evening, or east of UTC just after local midnight, the UTC date is off by one from the user's day. The 'last N days' window is then one day short or one day long, which gives the coach wrong data for gut-symptom questions. This is an edge-case error only.
confirmed.evidence: lib/server/coach-ports.ts:290 `new Date(Date.now() - days * 86_400_000).toISOString().slice(0, 10)` against `.gte("local_date", from)` at :292.
confirmed.fix: Derive today from the account day (accountDay or localDateIn with the stored zone), then step back by calendar days.
votes: confirmed: At lib/server/coach-ports.ts:289-292, `recentGut` computes `from` as the UTC date of now minus days×86400000 ms. It then filters `gut_log.local_date >= from`, and `local_date` is a user-local date. No upstream guard fixes this. The only caller is `lib/coach/executors.ts:153`, which passes `days` straight through. I found no docs/decisions ruling that accepts it; the grep hits for "gut" are unrelated to the lookback window. Tests only mock `recentGut`. A user west of UTC in the evening, or east of UTC just after local midnight, gets a window one day off from their own day. The effect is bounded to at most one day, on a soft "last N days" gut-symptom lookback. A `clock` with `date` and `tz` is already in scope in the same function (used by `compose` just below), so the fix is easy. The defect is real but cosmetic, so low severity stands.

confirmed: At lib/server/coach-ports.ts:289-292, `recentGut` builds `from` from `Date.now()` as a UTC date and compares it to the user-local `gut_log.local_date`. The same function already has the turn's local date available as `clock.date`, with `clock.tz`, in the enclosing `coachPorts` scope, and it does not use it. I ran the arithmetic with a user in Denver (UTC-6) at 22:00 local on 2026-10-10, which is 2026-10-11T04:00Z, and days=7. The code gives from=2026-10-04. The user-local window start is 2026-10-03, so the window is one day short. East of UTC just after local midnight the error goes the other way and the window is one day long. The impact is limited to the gut-symptom lookback for the coach. No owner ruling accepts this behaviour. The fix is to subtract days from `clock.date` using date-only arithmetic.

confirmed.title: Direct compose and suggestion-pool rotation fall back to the server UTC date
confirmed.defect: When no date is passed, the rotation date defaults to new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10), the UTC date. The same applies in lib/coach/compose-pinned.ts:27.
confirmed.failureScenario: For a user whose local day differs from the UTC day (evenings in the Americas), a compose or suggest call that omits the date seeds date-stable variety and the history windows from tomorrow's date. The cards shown and the plan resolved for the viewed day can then rank differently. This only affects ordering, not safety. The code comment accepts it as a fallback.
confirmed.evidence: lib/coach/suggest-pool.ts:46-48 and :122 `date: input.date ?? todayUtc()`; lib/coach/compose-pinned.ts:141 `args.date ?? todayUtc()`.
confirmed.fix: Require the caller to pass the viewed day, or derive the fallback from the account zone.
votes: confirmed: The defect is real but very small. In lib/coach/suggest-pool.ts:47 and lib/coach/compose-pinned.ts:27, todayUtc() is the fallback when no date is passed. No ruling in docs/ covers it. The finding overstates the compose path, though. coach-ports.ts:309 always passes `date: clock.date` to composeMeal, and plan-ideas passes the request date, so those two paths never reach the UTC fallback. Only the coach `suggest_options` tool can reach it: coach-ports.ts:347 forwards the model's raw `args`, and the model may omit `date`. The fallback then seeds `rankPlates` rotation from the UTC date. The effect is a different tie-break order among plates that already passed admission. It is not a safety issue and not a data issue. The code comment (suggest-pool.ts:43-44) accepts it as a fallback. Keep it as low severity: a one-line fix would default to `clock.date`.

confirmed: I traced the fallback through the real call paths. I did not run a snippet, because the code reading settles it.

The defect is real for the coach's suggest_options path. `lib/coach/suggest-pool.ts:122` uses `input.date ?? todayUtc()`, which is the server's UTC date. `SuggestInput.date` in `lib/coach/executors.ts` is documented as "not a model or wire field". `lib/server/coach-ports.ts` (suggest, ~line 347) calls `suggestOptions(args, ...)` without copying `clock.date` into `args`. It uses `clock.date` only for `composePoolPorts` (the focus read). So every coach suggest_options call seeds the plate rotation from the UTC date. In the evening in the Americas that is tomorrow's date, while `resolveDay` uses the viewed local date.

Two other cases do not have the problem:
- Coach `compose_meal` passes `date: clock.date` (`coach-ports.ts:309`), so the `compose-pinned.ts:141` fallback is not hit on that path.
- Plan-sheet chips pass `request.date` through `chipInput`, so `/api/plan/ideas` does not hit the pool fallback either.

The impact is limited to rotation and variety ordering. No safety verdict depends on it. The code comments in both files state the fallback is deliberate. Only the `suggest-pool.ts` fallback is reachable in practice, and the `compose-pinned.ts` one is dead on production paths. Severity stays low.

confirmed.title: MCP list_coach_messages is documented 'newest last' but with a limit returns the oldest messages
confirmed.defect: The tool orders created_at ascending and applies .limit(a.limit ?? 50). With the epoch floor as default `since`, the limit keeps the OLDEST N messages, not the newest N. The description says 'newest last, for a review'.
confirmed.failureScenario: An account has 300 coach messages. A review agent calls list_coach_messages with no args, or with limit 100, to read recent turns. It gets messages 1-50 (or 1-100) from the account's first days and never sees recent ones. A weekly review done through this tool judges stale turns. Passing sinceIso is the only workaround, and the schema does not say so.
confirmed.evidence: coach-tools.ts:71-79: `.gte('created_at', a.sinceIso ?? MESSAGES_FROM_FLOOR).order('created_at', {ascending: true}).limit(a.limit ?? 50)`. MESSAGES_FROM_FLOOR = '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' (line 20).
confirmed.fix: Order descending with the limit, then reverse the rows to present them oldest to newest. Or only apply the limit from the newest end.
votes: confirmed: lib/mcp/coach-tools.ts:71-79 does what the finding says. The query filters created_at >= sinceIso, defaulting to the 1970 floor, then sorts ascending and applies .limit(a.limit ?? 50). With no sinceIso, that returns the oldest N messages. The tool description says "newest last, for a review", and the spec (docs/specs/phase-7-coach.md:64) says the tool is meant to "read the week's turns for a review". No guard, test or ruling covers it. tests/coach/mcp-tools.test.ts mocks the query chain and only checks the user_id binding. Nothing in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts this ordering. The only workaround is to pass sinceIso, and the schema does not say so. The defect is real but bounded: it affects a read-only review tool and corrupts nothing, and a caller who passes sinceIso gets what they want. Suggested fix: order descending, apply the limit, then reverse the rows. Severity is low to medium; I would call it low.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code, not by running a repro. The query in lib/mcp/coach-tools.ts (lines 71-79) filters created_at >= sinceIso, defaulting to the 1970 floor, then orders created_at ascending and applies limit(a.limit ?? 50). Postgres applies the limit after the ascending sort, so it keeps the OLDEST N rows. An account with 300 messages therefore returns messages 1-50 (or 1-100 with limit 100) and never the recent ones. The only workaround is passing sinceIso, and the input schema does not say so. The tool description says "newest last, for a review", and the spec (docs/specs/phase-7-coach.md, line 64) says the tool is for reading "the week's turns". No owner ruling accepts this behaviour. The unit test only stubs the query chain and never checks which end the limit keeps. Impact is limited to a read-only MCP tool and needs an account with more than the limit in messages, so I rate it low to medium, with low as the corrected severity. The fix is to order descending, apply the limit, then reverse the rows.

confirmed.title: Meals export silently stops at 1,000 entries and reports no cursor
confirmed.defect: streamMeals does one select with .limit(opts.limit + 1). The route defaults limit to MAX_LIMIT = 5000 (app/api/export/route.ts:29,70). PostgREST max_rows = 1000 (supabase/config.toml:10) caps the response at 1000 rows whatever .limit asks for. hasMore is computed as entries.length > opts.limit, so 1000 > 5000 is false and next_cursor is null.
confirmed.failureScenario: An account with 1,400 non-deleted log_entries (about 280 days at 5 meals a day) downloads /api/export?kind=meals with no limit param. It gets the oldest 1,000 entries and a null next_cursor. The CSV carries no truncation notice, because the notice is only appended when a cursor exists. The user's 'full export' is missing their latest ~400 meals and nothing says so. The same happens for any explicit limit above 1000.
confirmed.evidence: export.ts:192-203: `.order(...).limit(opts.limit + 1)` then `const hasMore = entries.length > opts.limit; const page = hasMore ? entries.slice(0, opts.limit) : entries;`. route.ts:69-70: `if (raw === null) return MAX_LIMIT;` with MAX_LIMIT = 5000. csvResponse only adds TRUNCATION_NOTICE when nextCursor is truthy.
confirmed.fix: Cap the effective page size at 999 (or at the API row cap minus the sentinel row) in limitParam/MAX_LIMIT. Or read the page with fetchAllRows or keyset paging and compute hasMore from a sentinel row on the real page size.
votes: confirmed: Code read confirms the failure. streamMeals (lib/server/export.ts:189-203) does one select with .limit(opts.limit + 1) and no paging. The route (app/api/export/route.ts:29,70) defaults limit to MAX_LIMIT = 5000 and accepts any limit up to 5000. PostgREST max_rows is 1000 (supabase/config.toml:10, also the Supabase default), so the response is silently capped at 1000 rows. hasMore is `entries.length > opts.limit`, which is 1000 > 5000 = false, so next_cursor is null. csvResponse only appends TRUNCATION_NOTICE when nextCursor is set, so the CSV gives no sign of truncation. The oldest 1000 entries are returned and the rest are dropped without any warning. The same pattern is in export-water.ts:98 and export.ts:487; the buffered `page=` path uses PAGE_SIZE = 1000 correctly. The repo already knows max_rows truncates silently: tests/export/body-profile.test.ts:307 notes it, and lib/server/health-daily.ts uses keyset paging. I found no guard upstream, no test that covers meals above 1000 rows, and no ruling in docs/audit or docs/decisions that accepts this. Severity high fits: silent data loss in a user-facing full export, with a cursor that would let the client recover if it were reported.

confirmed: I traced the call path by reading the code. I did not run it against PostgREST. Default limitParam (app/api/export/route.ts:66-71) returns MAX_LIMIT = 5000. The route calls streamMeals once (route.ts:110-114). confirmed.title: Path traversal in fetchOwnedObject lets pantry/photo and coach/transcribe read another user's media with the service role
confirmed.defect: fetchOwnedObject only checks that the first path segment equals the caller's uid (`key.split("/")[0] !== userId`). It does not reject `..`, `.`, empty or other odd segments, and it does not check the media_objects row. The key then goes to the service-role storage client. supabase-js builds a URL string and fetch applies WHATWG dot-segment normalisation, so `<myuid>/../<victimuid>/<uuid>.jpg` downloads the victim's object. Every other mediaPath consumer (capture, plan-inspire, plan-document) is protected by the strict MEDIA_PATH regex (`media/<36 hex/dash>/<36 hex/dash>.ext`). Two routes skip it: POST /api/pantry/photo validates only `z.string().min(1).max(200)`, and POST /api/coach/transcribe validates only `z.string().min(1).max(512)`.
confirmed.failureScenario: Attacker (a shopping-pilot user) knows or obtains a victim's media path (uid plus random uuid, for example from a leaked log, support ticket or shared screenshot). They POST /api/coach/transcribe {"path":"media/<attackerUid>/../<victimUid>/<uuid>.m4a"}. The segment check passes, normalisation resolves the URL to the victim's object, and the victim's voice clip is transcribed and the text returned. The same trick on POST /api/pantry/photo sends the victim's photo to the vision model and returns the ingredient names it sees. The path unguessability limits this, but the ownership check is meant to be the boundary and it is bypassable.
confirmed.evidence: lib/server/media.ts:70-79 (segment-0 check only, then admin.storage.download(key)); app/api/pantry/photo/route.ts:23 `mediaPath: z.string().min(1).max(200)`; lib/server/coach-transcribe.ts:69 `path: z.string().min(1).max(512)`; lib/capture/types.ts:40 MEDIA_PATH regex used by capture, plan-inspire and plan-document but not these two. `new URL("https://x/storage/v1/object/media/AAA/../BBB/c.jpg").href` normalises to `.../media/BBB/c.jpg`.
confirmed.fix: In fetchOwnedObject, require `^media/<uid>/<uuid>.<ext>$` (or at least exactly 2 segments, with segment 0 === userId and the file segment matching the UUID.ext regex) and throw 403 or 400 otherwise. Also apply the MEDIA_PATH regex in the pantry/photo and coach/transcribe zod schemas.
votes:
confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run the storage client, because the worktree has no node_modules.

`fetchOwnedObject` (lib/server/media.ts:70-79) strips a leading `media/`, checks only that `key.split("/")[0] === userId`, and then calls the service-role `admin.storage.from("media").download(key)`. It does not reject `..` segments and does not check the `media_objects` row.

- **Guards on the two routes:** `POST /api/pantry/photo` validates `mediaPath` only as `z.string().min(1).max(200)`. `POST /api/coach/transcribe` validates `path` only as `z.string().min(1).max(512)`. Neither applies the strict `MEDIA_PATH` regex that capture, plan-inspire and plan-document use. The only other check before the fetch is `requireRecipeUser` or session auth.
- **Dot-segment resolution:** `new URL("https://x/storage/v1/object/media/A/../B/c.jpg").href` resolves to `.../media/B/c.jpg` (I ran this). By my recollection, storage-js `download` appends the path to the URL without encoding it, so `media/<myuid>/../<victimuid>/<uuid>.m4a` would reach the victim's object. I did not read that source here.
- **Rulings:** I saw no owner ruling that accepts this.

The bug is real, but exploiting it needs the victim's object path (their uid plus a random UUID), which an attacker would have to learn some other way. That limits the impact, so I rate it low rather than medium. A fix is to apply the strict regex in both routes, or to reject `.`, `..` and empty segments inside `fetchOwnedObject`.

confirmed: Reproduced. fetchOwnedObject (lib/server/media.ts:70) only checks key.split("/")[0] === userId, where key is objectKey(path) with the "media/" prefix stripped. "media/ME/../VICTIM/u.m4a" gives key "ME/../VICTIM/u.m4a", and segment 0 is ME, so the check passes. The key goes to admin.storage.from("media").download(key). In the installed storage-js 2.117.2, download builds the URL with a raw template string, with no segment sanitising. I ran the real StorageClient against a local HTTP server with download("ME/../VICTIM/u.m4a"). The server received /storage/v1/object/media/VICTIM/u.m4a, so fetch's dot-segment normalisation resolves to the victim's object. The client uses the service role, so RLS does not apply, and nothing checks the media_objects row. The two routes in the finding skip the MEDIA_PATH regex: pantry/photo accepts any string up to 200 characters, and coach/transcribe accepts any string up to 512 characters. Both call fetchOwnedObject directly. Exploitation needs the victim's uid and object uuid, so medium severity is reasonable, since unguessability limits it but the ownership boundary is bypassable. I found no owner ruling that accepts this.

confirmed.title: Oura 401 refresh is a no-op, the rotated-token write result is discarded, and rotation is not atomic with the DB write
confirmed.defect: Three related problems in token handling. (1) pullTwoDays passes `refresh: () => accessTokenFor(admin, source)`, but accessTokenFor returns the stored access token unchanged whenever its stored expires_at is more than 5 minutes away, so the single refresh-then-retry on 401 never refreshes. (2) The rotation update `.eq('oauth', source.oauth)` has no .select(), and the result is thrown away (`void data`). Zero matched rows is treated as success, and the new pair is lost. If the update errors after Oura has already rotated, the stored refresh token is dead. (3) `source` is a stale snapshot, so a refresh after an earlier in-run rotation re-sends the already-consumed refresh token.
confirmed.failureScenario: (1) A user revokes or re-authorises Oura, or the token is invalidated early, while the stored expires_at is still in the future. All three parallel ouraGet calls get 401, 'refresh' returns the same bad token, and the pull fails with 'Oura ... failed with 401' on every cron fire until the stored expiry passes. (2) Oura accepts the refresh and consumes the old refresh token, then the health_sources update fails on a transient DB error (HttpError 500) or the CAS matches nothing. The old refresh token is now invalid at Oura while the DB still holds it, so every later pull fails with exchange_failed until the user reconnects, with no flag or recovery path. (3) When the start-of-pull call rotated the token, a later 401 re-reads the old source.oauth and the exchange fails.
confirmed.evidence: oura.ts:105-107 returns current.access_token when expiry is more than the skew away. oura.ts:109-117 does the exchange, then `.update({ oauth: sealOauth(rotated) }).eq('id', source.id).eq('oauth', source.oauth)` with no select, followed by `void data; return rotated.access_token`. oura.ts:133 `refresh: async () => accessTokenFor(admin, source, { fetchFn: deps.fetchFn })` reuses the original `source`. lib/oura/client.ts:34-37 calls opts.refresh() once on 401. oura.ts:135 runs the three ouraGet calls concurrently via Promise.all.
confirmed.fix: Give the 401 path a force-refresh mode that ignores the stored expiry. Re-read the source row's current sealed oauth inside accessTokenFor. Serialise refreshes per source (a single in-flight promise). Check the rotation update with .select('id') and treat zero rows as lost, re-reading the stored pair (another worker rotated). Persist the rotated pair with a retry before returning, and mark the source needs-reconnect when it cannot be saved.
confirmed.knownBefore: docs/audit/2026-09-13/report.md R6 (CAS result discarded; code defect verified, high impact challenged). Parts (1) and (3) are new.
votes:
confirmed: I read lib/server/oura.ts and lib/oura/client.ts, and all three mechanics are real in the code. Impact is narrow, so I'd rate it low rather than medium.

(1) The 401 refresh is a no-op when the stored expiry is still in the future. accessTokenFor returns current.access_token whenever expiry is more than the skew away (oura.ts:105-107). The refresh callback calls it with the same source and no force flag, so ouraGet's single retry on 401 (client.ts:34-37) resends the same bad token. The pull then throws "Oura ... failed with 401".

(2) The rotation update has no .select() and does `void data` (oura.ts:109-117). A CAS that matches zero rows is treated as success. If the DB write errors after Oura has already rotated, the new pair is lost. The code path is the same one the 2026-09-13 audit listed as R6, which called the defect real and challenged only the "high" impact.

(3) `source` is a stale snapshot. If the start-of-pull call rotated the tokens and a later 401 triggers refresh, accessTokenFor re-reads the old source.oauth. Its expiry is old, so it re-sends the already-consumed refresh token.

Why it stays low: I found no guard, test or owner ruling that accepts these behaviours, so I could not refute it. But each failure needs a narrow trigger. These are an early server-side token invalidation while expiry is still valid, a DB failure in the window right after Oura rotates, or a 401 immediately after a fresh rotation. The harm is that Oura data stops syncing, which affects an advisory feature and not safety or targets. The user recovers by reconnecting, because completeOura overwrites the tokens. A re-authorise through completeOura also replaces the stored pair, which limits scenario (1).

confirmed: I traced the code in lib/server/oura.ts and lib/oura/client.ts but did not run a repro. All three parts hold.

(1) accessTokenFor returns the stored access token when the stored expires_at is more than OURA_REFRESH_SKEW_MS away. pullTwoDays passes `refresh: () => accessTokenFor(admin, source)`, so on a 401 ouraGet calls refresh once, gets the same token back, retries, and gets 401 again. `refreshed` is already true, 401 is not retryable, so it throws "Oura <path> failed with 401". The refresh never forces an exchange. The pull keeps failing on each cron fire until the stored expiry passes.

(2) The rotation update is `.update({oauth}).eq('id').eq('oauth', source.oauth)` with no .select() and no row-count check. `void data` discards the result. Zero matched rows returns the new access token and the new pair is never stored. If the update errors, it throws HttpError 500 after Oura has already consumed the old refresh token, and the DB still holds that dead token. Later pulls then fail at exchange. No flag or recovery path exists in this function.

(3) The refresh closure captures the original `source`. After a start-of-pull rotation, a later 401 reads the old, already-consumed refresh token from source.oauth. Its expiry is stale, so it exchanges again and fails. The three parallel ouraGet calls also each call refresh, so in the expired case the second and third exchanges reuse the already-consumed refresh token.

Severity is medium. Part 1 self-heals when the stored expiry passes. Parts 2 and 3 need a transient DB error or a 401 right after a fresh rotation. Their impact is permanent until the user reconnects.

confirmed.title: A failed time-zone read silently dates estimate and weekly-proposal jobs by UTC and locks the wrong day
confirmed.defect: readAccountZone swallows every read error and returns null, and resolveAccountDay then falls to UTC. The estimate and weekly-proposal jobs use that date as both the computation date (asOf) and the job_runs lock key, with no way to tell a real 'no zone' from a transient failure.
confirmed.failureScenario: During a brief PostgREST error for one account, the 07:00 UTC estimate run dates a Pacific/Auckland or America/Los_Angeles account by the UTC day, writes the estimate for the wrong local_date and takes lock key=UTC date; the later fire with a healthy read computes the account's real day and writes a second estimate row, so the account has estimates for two different 'today' values and the first (wrong-day) one may be the latest read by latestEstimate.
confirmed.evidence: account-day.ts:80-93 (`catch ... return null`), estimate/route.ts:62-63 and weekly-proposal/route.ts:130-131 (`storedZone: await readAccountZone(admin, userId)` then `asOf = day.date`, `claimLock(..., asOf)`).
confirmed.fix: In the jobs, read the zone with a throwing variant (like timeZoneFor) so a failed read returns 'retry' instead of dating by UTC.
votes: confirmed: The code does what the finding says. `readAccountZone` (lib/server/account-day.ts:80-93) catches every read error and returns null. In the estimate job, `resolveAccountDay` then dates the run by UTC, and the job passes that date to `claimLock` and `runEstimate`. Nothing in the job tells a transient read failure apart from an account with no stored zone. I found no upstream guard, and no ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit mentions this path. The "a zone read never fails the target read it serves" comment covers target reads, not the jobs. The estimate is keyed on (user_id, local_date) and the lock key is the date, so a later healthy fire takes a different lock and writes a second row. `latestEstimate` orders by `local_date` descending, so for zones west of UTC the wrong UTC-dated row is the newer one and gets read. For zones east of UTC, such as Auckland, the real date is later, so the correct row wins. I read only the estimate job route, not the weekly-proposal route. Impact is small: the estimate is stateless and advisory, the error is at most one day, and it needs a transient error on one account's read. Severity stays low.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run a repro.

- `readAccountZone` (account-day.ts:80-93) catches every error, including a PostgREST error, and returns null.
- `resolveAccountDay` then skips the stored and request zones and falls to UTC. It only logs a warning.
- estimate/route.ts:62-69 sets `asOf = day.date`, takes `claimLock(JOB_NAME, userId, asOf)`, and calls `runEstimate(asOf)`.
- `runEstimate` upserts one `expenditure_estimates` row per (user_id, local_date) (expenditure.ts:161).
- `latestEstimate` orders by `local_date` descending with limit 1 (expenditure.ts:206-207).

So a transient failure dates an America/Los_Angeles account by the UTC day. At the 07:00 UTC fire that date is one day ahead of the local date. The job writes an estimate row for the UTC date under that lock key.

A later healthy fire computes the real local date, which is a different lock key, and writes a second row. Until the real day catches up, the wrong-day row has the greater `local_date` and is what `latestEstimate` returns. The two rows can hold different TDEE values.

The weekly-proposal job locks on `weekStart` (route.ts:135), so the lock-key problem is milder there. It still passes the UTC `asOf` to `runEstimate` and `activeProfile`.

No owner ruling accepts this. The doc comment on `readAccountZone` says a zone read never fails the target read it serves. That fits the request path, but the jobs reuse the same function and cannot tell a missing zone from a failed read.

The effect is low: it needs a transient read error. It self-corrects once the local date reaches the UTC date, and it does not corrupt user data.

confirmed.title: First constraint_profiles write is an unconditional upsert, so two writers at rev 0 overwrite each other (allergens can be lost)

Both writers read rev 0, both pass baseRev===0, and the second upsert silently replaces the first row. `next` is built from the empty `current`, so any field the second request omits (`req.avoidAllergens ?? current.avoid_allergens`) resets to empty. No DB trigger enforces rev monotonicity.

confirmed.evidence: constraints.ts:162-166: `if (rev === 0) { const inserted = await client.from('constraint_profiles').upsert(next)...` versus line ~171 `.update(next).eq('user_id', userId).eq('rev', rev)` for rev>0. grep of supabase/migrations shows only food-world/condition-gate/rules-clock triggers on constraint_profiles, none checking rev.

In /Users/zero-suminc./projects/clients/Sasha/wt/audit-2026-10-10/lib/server/constraints.ts, putProfile at rev===0 does an unconditional upsert (insert ... on conflict (user_id) do update). Only the rev>=1 path uses the .eq("rev", rev) compare-and-swap. I found nothing that closes the gap:
- No migration inserts a default constraint_profiles row, and no grep hit for "insert into ... constraint_profiles". New accounts therefore start at rev 0.
- The only triggers on the table are the condition gate and the rules-clock trigger. Neither checks rev.
- app/api/constraints/route.ts calls putProfile with no advisory lock or serialisation.
- I found no ruling or prior audit that accepts this.

Two concurrent writers that both read rev 0 can both pass baseRev===0, and the second upsert overwrites the first. The overwrite also resets omitted fields to the values read as current, which were empty.

The high rating is overstated. The window is the milliseconds between getProfile and the upsert, on an account's first-ever rules write. That requires two truly concurrent first writers (phone plus MCP, or two devices). A single account makes that write once, so this is rare. Two different-field first writes will not normally land in that window. The real exposure is a lost allergen on that account's first write. I would call it low-to-medium. The fix is small: insert without upsert and treat a unique-violation as a conflict, or add an on-conflict guard such as a where clause on rev.

That upsert is keyed on the user_id primary key, so the default is ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE with no rev predicate. If the other writer inserted in between, the second upsert overwrites that row. Each `next` is built from the empty `current` read earlier, so fields the second request omits fall back to empty: `req.avoidAllergens ?? current.avoid_allergens` gives [], and so do conditions, banned_categories and custom_rules. The first writer's allergens are lost and both writers get status ok with rev 1. The compare-and-swap exists only on the rev>=1 `update ... .eq("rev", rev)` path. The only triggers on constraint_profiles are condition_gate, rules_clock and recipe_state_rules; none checks rev monotonicity. The condition_gate trigger takes an advisory lock, but it only serializes the writes and does not stop the second one from overwriting the first. putProfile has no lock or transaction of its own. Callers include app/api/constraints/route.ts, lib/mcp/coach-tools.ts and lib/server/food-world.ts. I downgrade to medium rather than high. The window is narrow: it needs two concurrent first-ever writes on one new account, and the write path is a PUT whose omitted fields keep the current value. The loss is silent, though, and it affects the allergen safety rule. The fix is a rev-0 insert that conflicts (`insert ... on conflict do nothing`, then return a conflict result when no row comes back) or a SQL function with a row lock.

confirmed.title: Backup pages by OFFSET over live tables, so concurrent writes skip or duplicate rows
confirmed.defect: tablePages reads each table with `.order(pk).range(offset, offset+999)` as separate requests against tables being written, with no snapshot and no keyset cursor. The dump header says consistency 'per-request'.
confirmed.failureScenario: While the dump is on page 2 of log_entries, a user deletes a row that sat on page 1, or inserts a row with a lower primary key. Every later row shifts by one. The row at the page boundary is skipped on delete, or written twice on insert. The backup is then missing a live row and still reports ok. The window is the whole upload, which grows with data size.
confirmed.evidence: app/api/jobs/backup/route.ts:74-81 uses offset += PAGE. The other jobs (lib/server/job-sweep.ts keysetRows) already use key > last paging.
confirmed.fix: Page by key (`gt` last primary key, composite keys via tuple comparison or a per-table ordered single key), as keysetRows does.

There is no snapshot transaction and no keyset cursor, so concurrent deletes or inserts shift later pages. A delete on an earlier page skips a live row at the next boundary. An insert at a lower key duplicates a boundary row. The run still records status "ok". I found no guard upstream or downstream. The cron lease only stops two backups running at once, not writes from users. No test covers the route. I found no ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts this. The 2026-09-13 audit only fixed the earlier truncation at max_rows. The header does say "consistency":"per-request", which documents the lack of a snapshot, but it does not say rows can be skipped. The route's own header comment says the real .sql dump comes from scripts/backup.sh on the Mac, which is what acceptance criterion 13 measures. confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code and did not run a repro. app/api/jobs/backup/route.ts:71-82 pages each table with `.order(pk).range(offset, offset+999)`. Inserts with random uuid ids can land on any earlier page, so duplicates are realistic. Many tables use soft deletes, which makes skips from deletes rarer. The same applies to hard-deleted rows. No owner ruling accepts this. The only prior mention is the 2026-09-22 phase-10 r4 spec review, which flagged cross-table inconsistency and asked for a database snapshot. The real recovery artifact is the pg_dump from scripts/backup.sh. The JSON dump is a secondary safety net. The cron runs nightly, so concurrent writes are infrequent. I rate it low rather than medium. The fix is to page by keyset (`key > last`, as lib/server/job-sweep.ts `keysetRows` does), or to take a snapshot.

The or() parameter is still ANDed with the RLS and user_id filters, so injection cannot reach another account's rows. The impact is a broken cursor contract and a 500 on bad input.

confirmed.title: Plan-sheet 'Not this' exclusion list outgrows the 2 KB body cap on /api/plan/ideas, so refills fail with 413
confirmed.defect: The route caps the request body at 2 KB (MAX_BYTES = 2 * 1024). The schema allows up to 40 excludeIds of up to 400 characters each (lib/plan/chips.ts:49). An ideaId is the plate key, the plate's food ids joined with '+' (lib/meals/plate.ts:310, lib/coach/suggest-pool.ts:195). With account-food uuids, a 3-food plate id is about 110 characters. PlanSheet keeps appending every skipped id to its `skipped` list (components/PlanSheet.tsx:415) and sends the last 40 on each refill (components/PlanSheet.tsx:216). The schema's own 40-id limit therefore cannot fit in the body gate.
confirmed.failureScenario: A user taps 'Choose for me' on a meal slot and keeps tapping 'Not this'. Each time all three cards are skipped, a refill goes out carrying every id skipped so far. After about 5-6 refills (roughly 18 skipped 3-food plates, about 2 KB of ids) readJson throws 413 too_large. The chip then shows an error and no further ideas appear for that ask. The ids are not trimmed to fit the byte budget, so the promise that a refill never shows rejected ideas again breaks, and the sheet cannot recover until it is closed and reopened.
confirmed.evidence: app/api/plan/ideas/route.ts:23 `const MAX_BYTES = 2 * 1024;` versus lib/plan/chips.ts:49 `excludeIds: z.array(z.string().min(1).max(400)).max(MAX_EXCLUDE_IDS)` with MAX_EXCLUDE_IDS = 40. components/PlanSheet.tsx:216 sends `excludeIds.slice(-MAX_EXCLUDE_IDS)`. lib/meals/plate.ts:310 builds `key: rows.map((row) => row.food.id).join("+")`.

confirmed: The mismatch is real. The route caps the body at 2 KB (route.ts:23). readJson returns 413 `too_large` from both the content-length check and the actual byte count (http.ts:49-57). The schema allows 40 ids of up to 400 characters, and PlanSheet.tsx:216 sends the last 40 skipped ids with no byte-budget trimming. An ideaId is `plate.key`, the plate's food ids joined with '+' (suggest-pool.ts:195). Since ideas require real food_refs uuids, each id is 36 characters per food, so a 3-food plate is about 110 characters and a 2-food plate about 73. The `skipped` list grows on every 'Not this' tap (PlanSheet.tsx:415) and resets only when a new chip is chosen or a found/doc flow starts (lines 318, 358, 447). A retry sends the same body and fails again, but choosing another chip resets `skipped`, so the user can recover without closing the sheet.

I found no guard that trims the ids and no owner ruling accepting this. I did not run a test; this rests on code reading and my own length arithmetic. Severity is low: it needs 6 or more consecutive full-skip refills in one ask, which is unusual, and picking another chip fixes it.

confirmed.title: Approving a pending target proposal built before a pace hold writes its deficit calories once the active revision has been re-derived to 0 pace
confirmed.defect: assertApprovalEligible only checks that the revision in force has goal_rate_bp_week = 0 when the account is held. recomputeAfterHoldChange re-derives the active revision to 0 pace at once, so that guard then passes. approve_target_proposal copies kcal/macros verbatim from the stored proposal (kcalTrain/kcalRest) and only copies the (now 0) pace label. Existing pending proposals are not superseded or rejected when a hold starts; write_target_proposal only rejects older pending rows when a new proposal is written, and the weekly job returns 'none' for held/minor cases without touching the old row. The source comment itself says 'A proposal built before the hold could carry a deficit'.
confirmed.failureScenario: User has a pending Sunday proposal at a deficit (e.g. 1,900 kcal against 2,300 maintenance). She taps Approve on the still-pending proposal: assertApprovalEligible sees active rate 0 and returns; the RPC writes a new revision with the 1,900 kcal numbers and goal_rate_bp_week 0, so a pregnant account is on a deficit target under a hold, and the 'held at maintenance' state is overwritten.

confirmed.fix: On approval under a hold, recompute/clamp the proposal's kcal to the active maintenance (or refuse with rate_not_eligible whenever the proposal was created before the hold / its stored rate differs); also reject pending proposals when a hold is applied (recomputeAfterHoldChange and the profile-instances route).

It checks only that the proposal is still pending. Nothing in lib/server, app/api or later migrations rejects or supersedes pending target_proposals when a hold begins. Only write_target_proposal rejects older pending rows, and only when a new proposal is written. The source comment says "A proposal built before the hold could carry a deficit" and relies on the next weekly proposal, which does not remove the still-pending row. No docs/decisions or docs/audit ruling accepts this. The result is a deficit-calorie revision on a held (for example pregnant) account, with the pace label showing 0. I rate it high rather than critical because it needs a user tap on a stale pending proposal and the window is limited, though the outcome is unsafe.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run it, because reproducing it would need a database. The call path is: decideProposal runs assertApprovalEligible and then the approve_target_proposal RPC. In lib/server/proposals.ts, assertApprovalEligible returns early when paceAllowed is true. When the account is held, it only rejects if the active revision's goal_rate_bp_week is non-zero. Nothing in lib/server/target-recompute.ts touches target_proposals. I found no other code that rejects or supersedes pending rows when a hold starts. The only rejections of older pending rows are in the migrations that write a new proposal (20261007090000, 20261024093200). confirmed.title: MCP route reads the whole request body before authentication and before any size check
confirmed.defect: readCappedBody does await req.text() and only then measures Buffer.byteLength against 64 KB. It never checks Content-Length, and it runs before withTokenUser. The same raw text is then JSON.parsed by toolNamesInBody pre-auth. The post-auth readJson is never reached for oversized bodies.
confirmed.failureScenario: An unauthenticated caller POSTs a multi-MB body (up to the platform limit of about 4.5 MB per request). The function buffers and decodes it into a string, then runs a byte count, then responds 413. The per-IP limit of 30/min allows about 30 such requests a minute from each IP, and many IPs multiply it. Nothing rejects on the declared Content-Length first. readJson in lib/server/http.ts does check it, and this route bypasses that.
confirmed.evidence: lines 89-100: const raw = bodyConsumed ? await req.text() : ''; if (Buffer.byteLength(raw,'utf8') > MAX_BODY_BYTES) throw 413. Line 105 calls it before withTokenUser at line 107.
confirmed.fix: Reject on Content-Length > MAX_BODY_BYTES first, and read the stream with a byte cap. Do the scope pre-parse only after the token is verified, or only on a body already known to be small.
votes: confirmed: The code matches the finding. app/api/mcp/route.ts readCappedBody (lines 89-100) calls `await req.text()` and only afterwards compares Buffer.byteLength against MAX_BODY_BYTES (64 KB). It never checks the Content-Length header. It runs before withTokenUser (guarded, line 105), and the raw text is then parsed pre-auth by scopeForBody/toolNamesInBody. lib/server/http.ts readJson does check the declared content-length (line 50), but the post-auth call at line 111 is never reached for an oversized body, so it does not help. I found no ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts this. The only guards are two pre-identity rate limits of 30/min, one keyed on the pre-identity key and one on the IP. Their sizes are limited by the Vercel platform body cap, which I recalled from general knowledge rather than checking in the repo. So the missing early reject is a real hardening gap. The impact is small. The body is bounded to a few MB and the rate limits cap the repeat rate. Per-request memory is transient. Nothing is persisted and nothing reaches a model. The correct severity is low, not medium. The fix is to reject early on an over-limit Content-Length, and to read the body with a size-capped stream.

confirmed: The code does what the finding says. In app/api/mcp/route.ts, readCappedBody (lines 89-100) calls `await req.text()` and only afterwards checks Buffer.byteLength against 64 KB. It never reads Content-Length. In guarded(), line 105 runs it before withTokenUser at line 107. readJson in lib/server/http.ts does check the declared Content-Length first (lines 50-53), but the route never reaches it for an oversized body. I traced the code but did not run a repro snippet. An unauthenticated caller can therefore make the function buffer a body up to the platform cap, about 4.5 MB on Vercel, before it answers 413. The impact is small. Two per-IP rate limits (30 per minute, lines 33 and 104) run before the read. The buffering is bounded by the platform cap. - `jsonError` (lib/server/http.ts:33-47) handles an error that is not an `HttpError` as an unhandled error. It returns a generic 500 and logs it. The documented answer for a bad cursor is 422 "malformed cursor".

Recipes cursor:
- `decodeTextCursor` (lib/server/export-cursor.ts) only checks that the string is not empty.
- `streamRecipes` passes it to `.gt("id", ...)` (:486), which would also give a 500 against a uuid column.

Injection:
- A caller can add predicates to the cursor's OR group, but the `.eq("user_id")` and `deleted_at` filters are separate AND filters, and RLS also applies. So there is no cross-account leak.
- The effect is limited to the caller's own rows, or to a 500.

Severity is low: a missing validation that gives a wrong status code, plus keyset-position tampering confined to the caller's own data.

The sibling plan-inspire and pantry-photo paths strip metadata first, and spec W12-F says the Plan sheet photo path must get the same server-side strip. The server trusts the phone's canvas re-encode, but the upload goes to a signed URL, so any client can upload a JPEG with EXIF.

confirmed.title: Media path accepted without format check on /api/coach/transcribe and /api/pantry/photo
confirmed.defect: transcribeRequestSchema takes any string up to 512 chars as the storage path, and pantry/photo takes any string up to 200 chars. fetchOwnedObject only compares the first path segment with the user id. Capture, plan/inspire and plan/document constrain paths with a media/<uuid>/<uuid>.ext regex. Capture also runs assertLiveMediaObject, which rejects tombstoned objects. These two routes do neither check.
confirmed.failureScenario: A path like 'media/<my uid>/../<other uid>/<file>.m4a' passes the first-segment check, and only the storage layer's key normalisation stands between it and another user's object. Even in the benign case, an object the user already deleted or that is past the sweep (media_objects.deleted_at set, but the file not yet removed) can still be read and sent to a model. Transcribe also has no per-user rate limit, only the 120/min per-IP pre-limit.
confirmed.evidence: coach-transcribe.ts:69 z.object({ path: z.string().min(1).max(512) }); pantry/photo/route.ts Body = z.object({ mediaPath: z.string().min(1).max(200) }); media.ts:74-76 key.split('/')[0] !== userId; capture.ts assertLiveMediaObject at line ~80-88 is not called here.

votes:
confirmed: The defect is real but narrow. I read the code and ran a URL check.

Confirmed:
- `fetchOwnedObject` (lib/server/media.ts:74-76) only compares the first path segment with the user id, then downloads with the admin client.
- Both routes pass a free-form path to it. The transcribe schema is `z.string().min(1).max(512)`, and the pantry/photo body is `z.string().min(1).max(200)`. Neither has the `media/<uuid>/<uuid>.ext` regex or an `assertLiveMediaObject` check. That check is in lib/server/capture.ts and runs only on the capture path.
- A path like `media/<me>/../<other>/f.m4a` passes the segment check. `new URL()` collapses it to `/object/media/<other>/f.m4a`. Because `fetch` normalizes URLs the same way, I expect the traversal to reach another user's object, but I did not run it against storage.
- A tombstoned object that is still in storage can be read and sent to a model, because the `media_objects.deleted_at` row is never checked.
- Transcribe has only the 120/min per-IP pre-limit. The model spend caps in `callModel` still apply. Pantry/photo does have a 10/min/user limit, so that part of the finding applies to transcribe only.

Why it stays low:
- Reading another user's object needs both their user id and the object's random v4 uuid, which an attacker cannot guess.
- Transcribe validates the bytes as audio. Pantry/photo validates them as an image and returns only ingredient names.
- The tombstone case only exposes the caller's own already-deleted media.
- I found no owner ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts this behaviour.

The fix is cheap: share the uuid path regex and the live-row check with the other routes, and add a per-user rate limit to transcribe.

confirmed: I traced the code; I did not run the exploit. The `..` bypass and the missing tombstone check both hold on the real call path. Cross-user reads need the victim's two UUIDs, so severity stays low.

1. **Path check.** `transcribeRequestSchema` and the `/api/pantry/photo` Body only bound the string length (512 and 200 chars). Both routes end in `fetchOwnedObject` (lib/server/media.ts:70-81). It calls `objectKey(path)` (which only strips a leading "media/") and compares `key.split("/")[0]` with the user id. It does not reject `..`.

2. **Traversal.** The path `<myuid>/../<otheruid>/<file>.m4a` passes the first-segment check. `fetchOwnedObject` then calls `admin.storage.from("media").download(key)` with the service-role admin client. storage-js 2.117.2 (dist/index.cjs:1203) builds the URL by plain string concatenation with no encoding. `fetch` normalises dot segments in URLs: `new URL('https://p.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/media/U1/../U2/f.m4a').href` returned `.../object/media/U2/f.m4a`. The request therefore reaches another user's object, and the admin client skips RLS. The attacker needs the victim's UUID and the file's UUID name, which are unguessable, so exploitation is hard. It is still a real cross-tenant read bypass, and the sibling routes use a strict `media/<uuid>/<uuid>.ext` regex.

3. **Tombstones.** `assertLiveMediaObject` exists only in capture.ts (lines 78-96) and is not called from coach-transcribe.ts or pantry-photo.ts. A user's own object with `media_objects.deleted_at` set, whose file the sweep has not yet removed, can still be downloaded and sent to a model.

4. **Rate limit.** app/api/coach/transcribe/route.ts has only `enforceRateLimit('coach:transcribe:pre:ip:...', 120, 60)`, with no per-user limit. `/api/pantry/photo` does have a per-user limit of 10/min.

I found no owner ruling in docs/decisions that accepts this behaviour.

confirmed.title: Per-op server 'error' results park the op after 3 attempts with no automatic release
confirmed.defect: app/api/sync/ops converts any RPC exception into an {status:'error'} result, including transient database errors such as statement timeout, serialization failure or connection reset. parkOrRetry counts those as permanent: after MAX_ERROR_ATTEMPTS=3 the op gets next_attempt_at = now + 365 days. Only the manual 'Sync now' action in SyncStatus calls retryParked. Nothing releases it automatically. The backoff steps are 1 s, 2 s and 4 s (with jitter), and the drain is only triggered by writes, visibility changes and online events.
confirmed.failureScenario: A short database hiccup (a few seconds) makes three consecutive passes return error for the same water_log, favorites_meals or plan_days op. The op is parked for a year. Later writes to the same entity chain onto its optimistic rev, so they conflict or park too. The edit never reaches the server, other devices never see it, and pendingCount() keeps counting it with no visible reason until the user finds 'Sync now'. This is the per-op variant of the confirmed whole-batch 4xx parking.
confirmed.evidence: app/api/sync/ops/route.ts:116-122 (catch -> errorResult for every exception); lib/sync/outbox.ts:190-204 (parkOrRetry); lib/sync/outbox.ts:208-218 and components/SyncStatus.tsx (retryParked is manual only); lib/sync/backoff.ts (1 s -> 60 s).

In lib/sync/outbox.ts, parkOrRetry (line 197) parks the op for 365 days once error_attempts reaches 3. retryParked is called only from the manual "Sync now" in components/SyncStatus.tsx. flushOnboardingWritesNow releases only food_membership ops. Nothing else releases a parked op: the visibility, online and save-debounce triggers in lib/sync/account-sync.ts skip it, because it is not due for a year. The code comment says only a human action clears a parked op, so the behaviour is deliberate. No ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts it as a fix for transient database errors. The 2026-09-13 audit noted the same park-forever path for a different cause. I traced this by reading the code and did not run a test. The impact is smaller than the finding claims. The three error passes must fall inside one transient window, and the 1 s then 2 s backoff means they need roughly three separate drain triggers, such as writes or a visibility change, within a few seconds. The parked op still counts in pendingCount, and the "Sync now" button releases it. So the edit is delayed until the user presses the button. It is not lost, and it is not hidden indefinitely. Severity is low rather than medium.

confirmed: Confirmed by code trace. app/api/sync/ops/route.ts catches any applyOp exception and pushes errorResult, so a transient DB error becomes {status:'error'}. In lib/sync/outbox.ts:306-307 that goes to parkOrRetry. At error_attempts >= MAX_ERROR_ATTEMPTS (3) it sets next_attempt_at = now + PARK_MS (365 days). confirmed.title: Applying an older op result overwrites newer optimistic mirror edits (lost water cup, UI regress)
confirmed.defect: applyApplied for create/update does putRow({...local, ...op.payload, rev: result.rev}). It does not check whether a newer op for the same entity is still queued. The mirror already holds that newer op's optimistic payload, and the older payload is written over it.
confirmed.failureScenario: Water at 4 cups. Tap 1 queues op1 (cups 5) and a pass sends it. Tap 2 during the round trip sets the mirror to 6 and queues op2 with base_rev r+1. op1's 'applied' arrives and putRow rewrites the mirror to cups 5, rev r+1. Tap 3 reads current=5 in writeCupsNow and writes 6, not 7. The server ends at 6 after three taps from 4: one cup is lost and the tile visibly drops back. Other whole-row mirror users (plan_days, favorites sort, user_foods) regress the same way until their pending op lands.
confirmed.evidence: lib/sync/outbox.ts:275-277; lib/water-client.ts:136-149 (reads mirror cups as the base, optimistic rev+1 write); no pending-op check anywhere in applyApplied.
confirmed.fix: In applyApplied, if any queued op for the same entity and id remains (other than the one just settled), update only rev, or merge the result under that pending payload. Alternatively, recompute the mirror as the server row plus pending payloads.
votes:
confirmed: applyApplied (lib/sync/outbox.ts, create/update path) does getRow, then putRow({...local, ...op.payload, rev: result.rev}), then deleteOp. It never checks whether a newer op for the same entity is still queued. Only user_settings is protected: settleUserSettings rebuilds the mirror from the baseline plus queued intents. Every other entity, water_log included, is not.

drainOutbox pushes outside any lock that the water write path shares. waterQueue only serializes water writes against each other, and a pass can be in flight while writeCupsNow runs.

The sequence holds. Op1 (cups 5) is in flight. Tap 2 reads the mirror at 5, writes the mirror as cups 6 with rev r+2, and queues op2 on base r+1. Op1's 'applied' then arrives and the mirror is overwritten to cups 5, rev r+1.

Tap 3 reads current=5 and writes 6, so op3 carries cups 6 rather than 7. The server's greatest() rule keeps the final count at 6 after three taps from 4. One cup is lost and the tile visibly drops.

I found no pending-op check, no overlay or reapply step after the drain, and no owner ruling in docs/audit or docs/decisions that accepts this. The window is narrow, one tap during the push round trip. The effect is a real lost write for any other whole-row mirror entity too.

confirmed: Confirmed by tracing the code. I did not run a repro, because vitest only includes tests inside the repo and I may not write there.

Why the race is open:
- `drainOutbox` awaits `push` with no lock on the mirror or the queue.
- While that request is in flight, a second `writeCupsNow` runs freely. It reads mirror cups 5, rev r+1. It writes `putRow({cups: 6, rev: r+2})` and enqueues op2 with base_rev r+1.
- When op1's `applied` result arrives, `applyApplied` (`lib/sync/outbox.ts` ~275-277) does `getRow`, then `putRow({...local, ...op.payload, rev: result.rev})`.
- `op.payload` is op1's `{cups: 5}`, so the mirror goes back to cups 5, rev r+1.
- The function never checks `allOps` for a newer queued op on the same entity_id. The only guard is the `user_settings` special case, which hands off to `settleUserSettings`. `water_log`, `plan_days` and other whole-row entities have no such guard.

Effect on the scenario:
- The UI shows 5 until op2 lands, and then jumps to 6.
- If tap 3 lands in that window, `writeCupsNow` reads current=5, so `mergeCups(5, 6)` gives 6. It queues a duplicate cups-6 op with base_rev r+1.
- The server ends at 6 after three taps from 4, so one cup is lost.

Severity is limited. The mirror self-heals once op2 applies. The loss needs a tap inside the push round trip. Medium is fair, and it could arguably be rated low.

hurt on 9/12' with the server's 'fine 9/04' and returns 'fine 9/04
hurt on 9/12
fine 9/04'. Each further rev bump adds another copy, in symptom-evidence notes on user_food_prefs, log_entries and gut_log.

confirmed.title: Food membership revision is the device clock in ms, so a skewed device can override or discard another device's explicit Avoid
confirmed.defect: The membership rev is Math.max(Date.now(), cachedRev+1, localClock+1) and is written verbatim to food_membership_revisions. The server accepts a write only if membership.rev < excluded.rev, with no bound or server-side clock. Cross-device ordering is therefore decided by raw device clocks. The route reports the loser as 'rejected', and reconcileFoodMembership reverts the local mark to the server's status. The membership cache is localStorage only, so a device that has not seen the other device's mark has no floor.
confirmed.failureScenario: Device A's clock is 1 hour ahead (manual time, travel or a dead clock). The user marks 'peanut butter' as eats on A (rev = T+1h). Ten minutes later on correctly-clocked device B, the user taps Avoid. B mints rev = T+10min, which the server rejects as older, and B's UI silently reverts the Avoid to eats. The user's most recent explicit rule change is lost. Only a second tap works, after the cache holds the server rev.
confirmed.evidence: lib/foods/prefs-client.ts:126-131 and 467; supabase/migrations/20261205090000_food_membership_result.sql (on conflict ... where membership.rev < excluded.rev); app/api/sync/ops/route.ts:80-90 (rejected when row.rev !== rev); lib/foods/prefs-client.ts:535-552 (reconcile reverts the local mark).
confirmed.fix: Let the server assign the revision (previous rev + 1) or take max(client rev, server rev + 1) in the RPC, with a bounded clock if timestamps are kept. At minimum, do not silently revert a fresher explicit tap: surface the rejection or retry at serverRev + 1.

A device whose clock runs ahead therefore wins by rev, and the correctly-clocked device's later Avoid comes back as `rejected`. `reconcileFoodMembership` then reverts the local mark to the server status, and it does so silently. The sync pass (`refreshFoodProjection`) refreshes foods and status from the server but does not raise the membership rev floor. The prefs-client.ts comment near line 463 already concedes that the clock is per tab and a follow-up is deferred. I found no ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit that accepts device-clock ordering for membership. The finding is real, but it needs a materially skewed clock (hours) or near-simultaneous cross-device taps, and the user can recover with a second tap, which succeeds once reconcile has cached the server rev. confirmed.title: plan_days conflict handling loses edits: whole-field newer-wins on full-row payloads, optimistic-rev aliasing, no legacy-store projection
confirmed.defect: Every plan_days op carries all five plan fields from the legacy store, with a base_rev taken from the mirror's optimistic rev+1. On conflict, mergeEntity runs newerWinsFields over those fields, comparing the device client_ts with the server updated_at. swaps, slot_notes and item_overrides are replaced whole, with no per-slot merge, and the fields the user did not touch count as 'defined' on both sides. The merged result is written only to the IDB mirror and the rebased op. The legacy store that Today renders is not re-projected. applyPulledPlanDay also skips every pulled change while an op is pending for that date.
confirmed.failureScenario: (1) Device A offline sets floor_day=true and swaps meal-1 at 10:00. Device B sets swaps meal-2 at 10:05. On reconnect A's pull of B's change is skipped (op pending), then A's op conflicts. The server row is newer, so the server's swaps and floor_day win. A's floor_day and meal-1 swap are discarded, the mirror shows B's values, and A's Today still shows its own local values. (2) Two queued ops op1 (base r) and op2 (base r+1, the optimistic rev) while a remote device moved the server to r+1: op1 conflicts, but op2's base_rev matches the remote's revision by coincidence and applies from stale mirror data, silently overwriting the remote swaps and eaten ticks. The rebased op1' gets client_ts=now and a fresh tail seq, so it then reapplies its older content over op2's newer intent.
confirmed.evidence: lib/sync/merge.ts:125-136 (plan_days only merges eaten_slots specially); lib/sync/outbox.ts:180-189 (rebaseOp re-enqueues at the tail with client_ts=now); lib/plan-day-client.ts:85-110 (full-row payload plus optimistic rev+1 base); lib/sync/plan-days.ts:34-38 (pull skipped when an op is pending); tsx run of mergeEntity('plan_days', {floor_day:true, swaps:{'meal-1':'a'}}, {floor_day:false, swaps:{'meal-2':'b'}, rev:5, updated_at:'10:05'}, '10:00', '10:05') returned floor_day:false, swaps:{'meal-2':'b'}, so both of A's edits were dropped.
confirmed.fix: Send only the changed plan fields (omit/keep is already supported server-side) and merge swaps/slot_notes/item_overrides per slot. Coalesce successive plan_days ops, or rebase every queued op for the entity on a conflict. After a plan_days conflict or applied settle, re-project the merged row into the legacy store.

confirmed: The core defect holds. lib/sync/merge.ts runs a generic newerWinsFields on plan_days. Only eaten_slots gets a per-slot merge, so swaps, slot_notes and item_overrides are replaced as whole maps. lib/plan-day-client.ts sends all five fields in every payload with base_rev set to the mirror's optimistic rev. The drain in lib/sync/outbox.ts has no guard that stops a second op on the same entity after the first conflicts. syncOnce pulls before it pushes, and applyPulledPlanDay skips a date while an op is pending, so the mirror stays at rev r. The queued ops therefore carry base_revs r and r+1. If a remote device moved the server to r+1, op1 conflicts but op2 matches by coincidence and applies its full-row payload. That overwrites the remote device's swaps and notes with stale content.

No owner ruling or audit accepts this. docs/decisions has nothing on plan_days merge. The only nearby note is docs/specs/coach-undo-receipt.md, which names the stale-phone overwrite as a known risk. The architecture §3.7 merge table has no plan_days row, so the generic newer-wins rule applies by default.

Parts of the finding are overstated. Whole-field newer-wins on floor_day is last-writer-wins by design, because B's full-row payload explicitly carries floor_day. The claim that A's Today stays on stale local values is only transient. The rebased op applies and bumps the server rev, and the next pull projects the merged row into the legacy store.
