Only the plan_days branch (plan-days.ts:34) skips a pulled row when an op is queued for it or the mirror rev is higher. addCups reads the mirror row (water-client.ts:138-149) to compute the next count. I found no feed filter that drops a device's own ops, and no owner ruling that accepts this behaviour. The pull-while-queued timing is plausible, since a tap can land between a push and the next pull.

confirmed.title: Chained log-entry ops aimed at speculative revs overwrite another device's edit (a coach move is silently reverted)
confirmed.defect: A second note edit (and coach move_entry or delete_entry, lib/coach/apply-entries.ts:166) on an entry with a queued op builds its op from the pending op's payload, with base_rev = pending.base_rev + 1, a rev the server only reaches if the first op applies. Both ops go out in one /api/sync/ops batch in seq order. If another device wrote the entry in between, the first op answers 'conflict' and its rebase (log-entry-ops.ts:123) keeps it queued. The second op's base_rev then equals the OTHER device's revision, so apply_sync_op's compare-and-swap passes and writes the phone's stale whole row (local_date, slot, eaten_at, items from rev 2) over the other device's write.
confirmed.failureScenario: The phone is offline and the user types a note on an entry twice: N1 (base 2), then N2 (base 3, payload = N1's row plus the new note). Meanwhile on the tablet the coach moves that entry from 2026-10-09 dinner to 2026-10-10 lunch (server rev 3). The phone comes online and sends [N1, N2]. N1 conflicts with rev 3. N2's base 3 matches, so it applies and rewrites local_date 2026-10-09 and slot dinner. The move is silently undone on the server and on every device, and the meal's calories count on the wrong day. N1's later rebases then join notes onto N2's text, so text the user replaced comes back.
confirmed.evidence: log-note-client.ts:34-39: `if (pending) { ... row = { ...pending.payload, rev: (pending.base_rev ?? 0) + 1 }; }`, then `base_rev: rev` with a payload of serverFields(row). apply_sync_op (20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:472) checks only `v_base <> current rev`. The log_entries upsert branch replaces local_date, slot, eaten_at and items wholesale from the payload (20261025090200_log_entries_title.sql, log_entries branch). drainOutbox (outbox.ts:392-394) sends both ops in one batch, and rebaseLogNote (log-entry-ops.ts:123) re-aims only the conflicting op, not its successor. The known merge.ts:128 'optimistic-rev aliasing' finding names plan_days only. Water and gut_log ops chain the same way.
confirmed.fix: Never let an op aim at a rev only its own predecessor can produce. Either coalesce successive note, move and delete edits into the single pending op for the entry (the user_settings model), or make the drain send at most one op per (entity, entity_id) per batch. When an op for a key answers conflict, rebase every later queued op for that key onto the server's row before sending it.
votes:
confirmed: The code matches the finding and I found no guard that stops it. I did not run a repro.

- **Op construction:** lib/log-note-client.ts:34-39 builds a second note op from the pending op's payload, with rev = pending.base_rev + 1 and base_rev set to that value. lib/coach/apply-entries.ts:166 does the same for move and delete.
- **Batching:** drainOutbox (lib/sync/outbox.ts:360-372) sends every due op in one batch, sorted by seq. The only filter, `drainable`, skips an entry only while its own commit POST is in flight. Nothing holds back a later op on the same entry after an earlier one conflicts.
- **Server:** app/api/sync/ops/route.ts:98 runs each op independently with its own try/catch, and a conflict on one op does not stop the next. apply_sync_op (20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:472) rejects only when base_rev differs from the current rev. After another device writes rev 3, N1 (base 2) conflicts and N2 (base 3) passes the check. N2's payload is serverFields of N1's stale row plus the new note, so it overwrites the other device's local_date, slot and items.
- **Rebase:** rebaseLogNote (lib/sync/log-entry-ops.ts:123) re-aims only the conflicting op, not N2.
- **Rulings:** I found no owner ruling that accepts this. The "optimistic-rev aliasing" finding at merge.ts:128 covers plan_days only.

Trigger conditions are narrow. Two edits to one entry must be queued while offline, and another device must write that entry in between. When both hold, the other device's write is silently reverted. That keeps this at medium.

confirmed: Traced by reading the code; I did not run it. Each step matches the finding.

1. lib/log-note-client.ts:34-39. When an op is already queued for the entry, the second note edit sets `row = {...pending.payload, rev: pending.base_rev + 1}`. It then enqueues N2 with `base_rev` of that value (3 in the scenario) and a payload that is N1's whole row plus the new note.
2. drainOutbox (lib/sync/outbox.ts:360-372) sends every due op in one batch, sorted by seq. `drainable` only skips entries whose commit is in flight, so nothing holds N2 back when N1 conflicts.
3. apply_sync_op (20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:472) checks only `v_base <> current rev`. If another device moved the entry to rev 3, N1 (base 2) returns `conflict`. N2 (base 3) then equals the current rev, so the compare-and-swap passes.
4. N2 goes through `_sync_upsert` with the phone's stale whole-row payload. That payload carries local_date, slot and items from rev 2, so it overwrites the other device's move on the server.
5. rebaseLogNote (lib/sync/log-entry-ops.ts:123) re-aims only the conflicting op (N1). N2 has already applied by then, so there is nothing for it to repair. N1's later note merge then joins onto N2's text.

No owner ruling in docs/decisions or docs/audit accepts this behaviour. Severity medium fits: it is a silent lost update of a move, reachable when two devices edit the same entry while the phone is offline.

confirmed.title: Retiming a log into the spring-forward gap moves it an hour earlier in America/* zones but an hour later in Pacific/Auckland
confirmed.defect: instantAt runs a fixed two-pass offset correction. For a wall-clock time that does not exist (the DST gap), the second pass overshoots back across the transition in zones west of UTC. The time is then saved before the gap, not shifted forward the way JavaScript Date and Temporal 'compatible' disambiguation do. Zones east of UTC land after the gap, so the result depends on the zone. Every manual and coach retime (saveExtraTime, move_entry) and every coach log_meal time goes through this function.
confirmed.failureScenario: An America/Los_Angeles user drags a snack to 02:30 on 2026-03-08 (spring-forward day). instantAt returns 2026-03-08T09:30Z, which is 01:30 PST, and the card then shows 01:30, an hour before the time the user chose. The same drag in Pacific/Auckland on 2026-09-27 gives 03:30 NZDT. A move to 01:30 or 03:30 on that day is unaffected.
confirmed.evidence: Repro: instantAt('2026-03-08','02:30','America/Los_Angeles') -> 2026-03-08T09:30:00Z (01:30 local); instantAt('2026-09-27','02:30','Pacific/Auckland') -> 2026-09-26T14:30:00Z (03:30 local). Pass 1: 02:30Z reads as Mar 7 18:30 PST, +8h -> 10:30Z (03:30 PDT). Pass 2: target 02:30 minus shown 03:30 = -1h -> 09:30Z (01:30 PST), and dateInZone still equals the date, so it is accepted.
confirmed.fix: After the two passes, if the formatted local time does not equal the requested time (a gap), pick the later candidate (the instant + the offset difference), or use the 'compatible' rule: resolve with the offset in force before the transition, then move forward.
votes: confirmed: I copied the instantAt body from lib/coach/apply-shared.ts into a scratch script and ran it. It returned 2026-03-08T09:30:00Z (01:30 PST) for America/Los_Angeles 02:30, and 2026-09-26T14:30:00Z (03:30 NZDT) for Pacific/Auckland 02:30, exactly as reported. The fixed two-pass correction accepts the overshoot because dateInZone still matches the date. A search of docs/decisions and docs/audit found no ruling that accepts this DST-gap behaviour. It is an edge case that only affects a wall-clock time inside the spring-forward gap, and the result flips direction by zone. The earlier-than-chosen result in America/* zones is the clearly wrong one. Low severity stands.

confirmed: I copied the instantAt logic from lib/coach/apply-shared.ts into a snippet and ran it. instantAt('2026-03-08','02:30','America/Los_Angeles') returned 2026-03-08T09:30Z, which shows as 1:30 AM PST, an hour before the requested time. instantAt('2026-09-27','02:30','Pacific/Auckland') returned 2026-09-26T14:30Z, which shows as 3:30 AM NZDT, an hour after. The same nonexistent wall-clock time therefore lands on opposite sides of the gap depending on the zone. The date check passes in both cases, so the result is accepted. The impact is small: only a time inside the DST gap is affected.

confirmed.title: Server day context picks the cached target by the server's UTC date, so east-of-UTC accounts lose their meal layout on the morning a revision is dated
confirmed.defect: serverStoreFor calls settingsWithTargetRevision(baseSettings, targets.revision) with no `today`. The default is todayIso(), which is the server process's local date, and Vercel runs in UTC. activeTargets(admin, userId, date) correctly returns the revision in force on the viewed date. But when that revision's effectiveFrom is later than the server's UTC date, withTargetHistory finds nothing in force on that 'today' and returns activeTargetProfile = null. The history still holds the revision, so resolveTargets(date) still finds the day's macros. mealCountFor/slotListFor/resolveSlotTimes read settings.activeTargetProfile instead, so the server falls back to the 3-meal layout whenever mealsPerDay is unset.
confirmed.failureScenario: Pacific/Auckland account, no meals_per_day set, training 2400 / rest 2100 kcal; the phone shows 4 meals at 08:00, 11:30, 15:00 and 18:30. At 09:00 NZDT on 2026-10-11 (2026-10-10T20:00Z) the user weighs in, which writes a revision dated 2026-10-11. Until 13:00 NZDT, every buildDayContext for 2026-10-11 (coach turn, compose_meal, suggest_options, Plan-sheet ideas, preview_skip) resolves only meal-1@08:00, meal-2@12:30 and meal-3@18:30. Each open slot is sized to one third of the day instead of one quarter: about 700 instead of 525 kcal on a rest day. composeTarget/suggestionTarget for meal-4 find no named slot and fall to remainingMealShare over 3 slots. previewSkip refuses meal-4 because plannedSlotIds lacks it. meal-3 reads as dinner (18:30) on the server but as a snack (15:00) on the phone. The same happens on onboarding day and for Asia/Kolkata before 05:30 IST. This is distinct from the known lib/plan.ts:55 finding (the phone using today's cache for other dates): here the server's cache is wrong even for the account's own today.
confirmed.evidence: Repro (TZ=UTC, system time 2026-10-10T20:00Z, revision effectiveFrom 2026-10-11, training 2400 kcal): settingsWithTargetRevision(base, rev) -> cache null, history 1; resolveDay(store,'2026-10-11') slots = meal-1@08:00, meal-2@12:30, meal-3@18:30. The same revision with today='2026-10-11' (the phone) gives meal-1@08:00, meal-2@11:30, meal-3@15:00, meal-4@18:30. Code: lib/targets/revision.ts:341 `today: string = todayIso()` (getFullYear/getDate, the process zone); lib/plan.ts:58 mealCountFor reads settings.activeTargetProfile?.training?.kcal; lib/plan/slot-share.ts:71 plannedSlotIds -> slotListFor(dayType, store.settings); lib/server/coach-ports.ts:150-157 composeTarget falls back to remainingMealShare when the named slot is missing.
confirmed.fix: In serverStoreFor, pass the viewed date as `today`: settingsWithTargetRevision(baseSettings, targets.revision, date). This makes the cache the revision in force on that date, so the meal count and slot clocks match what the phone shows for that day.
votes: confirmed: The code path is as described. At lib/server/day-context.ts:294 `settingsWithTargetRevision(baseSettings, targets.revision)` is called with no `today`. The default in lib/targets/revision.ts:355 is `todayIso()` from lib/settings/date.ts, which is `localIsoDate(new Date())`, the server process's local date (UTC on Vercel). `withTargetHistory` then calls `revisionOn(history, since, today)`. When the only revision is dated after that server date, nothing is in force, so `withoutCurrentTarget` sets `activeTargetProfile = null` and clears the pins, while the history still holds the revision. `mealCountFor` (lib/plan.ts:55-60) reads `settings.activeTargetProfile?.training?.kcal` when `mealsPerDay` is unset, so it returns 3, and `slotListFor` and `resolveSlotTimes` use that count. `activeTargets(admin, userId, date)` is keyed to the viewed date, so the revision is found there but dropped from the cache. I did not run a repro or read the other call sites it cites (coach-ports, previewSkip, slot-share). The owner ruling in `targetDayFor` says the phone's day governs revision dates, and the code applies no matching rule on the server. I found no upstream guard. I set severity to medium, not high: it needs `mealsPerDay` unset, a revision dated after the server's UTC date, and a window of a few hours. The result is wrong slot layout and sizing, with no data loss.

confirmed: Reproduced. lib/server/day-context.ts:293-294 calls settingsWithTargetRevision(baseSettings, targets.revision) with no `today`, so it defaults to todayIso(), the process-local date (UTC on Vercel). I ran a tsx snippet (scratchpad/repro/tzday.ts) with a revision dated 2026-10-11 (training 2400 kcal), no mealsPerDay, and the server's today set to 2026-10-10. The server-style call gave activeTargetProfile = null and slotListFor returned 3 slots. The same revision with today = 2026-10-11, as the phone passes it, gave a 2400 kcal cache and 4 slots. The cause is in lib/targets/revision.ts. revisionOn finds nothing in force on 10-10, and `since` equals the revision's effectiveFrom (10-11), which is later than today, so it returns null. withTargetHistory then calls withoutCurrentTarget, which clears the cache. lib/plan.ts:55-60 mealCountFor reads activeTargetProfile.training.kcal and falls back to 3 meals when it is missing. The server's slot layout therefore differs from the phone's for the east-of-UTC window between local midnight and UTC midnight on a revision's start date. The harm is limited to accounts with mealsPerDay unset, and it lasts only for that window.

confirmed.title: plan_days pull skip plus a 'duplicate' answer permanently drops another device's change to that day
confirmed.defect: applyPlanDay returns true without writing when any plan_days op for the date is queued, so pullChanges advances and saves the cursor past that change. If the queued op then settles without re-reading the server row, the skipped remote change is never applied. That happens on 'duplicate' (outbox.ts:317 → dropOp → deleteOp only), the expected answer when a push committed but its response was lost; the ops route admits a cut-off batch loses committed results. Nothing re-fetches the row, and no later change for the date arrives to repair it.
confirmed.failureScenario: The phone toggles Floor Day on 2026-10-10 (op P, base 1). P commits on the server as rev 2, but the response is lost, so P stays queued. The tablet ticks meal-1 as eaten (rev 3). The phone's next pass pulls seq 11 (rev 2) and seq 12 (rev 3). Both are skipped because P is pending, and the cursor moves to 12. P is re-pushed and answers 'duplicate', so the op is deleted. The phone's mirror stays at its speculative rev 2 without the tick, and Today (store.days) never shows meal-1 as eaten. That changes the day's rings and totals until some later edit to that date happens to resync it.
confirmed.evidence: Reproduced (scratchpad/repro/plan-dup-skip.test.ts, passing): after pull and the duplicate push, cursor = 12, outbox empty, mirror.rev = 2, and loadStore().days[D].eaten['meal-1'] is undefined. plan-days.ts:34-38 skips the write and returns true; client.ts:323-324 saves the cursor anyway; outbox.ts:317 `return dropOp(h, op); // 'duplicate'` deletes the op without refreshing the row. The known merge.ts:128 finding covers the conflict path, not this skip-then-duplicate loss.
confirmed.fix: When a pulled plan_days change is skipped for a pending op, remember the highest skipped rev for that date (for example in meta). On 'duplicate' (or any settle that does not carry the server row) for a plan_days op, re-read the row, or roll the cursor back to just before the skipped seq, as the restore path does, so the next pull re-applies it. An alternative is to project the newest skipped row once the outbox no longer holds an op for the date.
votes: confirmed: The mechanism holds. applyPlanDay (lib/sync/plan-days.ts:34-38) returns true without writing while a plan_days op is queued for the date. pullChanges (lib/sync/client.ts:263-266, 323-324) then saves the cursor past those changes. A 'duplicate' answer reaches outbox.ts:317, which only calls dropOp and deleteOp. It does not refresh the mirror or the row from the server. Nothing re-fetches the day: plan-cache.ts restoreCachedPlanDays only runs from the mirror after the legacy store is lost, and no other plan_days refresh exists in lib/sync. I also found no owner ruling or audit entry that accepts this behaviour. The only audit hits are about the 'gone' status. The saved repro (scratchpad/repro/plan-dup-skip.test.ts) models this sequence. I could not get its run to finish, so my confirmation rests on reading the code and the repro's assertions. The repro asserts cursor 12, an empty outbox, mirror rev 2 and no tick on Today. Severity is low rather than medium because it needs a lost push response and a second device editing the same date before the next sync. The stale day also repairs itself on the next server change to that date.

confirmed: I re-ran the existing repro in the worktree, copied temporarily into tests/ and removed afterwards, so the repo is unchanged. The vitest file passes and its assertions encode the reported outcome. A pull with a queued plan_days op skips the remote rev 2 and rev 3 rows (plan-days.ts:34-38, returns true with no write). The cursor still advances to 12. The re-push is answered 'duplicate', and outbox.ts:317 `return dropOp(h, op)` deletes the op without re-reading the row. Afterwards the outbox is empty, the mirror is stuck at rev 2, and `loadStore().days[D].eaten['meal-1']` is undefined, so the tablet's tick never reaches the phone. Nothing re-fetches that row, so the loss lasts until a later change to that date arrives. Severity medium is right: it needs a lost push response plus a concurrent edit from a second device, and it is permanent until a later edit to that date.

plausible.title: Caller-side aborts are recorded as `timeout` rows and count toward the shared provider circuit
plausible.defect: A caller abort (`callerAborted`, or `turnAborted` in `generateGrounded`) is a named `AbortError`. `classifyFailure` maps every AbortError to `timeout`. `circuit.ts` counts `timeout` rows in `PROVIDER_FAILURES`, per provider and model across all users, and opens the circuit at 5 in 10 minutes. A user or coach-turn abort is therefore indistinguishable from a provider stall in the ledger.
plausible.failureScenario: The coach turn aborts its lookup hop through `turnAborted` whenever the tool batch stops waiting (`generateGrounded` passes `args.signal`). Five such aborts in 10 minutes, from any accounts, write five `timeout` rows for `google` / `gemini-3.8-flash`. `assertCircuitClosed` then throws 'circuit open' for every user's lookup. That model is also the capture pin and the converse fallback, so capture and coach calls are refused until the window passes. The same applies to Jev calls with a caller signal: five cancelled requests open the Jev circuit for everyone.
plausible.evidence: lib/ai/call.ts:71 `e.name === "AbortError"` returns "timeout". lib/ai/call.ts:111-115 and lib/ai/gemini-grounded.ts `turnAborted` set name = AbortError. lib/ai/circuit.ts:21 `PROVIDER_FAILURES = ["provider_error","timeout","error"]` and :35-50 count per provider and model with no user filter.
votes:
refuted: The mechanism is real: mid-attempt caller aborts are recorded as `timeout` by `classifyFailure`, and `timeout` counts toward the circuit. But this is deliberate, tested behaviour, and the failure scenario does not hold.

- `turnAborted` in `lib/ai/gemini-grounded.ts` is documented as "A turn abort, as the AbortError `classifyFailure` reads as a timeout".
- `lib/ai/adapter.test.ts` (about lines 585-600) asserts that a turn abort writes a zero-cost row with `status: "timeout"`. It is a designed contract.
- The abort sources are all deadline-driven, not user-driven. I read `tool-batch.ts:140` (wall-clock budget exceeded), `fast-path.ts:45` (reply deadline), `final-step.ts:135` (grounding returned late) and the `reply.ts` abort handlers, and all of them abort only after a deadline expires. In those cases the lookup was too slow to finish in time, which is the same condition `withDeadline` already records as `timeout`.
- Opening the circuit after 5 such stalls in 10 minutes is the circuit working as intended. The abort is not a user cancel that gets misread as a provider failure.
- An abort that happens before any attempt starts throws before any row is written, so it never counts.
- The "five cancelled requests open the Jev circuit for everyone" claim has no supporting path. I found no user-initiated cancel feeding `signal` into `callModel` for Jev; `typesafe.ts` passes only `options.signal`, and the coach-turn aborts are the deadline ones above.

At most this is a low-severity labelling imprecision: the ledger does not separate a provider stall from the turn's own wall-clock limit. I found no incorrect circuit opening.

confirmed: The mechanism is real and I traced it in the code. I did not run a repro.

- `attempt` in `lib/ai/call.ts` rejects with `abortError()` (`callerAborted` or `turnAborted`) when the caller's signal aborts mid-flight. The error has `name = "AbortError"`.
- The catch falls through to `record(classifyFailure(lastError), …)`, and `classifyFailure` returns `timeout` for any AbortError.
- `writeAiCall` stores that row with provider and model. `recentFailureCount` in `lib/ai/circuit.ts` counts `timeout` rows by provider and model with no user filter, and opens the circuit at 5 in 10 minutes. So caller aborts are indistinguishable from provider stalls in the ledger and in the circuit.
- The existing test "stops at the turn's own abort… still writes its row" in `lib/ai/adapter.test.ts` (about line 584) pins `status: "timeout"` for a turn abort. The comment on `turnAborted` in `lib/ai/gemini-grounded.ts` says the same: "as the AbortError `classifyFailure` reads as a timeout". The row for an abort is written by design.
- `lib/server/lookup-lane.ts` passes the coach turn's abort signal into `generateGrounded`, and `reply.ts` passes `kit.turnAbort.signal` onward.

Why I rate it low:
- A coach-turn abort on the lookup hop mostly happens because the lookup was slow and the batch stopped waiting. Counting that as a timeout is arguably the intended signal.
- The scenario needs five such aborts from any accounts within 10 minutes. Pure user cancels, which are not provider slowness, are the real false positive.
- A pre-aborted call throws before any row is written, so it does not count.

The "five cancelled requests open the Jev circuit" claim is only true if Jev callers pass a signal that actually aborts. I did not verify that.

plausible.title: Eats-set reads are one unbatched .in() over every ref id, so a large Favored/Eats set can fail the eligible endpoint
plausible.defect: eligibleFoods passes the whole Eats ref list to a single food_refs `.in("id", refIds)`, and again to `.in("catalog_food_id", catalogIds)`. The same pattern is in meal-snapshot.ts snapshotFoods (lines 97-99, 120) and in loadSuggestionEvidence (lib/coach/suggest-policy.ts:105 and the revision and food-key reads). The rest of the codebase batches id reads at ID_BATCH = 100, documented as 'well under any gateway's request-line limit', and uses readByIdBatches or fetchAllChunked.
plausible.failureScenario: An open-world account with many Favored families accumulates a few hundred Eats refs (set_food_membership alone writes up to 50 refs per family). A 300-uuid `.in()` is a URL of about 11 KB. A gateway or PostgREST request-line limit rejects it, so eligibleFoods throws. GET /api/foods/eligible (v1, v2 and v3), candidateFoods and the taste and Favor paths that call it then answer 5xx or 503. The account gets no new suggestions at all, with no partial result.
plausible.evidence: eligible-foods.ts:91-93 `client.from("food_refs").select(...).in("id", refIds)` with refIds = every Eats pref; meal-snapshot.ts:97-99; compare date-chunks.ts ID_BATCH = 100 and candidate-foods.ts readRefFacts, which batches.
plausible.fix: Use readByIdBatches/fetchAllChunked for the food_refs, catalog_food_revisions and user_food_prefs reads in eligibleFoods, snapshotFoods and loadSuggestionEvidence.
votes: uncertain: The code pattern is real. In lib/server/eligible-foods.ts, `.in("id", refIds)` and `.in("catalog_food_id", catalogIds)` take every Eats ref in one call. lib/server/meal-snapshot.ts has the same pattern at lines 97-99 and 120. Other files batch their id reads, for example taste-favor.ts, taste-resolve.ts and mixed-dish-inputs.ts, using ID_BATCH = 100 from date-chunks.ts. I found no cap on the size of the Eats set in lib/foods, eligible-foods.ts or the migrations. The user_food_prefs read is paged, so a large set would reach the unbatched `.in()`. I did not prove the failure. The trigger needs roughly 300-400 or more Eats refs, which is about 12 KB or more of URL. I found no gateway limit documented in the repo, so I could not confirm that such a URL is rejected. Heavy real accounts probably hold tens to low hundreds of refs, so reaching the limit is unlikely today. I also did not run any test against a large Eats set. This is a latent scalability gap, not a demonstrated bug. Other unbatched `.in()` reads (allergen-evidence.ts, export.ts, day-context.ts, log-evidence.ts) show the codebase does not apply batching everywhere. Low severity is right. The fix is cheap: use readByIdBatches.

confirmed: Code confirmed: eligible-foods.ts:93 and :105 issue single unbatched .in() over all Eats refIds and catalogIds (also meal-snapshot.ts:99,100,123 and suggest-policy.ts:99-126), while date-chunks.ts defines ID_BATCH=100 with readByIdBatches for exactly this. No cap on Eats ref count found, and a failed read throws with no partial fallback. The actual gateway rejection at ~11KB URLs could not be exercised read-only, so the 5xx impact is plausible, not demonstrated. Low severity fits.

plausible.title: Pantry items set to 0 g still count as on hand for shopping focus and 'Use what I have'
plausible.defect: The pantry reads for focus keys and for on-hand foods select every live row inside the 14-day box. They ignore confirmed_grams. The pantry API accepts confirmedGrams 0 (nonnegative), which is how a user says the stock is used up, and the planner treats 0 g as no stock (confirmedGrams > 0 everywhere in aggregate.ts and planner.ts).
plausible.failureScenario: A user sets rice to 0 g in the pantry after finishing it. For the next 14 days with focus on, plates containing rice get list/pantry coverage, and 'Use what I have' suggests rice. The shopping planner meanwhile says the pantry has none.
plausible.evidence: lib/server/shopping-focus.ts:75-78 and lib/server/plan-on-hand.ts:56-61 select name,confirmed_at with no grams filter. lib/shopping/focus.ts focusKeysFrom adds a key for every pantry item. lib/shopping/aggregate.ts:132 and lib/shopping/planner.ts:106 use confirmedGrams > 0.
plausible.fix: Skip pantry rows with confirmed_grams equal to 0 in both reads. Treat null (unknown amount) as the owner decides.
plausible.knownBefore: Spec D7 (docs/specs/phase-18-open-world-foods.md:352) defines the pantry time box by confirmed_at and deletion only; no grams condition.
votes: refuted: The code reads are as described. shopping-focus.ts:75-78 and plan-on-hand.ts:56-61 do not filter on confirmed_grams, and the migration check allows >= 0. But the owner spec (docs/specs/phase-18-open-world-foods.md D7, line 352) defines the pantry signal as "14 days after confirmed_at; confirming again restarts it; deleting ends it". Grams are not a condition, and only deletion ends the signal. Pantry photo rows carry confirmedGrams null and deliberately count as on hand ("pantry_photo" source), so the unfiltered read is an intended design, not a slip. The shopping planner's confirmedGrams > 0 checks answer a different question (stock to subtract from the buy quantity). Their wording differs from the D7 presence signal. The 0 g mismatch is a minor spec gap at most. It only nudges ranking, and never changes a safety verdict or hides a food. I did not find a UI path that sets 0 g, though my grep for callers of confirmPantryForLine failed, so that part is unchecked. The finding follows the spec as written, so it is refuted as a bug.

confirmed: Confirmed by code trace. I ran no snippet, because the path is straight reads and filters.

The pantry accepts 0 g. validation.ts:45 allows nonnegative numbers, and the DB check is confirmed_grams >= 0. An update (repository.ts:289-295) stores 0 and resets confirmed_at to now. So a 0 g row is a live row with a fresh 14-day box.

The two focus readers ignore grams. shopping-focus.ts:75-78 and plan-on-hand.ts:56-61 select only name,confirmed_at (plus source). Neither filters on confirmed_grams. focusKeysFrom (focus.ts:154-166) adds a key for every pantry item. readPantry in plan-on-hand.ts returns every row that passes pantryActiveOn, which tests dates only. So a 0 g rice row gives rice a focus key and an on-hand entry for 14 days.

Everything else treats 0 g as no stock. aggregate.ts:132 and planner.ts:119-120 and 309 require grams > 0. ShoppingView.tsx:156 and ShoppingIngredientPicker.tsx:66-67 hide 0 g rows from the confirmed pantry display. So focus disagrees with both the planner and the UI.

The spec's D7 pantry rule (docs/specs/phase-18-open-world-foods.md:346+) says only "14 days after confirmed_at; deleting ends it". It does not address grams, and I found no ruling that accepts the behaviour.

The impact is small: a ranking preference and a suggestion input, not a safety path. Low is right.

A fix would filter out grams = 0 in both readers. Null grams (a photo item with no confirmed amount) is a separate question and arguably should still count as present.

plausible.title: Account with 14+ counted days but no valid observation is reported `held` at the seed instead of `starting` with a null number
plausible.defect: E2 says `starting` applies with fewer than 14 qualified days, or no valid observation yet. In that phase `tdeeKcal` is null and the status is `burn_in`, so the card shows "From your profile". The code returns `status: held`, `phase: provisional` and `tdeeKcal = roundKcal(seed)` for an account that has 14+ counted days but has never had a valid window. A new account that logs food but never weighs is the typical case.
plausible.failureScenario: A user logs 20 complete days and never weighs. The engine returns held/provisional with tdeeKcal = the formula seed and the reason "Holding the starting estimate - ...". In components/TdeeLines.tsx, `learnedLine` labels any `held` row with a non-null tdee as "Last learned" and "Holding steady". The UI therefore shows the formula number as something the app learned.
plausible.evidence: lib/expenditure.ts:433-438 (`held`, `phase: "provisional"`, `tdeeKcal: roundKcal(seed)`) versus docs/specs/phase-16-adaptive-handoff.md E2 rows 1 and 4. TdeeLines.tsx `learnedLine` handles `status === "held"` with `tdeeKcal !== null`.
votes: uncertain: The code does what the finding describes. At lib/expenditure.ts:433-438, an account with 14 or more counted days and no valid observation anywhere in the lookback gets held / provisional / tdeeKcal = seed. That conflicts with the literal wording of E2 row 1 ("no valid observation yet" means starting, null, burn_in). But it is not an accident. The inline comment ("holds at the seed; it is not sent back to 'starting' by a long gap") cites a GPT-6 Sol engine review, finding 2. A test pins the behaviour: tests/expenditure/server-expenditure.test.ts:252 expects held, provisional and 1850. Spec row 4 also lists "else the seed (R8)" under held. R8 only covers a gap after the data was once valid, so the never-valid case, such as someone who logs but never weighs, is not explicitly ruled on. The claimed user harm is weak. When a phase is present, the UI most likely goes through learnedPhaseLine. That line labels the number "Last estimate", marks it stale and shows the reason "Holding the starting estimate - ...", so the formula number is not clearly passed off as learned. I did not trace which path TdeeLines takes, so the "Last learned" label may still appear. Overall this is a real but low-severity spec and UX gap, not a defect.

confirmed: I traced this by reading the code. I did not run a snippet. The engine does what the finding says, but the UI impact is overstated.

**Confirmed.** In `lib/expenditure.ts`, `estimateExpenditure` returns `burn_in` / `starting` / `tdeeKcal: null` only when lifetime qualified days are below 14. Take an account with 14 or more counted days and no weigh-ins, so the 14-day and 28-day windows are both invalid. The `pointOn` lookback over the last `HELD_LOOKBACK_DAYS` finds no earlier valid point. The engine then falls through to the last return, which gives `status: held`, `phase: provisional`, `tdeeKcal: roundKcal(seed)` and the reason "Holding the starting estimate - ...". Spec E2 row 1 says `starting` also applies when there is "no valid observation yet". Spec row 4 (`held`) covers an observation "invalid after it was once valid". The code contradicts row 1 for a never-valid account.

**Intent.** The code comment above that return says it is deliberate: an account that has earned 14 counted days "holds at the seed; it is not sent back to 'starting' by a long gap." R8 in `docs/decisions/2026-10-04-adaptive-handoff-rulings.md` only says "else the seed". It does not rule on a never-valid account. So this looks like a spec/code mismatch that was chosen on purpose, not an owner-ruled behaviour.

**UI claim is wrong.** In `components/TdeeLines.tsx`, `learnedPhaseLine` handles `held` as label "Last estimate", `stale: true`, no meter, with the detail text "Holding the starting estimate - ...". It does not say "Last learned" or "Holding steady". The formula number is not shown as something the app learned. The visible effect is a stale-styled number with honest wording, where the spec wanted "From your profile".

I rate it low: spec mismatch with minor presentation impact, and no wrong target or proposal. `proposalEligible` is false in this branch.

plausible.title: Recipe catalog cap counts every historical revision, so republishing can take the whole recipe catalog offline
plausible.defect: searchCatalog() pages all rows of recipe_catalog_revisions (superseded and withdrawn included) against a hard cap of 64. hydrate() then drops every non-current revision. Selections hold foreign keys to old revisions, so old revisions must stay in the table.
plausible.failureScenario: The 24-recipe pilot has headroom now. Once enough recipes get new revisions (for example 24 recipes with 3 revisions each = 72 rows), searchCatalog throws 503 recipe_catalog_cap. Search, detail-by-search, the shopping planner and the coach all fail, although fewer than 64 recipes are published.
plausible.evidence: lib/recipe-catalog/repository.ts:91-111: the query has no filter on current revisions, and 'revisions.length > pilotCap' throws. hydrate() at :35-56 filters on root.current_revision_id afterwards.
plausible.fix: Filter to current revisions (join to recipe_catalog.current_revision_id and publication_state = 'published') in the query, or apply the cap after hydration.
votes: confirmed: The mechanism is real. searchCatalog (lib/recipe-catalog/repository.ts:91-111) pages all of recipe_catalog_revisions with no current-revision filter and throws 503 recipe_catalog_cap when more than 64 rows come back. hydrate() drops non-current revisions only after that check. Old revisions must stay in the table because of the on-delete-restrict foreign keys from items, steps and selections. Revisions accumulate: scripts/repair-recipe-food-mapping.ts:185 inserts new revisions for existing recipes, and the unique (recipe_id, rev) constraint allows many per recipe. The seeder creates one revision per recipe, so the table currently holds about 24 rows. No ruling accepts the behaviour. The cap is described as a deliberate "reviewed pilot limit" that fails loudly, and tests/recipe-catalog/pagination.test.ts:52 pins the over-cap error, but nothing says superseded rows should count toward it. I did not run the test. The impact is a latent outage that needs roughly 40 extra revisions, which has no current production path other than the repair script. Low severity is right.

refuted: The premise fails. searchCatalog runs on the signed-in user's Supabase client, not the admin client. The callers (app/api/recipes/route.ts, lib/server/recipe-plan.ts, lib/server/coach-ports.ts) pass that auth client; recipe-plan.ts:113 says "All account reads above use the auth client". Row-level security on recipe_catalog_revisions (migration 20261127090000_recipe_catalog_shopping.sql:403-406) lets authenticated users select only a revision whose root is published and whose current_revision_id equals that revision. Superseded, withdrawn and draft revisions are invisible to this query. The paged read therefore returns at most one row per published recipe, so the 64-row cap counts published recipes. Old revisions can pile up in the table (the repair script and seeding insert new ones), but they never reach the count. 24 recipes with 3 revisions each would still read as 24 rows. Hydrate()'s later filter is redundant for this path, since RLS already removed those rows. The pinned-revision path (getPinnedRecipeRevisions) does not use the cap. The cap does count published recipes, so a catalog of more than 64 published recipes would throw 503 recipe_catalog_cap. That is deliberate and documented in the code comment, not the finding's defect. One residual: if searchCatalog were ever called with a service-role client, the finding's scenario would apply. No such caller exists in the repo. I did not run a database test, so this rests on the migration policy and the call sites.

plausible.title: Every sync pass triggers an uncoalesced, unthrottled full server snapshot recompute on Today
plausible.defect: Today re-runs `loadEligibleLocalFoodIds` on every SYNCED_EVENT with no dedupe, throttle or in-flight coalescing. Every sync pass dispatches SYNCED_EVENT in its `finally`, including no-op passes. Only an open-world v3 snapshot can be served from a held copy. Closed accounts store a v2 snapshot, and `heldOpenSet` rejects anything that is not v3, so they always do a network round trip.
plausible.failureScenario: A closed-world user ticks four meals in a row, or switches back to the app. Each save triggers a sync pass 1.5 s later (SAVE_DEBOUNCE_MS), and a `runAgain` pass follows. Each pass dispatches SYNCED_EVENT, so each one fires GET /api/foods/eligible?v=3. The server runs `mealSnapshot`, which does a paged Eats read, a policy-evidence load, 90-day history affinity and the facets read. There are also two rate-limit RPCs per request. In-flight requests overlap, because `latestRead` only discards stale results and does not cancel them. The route allows 30 requests per minute per user, so a burst yields 429s. `readEligible` then sets `starterGate` to 'unavailable', and the 'Couldn't check your food rules' / retry notice shows on Today.
plausible.evidence: app/page.tsx:268-311 (`readEligible` registered on SYNCED_EVENT, no throttle, unlike the `wait()`/`lastKey` dedupe in components/MyFoods.rule-marks.ts). lib/sync/client.ts:522 dispatches SYNCED_EVENT after every pass. lib/foods/eligible-client.ts:232 returns `held:false` for any non-v3 stored snapshot, so a closed account never reuses its stored v2. app/api/foods/eligible/route.ts limits to 30 per minute per user.
votes:
uncertain: The mechanism is real, but the stated impact is overstated.

What holds:
- app/page.tsx registers `readEligible` on SYNCED_EVENT with no throttle or dedupe, and `latestRead` only drops stale results.
- lib/sync/client.ts dispatches SYNCED_EVENT in the `finally` of every pass, including no-op passes.
- `heldOpenSet` in lib/foods/eligible-client.ts returns no set for any stored snapshot that is not v3. A closed account therefore does a network GET /api/foods/eligible?v=3 after every pass.

What does not hold:
- Passes already coalesce. A second `syncOnce` call during a running pass only sets `runAgain`, so there is at most one follow-up pass per burst. Each pass needs a push or pull round trip, and the save debounce is 1.5 s.
- Reaching the 30/min per-user limit in app/api/foods/eligible/route.ts needs about 30 completed passes in 60 s. Four meal ticks do not get close.
- Even if a 429 occurs, the catch block keeps the last good eligible set. It shows only a retry notice, which clears on the next successful read.
- Snapshot invalidation on local writes is by design (the `lib/sync/idb.ts` hook forgets the snapshot). A refetch after a real change is intended. Only the refetch after a no-op pass is wasteful.

What remains is minor redundant server work for closed accounts, not a request storm that breaks Today. I found no owner ruling in docs/audit or docs/decisions that accepts it. I did not run the route or tests.

confirmed: I traced this by reading the code. I did not run it. The mechanism is real, but the 429 consequence is overstated.

Confirmed:
- app/page.tsx registers `readEligible` on SYNCED_EVENT. It has no throttle, no dedupe and no in-flight coalescing. `latestRead` only discards stale results.
- lib/sync/client.ts:522 dispatches SYNCED_EVENT in a `finally` after every pass, no-op passes included.
- In lib/foods/eligible-client.ts, `heldOpenSet` returns `{set: null}` unless the stored snapshot has `schemaVersion === 3`. A closed account stores v2, so it never reuses it. Every `readEligibleOnce` call therefore does `accountFetch("/api/foods/eligible?v=3")`.
- Each pass causes one full server snapshot recompute. The route also runs two rate-limit calls per request (per-IP 120/min, per-user 30/min).
- Overlapping requests are possible, since nothing cancels an in-flight read.

Not confirmed:
- The 429 and "Couldn't check your food rules" outcome needs more than 30 requests in 60 seconds from one user.
- Ticking four meals in a row gives roughly 4 to 8 passes, because of the 1.5 s save debounce plus `runAgain`. That is well under 30.
- If a 429 did happen, `!response.ok` would throw and `setStarterGate("unavailable")` would show the notice. That consequence is plausible only in unusual bursts.

What remains is a modest, real inefficiency: redundant, uncoalesced server recomputes per sync pass for closed-world accounts. I rate it low severity, not medium.

I found no owner ruling that accepts this behaviour. Fix would be a short throttle or coalescing on the SYNCED_EVENT read, or reusing a fresh stored v2 snapshot.

plausible.title: Pulling plan days costs one full-store parse and write plus a whole-outbox read per change
plausible.defect: `applyPulledPlanDay` runs once per pulled plan_days change. Each call does `getAll()` on the whole outbox to look for one pending op. It then calls `loadStore()`, which re-reads localStorage and does `JSON.parse` plus `normalizeStore` on every call, and `saveStoreFor`, which does a full `JSON.stringify` and `setItem` of the whole store. The cost per change grows with the store size and the outbox length, so a bulk pull is quadratic.
plausible.failureScenario: A new device, or one that cleared its cursor, pulls a year or more of plan_days in 500-row pages. Every row triggers an outbox scan, a full-store parse and a full-store write to localStorage on the main thread. The first sync freezes the UI for seconds. The same holds for `restoreCachedPlanDays` at startup (lib/sync/plan-cache.ts:27 reads the entire outbox per cached day).
plausible.evidence: lib/sync/plan-days.ts:28-31 (`tx.objectStore(OUTBOX_STORE).getAll()` per change) and 44-52 (`loadStore()` then `saveStoreFor`). lib/store.ts:178-181 (`loadStore` always `JSON.parse`s). lib/sync/client.ts:262-266 (called per change in the pull loop).
votes: uncertain: Partly refuted, partly true. FALSE part: loadStore() (lib/store.ts:~160-181) returns the in-memory `cached` store when it belongs to the current account. It only does JSON.parse and normalizeStore on a cold start, after an account change, or when no cache exists. So "parse + normalize on every call" does not hold for a normal pull loop. TRUE part: applyPulledPlanDay (lib/sync/plan-days.ts:28-31) calls getAll() on the whole outbox for each change. It also calls saveStoreFor -> saveStore, which does a full JSON.stringify and localStorage.setItem of the entire store per change (store.ts:247). There is no batching or debounce. restoreCachedPlanDays (plan-cache.ts:27) likewise reads the whole outbox per cached day and writes the store per restored day. So the cost is O(changes x store size), plus O(changes x outbox length). The outbox is normally near-empty on a fresh device, which is the scenario the finding names. The store stringify is the real cost. For a year of plan days, that is hundreds of writes of a store of unknown size. This is a plausible minor perf inefficiency, not a correctness bug. It is not a multi-second freeze: the pull loop awaits IDB transactions between changes. No owner ruling or audit accepts it. I found no measurement. Low-severity, unmeasured perf issue; the stated mechanism is overstated.

confirmed: I traced the call path in the code and did not run a timing repro. The code does what the finding says. In lib/sync/client.ts:263-264 the pull loop awaits `applyPulledPlanDay` once per plan_days change. Each call (lib/sync/plan-days.ts:28-31) does a whole-outbox `getAll()`. It then calls `loadStore()`. In lib/store.ts, `loadStore` returns the cache only for an unbound account or after a failed persist. Otherwise it reads localStorage and runs `JSON.parse` and `normalizeStore` every time, so the in-memory `cached` copy is not used on this path. `saveStoreFor` then calls `saveStore`, which does a full `JSON.stringify` and `setItem` (store.ts:247). The store grows by one day per pulled row, so a bulk pull is quadratic in rows. `restoreCachedPlanDays` (plan-cache.ts:27-38) has the same per-day outbox `getAll()` and `loadStore()` plus `saveStoreFor`. Severity stays low. This is a performance cost on first sync or a cleared cursor, not a correctness bug, and no owner ruling accepts it. I did not measure how long the freeze lasts.

plausible.title: media-sweep deletes any storage path named in a media_objects row, and users can insert such rows for arbitrary paths
plausible.defect: The media_objects_rw policy lets an authenticated user insert or update rows where user_id equals their own id. The path column is the primary key and nothing ties it to the user's folder, and created_at and entry_id are also writable. app/api/jobs/media-sweep/route.ts selects unattached rows older than 24h and calls deleteMedia(admin, row.path), which removes objectKey(path) from the bucket with the service-role client. It never checks that the path starts with the row's own user_id. A user can also set entry_id on their own rows to exempt them from the sweep.
plausible.failureScenario: Account A inserts a media_objects row with path = 'media/<B-uid>/<known-uuid>.jpg', user_id = A, created_at backdated more than 24h and entry_id null. The next daily sweep deletes B's stored capture image. This needs B's object path (a random uuid), so it is not practically guessable today. The sweep still lets a row owner trigger a service-role delete outside their own folder, which is a missing owner binding.
plausible.evidence: 20260920090100_phase4_media_bucket.sql:28-31 (media_objects_rw for all, grant insert/update/delete to authenticated, path is the primary key). media-sweep/route.ts:75-85 (select path only, deleteMedia(row.path)). lib/server/media.ts:90-100 (deleteMedia has no owner or prefix check).
plausible.fix: Select user_id with path in the sweep and skip, with an error log, any row whose objectKey does not start with `${user_id}/`. Add a CHECK constraint or WITH CHECK clause that path starts with 'media/' || user_id || '/'. Also consider restricting the storage.objects media_own_folder policy to select/delete, since direct client uploads skip the media_objects row and the sweep.
votes:
confirmed: The missing owner binding is real, but exploiting it needs the victim's object path, which is unguessable. Nothing I found blocks the insert.

- **Insert is open.** `media_objects_rw` (supabase/migrations/20260920090100_phase4_media_bucket.sql) allows any authenticated user to insert, update and delete rows where `user_id` is their own id. `path` is a free-text primary key and `created_at` and `entry_id` are client-writable.
- **No later guard.** The only later trigger on the table is `same_owner` (20261103090100). It checks `entry_id` against `user_id` only, and the 20261218090200 migration only adds an index. Nothing ties `path` to the row owner's folder. I found nothing in docs/decisions covering this table.
- **Sweep trusts the path.** `app/api/jobs/media-sweep/route.ts` selects `path` from rows with null `entry_id` older than 24h. It calls `deleteMedia(admin, row.path)`, which runs `admin.storage.remove([objectKey(path)])` with the service role. `objectKey` only strips a `media/` prefix. `deleteMedia` has no owner check, unlike the download helper in `lib/server/media.ts`, which checks `key.split("/")[0] === userId`.
- **Why low.** Storage RLS (`media_own_folder`) stops the attacker deleting the object directly. The sweep bypasses it. The attacker needs the victim's `<uid>/<uuid>.<ext>` path, and I found no path in the app that exposes it to other users. The impact is also limited to one stored capture image.

A fix would add a check that `split_part(path,'/',2)` (or the key's first segment) equals `user_id`, in the table's check constraint or a trigger, or a prefix check in the sweep.

refuted: The missing binding is real. The media_objects_rw policy only checks user_id, nothing ties path to the user's folder, and deleteMedia in lib/server/media.ts removes any path with the service role. But the stated attack does not work. path is the table's primary key. signUpload inserts a media_objects row for every object before it creates the upload URL, and the sweep only tombstones rows (deleted_at), never deletes them. So when B's object exists, B's row already holds path 'media/<B-uid>/<uuid>.ext'. A's insert of the same path then fails with a unique violation. A's update or upsert of that row is hidden by RLS (user_id = auth.uid()), and the same-owner migration 20261103090100 adds no path check. A can only claim a path that has no row yet, and in normal operation every stored object has a row. The one gap is a row B deleted himself, which is B's own action. Exploiting it would also need B's random uuid object name. I traced this by reading the code and did not run a repro. At most this is a defense-in-depth hardening gap (a path-prefix check or CHECK constraint), not a reproducible cross-account delete.

plausible.title: Restore op on a missing local row can roll the cursor back to -1 and break pull permanently
plausible.defect: For a restore that the server treats as an idempotent no-op, apply_sync_op returns seq = coalesce(max(change_log.seq ...), 0). The client does `setCursor(h, result.seq - 1)` when `!local`. With seq 0 the cursor becomes -1, and /api/sync/changes rejects since=-1 (`^\d+$`) with 400. The pull then throws every pass, and because pull runs before push, sync stops entirely. Even for a normal seq it rewinds the cursor to just before that entity's last change and re-downloads the whole feed since then.
plausible.failureScenario: A restore op is acknowledged for a live row that has no change_log rows (a directly written row) and no local mirror row. The cursor is set to -1 and every later syncOnce fails at pull with 400 `since must be a non-negative integer`.
plausible.evidence: outbox.ts:256-262; app/api/sync/changes/route.ts parseCount regex; rpc.sql restore branch `coalesce((select max(seq) ...), 0)`.
plausible.fix: Clamp with Math.max(0, result.seq - 1), and only rewind when result.seq > 0.
votes: refuted: The seq-0 branch cannot be reached through the sync path, and the ordinary rewind is deliberate. The only way to get seq 0 is a restore on a live row with no change_log rows. A client only queues a restore after it has seen or made a tombstone. The client gets a tombstone from its own delete op or from a pull, and both write a change_log row. Nothing prunes change_log: I found no migration that deletes from it. So max(seq) for that entity key is at least 1 whenever a restore is legitimately queued. The "directly written row" in the failure scenario is not something a client can tombstone and then restore. For a normal seq, outbox.ts:256-262 rolls the cursor back on purpose, with a comment saying so, to re-fetch the entity's snapshot. That costs a re-download and breaks nothing. setCursor has no guard against a negative value, and the code has no defensive clamp (result.seq - 1 would be -1 for seq 0). That is a latent hardening gap, not a reachable defect.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run it. The path is real: lib/sync/outbox.ts:256-262, restore branch with no local row. The code sets the cursor to `result.seq - 1` whenever that is below the current cursor, with no clamp. `setCursor` in lib/sync/idb.ts:493 stores the value as given. In `apply_sync_op` (supabase/migrations/20260919090300_phase3_sync_entities.sql:466-470), a restore on a row that is not tombstoned returns `seq = coalesce(max(change_log.seq) for that entity/key, 0)`. If the row has no change_log entries (for example a legacy-backfilled or directly written row), seq is 0. The client then stores cursor -1, because `0 - 1 < cursor` for any cursor >= 0. `pullChanges` (lib/sync/client.ts:248) then requests `/api/sync/changes?since=-1`. The route's `parseCount` (app/api/sync/changes/route.ts:18-23) rejects it with 400 `since must be a non-negative integer`. The cursor is persisted, so every later pull hits the same 400 until it is repaired. With a normal seq the cursor rewinds to just before that entity's last change, which is harmless: it re-pulls the feed and the code comment says that is intended. Severity stays low because three conditions must hold together. The server must have no change_log row for the entity. The restore op must still be queued. The local mirror row must be gone. Normal ops always write change_log, so this needs legacy or direct-write data. I found no owner ruling that accepts this behavior. A fix is a clamp such as `Math.max(0, result.seq - 1)`, or skipping the rewind when seq is 0.

plausible.title: Signed upload URL is documented as 60 s but Supabase issues a 2-hour token
plausible.defect: `signUpload` returns `expiresInSeconds: 60` and `SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS = 60`. `createSignedUploadUrl` takes no expiry option, and the token it returns is valid for the Storage default of about 2 hours. The row stores the declared size, but the real upload can be any size up to 8 MB.
plausible.failureScenario: A leaked or logged upload URL stays usable for about 2 hours, not 60 s. The client trusts the 60 s figure and the declared `bytes` is only a claim, so the `media_objects.bytes` accounting can be wrong by up to 8 MB per object.
plausible.evidence: lib/server/media.ts:20 `SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS = 60`. lib/server/media.ts:57-69 `createSignedUploadUrl(objectKey(path))` with no expiry argument, then `expiresInSeconds: SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS`.
plausible.fix: Stop reporting a fixed 60 s, or enforce it on the server. Treat `bytes` as advisory, or read the real size from storage metadata when the row is attached or swept.
plausible.knownBefore: docs/audit/2026-09-13 (findings-full.json, same finding) and docs/plans/2026-09-11-phase-3-4/lane-M-capture-server.md Open Question #1 ("accept as documented")
votes: refuted: The technical claim is accurate: createSignedUploadUrl takes no expiry, so the 60 s figure is only a label and the token lives about 2 hours. This is not a new bug, though. The 2026-09-13 audit (docs/audit/2026-09-13/findings-full.json ~3755-3765) reported the same finding, and docs/plans/2026-09-11-phase-3-4/lane-M-capture-server.md:3462 (Open Question #1) records the decision "accept as documented". The enforced boundary is the owner-folder path scoping, the media_objects row, and the 24 h sweep. The impact is also narrow. The URL is for one random-UUID object under the caller's own uid and upsert is off, so a completed upload cannot be overwritten. Reads re-check ownership. The bucket's own file_size_limit and allowed_mime_types (migration 20260920090100) cap the real upload size, so the bytes accounting error is bounded. Nothing depends on the 60 s figure for a security decision.

confirmed: The code matches the finding, but I did not issue a real token. The 2-hour lifetime comes from Supabase Storage's default, which I know of but did not measure. In lib/server/media.ts, `SIGNED_UPLOAD_SECONDS = 60` is only a constant echoed back as `expiresInSeconds`. The installed storage-js (2.117.2) `createSignedUploadUrl(path, options)` accepts only `{ upsert }`, so there is no way to set an expiry. It POSTs an empty body to `/object/upload/sign/...`, and the server picks the lifetime, which is its default of about 2 hours. So the documented 60 s is not enforced. The declared `bytes` is only a claim: `media_objects.bytes` stores the declared value, and the bucket allows up to 8 MB (`file_size_limit` 8388608, with a MIME allowlist), so the stored size can differ from the real upload by up to 8 MB. Impact is limited. The URL is bound to one server-generated path (`<uid>/<uuid>.<ext>`), upsert is not enabled, and a second upload to the same path should be refused. The bucket caps size and MIME type. The server re-validates the content in `lib/media/validate.ts` before using it. So this is a low-severity mismatch between the documented and actual expiry, plus loose size accounting.

plausible.title: client_timings check constraints re-added without NOT VALID, a full-table scan under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE with no lock or statement timeout
plausible.defect: The migration drops and re-adds client_timings_path_check and client_timings_step_check as ordinary validated CHECKs. ADD CONSTRAINT then scans the whole table while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. client_timings is the append-only telemetry table that every capture, scan, log and coach hop writes to. The file also lacks the 'set local lock_timeout / statement_timeout' preamble every other recent migration uses. Its header claims 'Live-safe: a check widened, no data moved', which is false for the lock.
plausible.failureScenario: With a large client_timings table, the migration blocks every concurrent POST /api/timings insert for the duration of two full scans. With no lock_timeout it can also queue behind a long-running reader. While it waits, it blocks all new inserts behind itself, the lock-queue convoy.
plausible.evidence: 20261229090000_client_timings_plan_chips.sql:8-19 has 'alter table client_timings drop constraint if exists ...; add constraint ... check (...)' twice and no NOT VALID, no VALIDATE step and no set local lock_timeout. The convention in 20261217090000 and 20261224090000 is NOT VALID, then a separate VALIDATE file.
plausible.fix: Add 'set local lock_timeout = 3s' and use 'add constraint ... not valid', then validate in a follow-up file. Because the constraints are only widened, existing rows already satisfy them.
plausible.knownBefore: Same pattern in migrations 20261021090000 and 20261023092000, already applied.
votes:
refuted: The mechanics are true. The migration re-adds validated CHECKs, which scan the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and it has no lock_timeout. But the claimed failure does not hold up in practice.

- The same drop-and-add pattern was already used on this table in 20261021090000_client_timings_dictation.sql and 20261023092000_client_timings_attach_step.sql. No ruling or audit flags it.
- The table holds only short, bounded telemetry rows. Only a handful of accounts exist, so each scan lasts milliseconds.
- The header says order does not matter, and telemetry is lossy by design. POST /api/timings answers 202 whatever the insert does, so a brief stall can lose measurements but never blocks a user's tap.
- Reads of this table go through a service-role script, so no user-facing reader can queue behind the lock.

The "lock-queue convoy" scenario needs a long-running transaction on a tiny telemetry table, which is not a realistic risk. The header's "live-safe" wording is loose, but this is style drift, not a defect.

confirmed: Read the migration at supabase/migrations/20261229090000_client_timings_plan_chips.sql. It drops and re-adds client_timings_path_check and client_timings_step_check as ordinary validated CHECKs. It has no NOT VALID, no VALIDATE step and no set local lock_timeout or statement_timeout. In Postgres, ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK without NOT VALID scans the whole table while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Two such scans run in one transaction. While the migration waits for or holds that lock, new POST /api/timings inserts queue behind it. The header's "Live-safe" claim holds for data (nothing is moved) but not for locking. I did not run it against a database. The 20261229 file does lack the timeout preamble that the 2026122* migrations 20261220090300 and 20261226090000 also lack, so the "every other recent migration uses one" claim is overstated. Severity stays low for three reasons. Earlier migrations in this family (20261021090000 and 20261023092000) used the same drop and re-add pattern. The table is narrow, append-only telemetry. Inserts that fail only lose measurements, since the route answers 202 and the insert is dropped. Impact is a short, self-clearing stall that grows with table size, and the table has no retention job.

plausible.title: Oura 401 refresh path cannot actually refresh and can silently drop rotated tokens
plausible.defect: pullTwoDays fires three ouraGet calls in Promise.all, each with `refresh: () => accessTokenFor(admin, source)` using the ORIGINAL `source` snapshot. accessTokenFor only exchanges when the snapshot's expires_at is within the skew; otherwise it returns the same (rejected) access token, so the 'one refresh then retry' on 401 retries the same bad token. If the token was near expiry, up to four concurrent exchanges reuse the same single-use refresh token (the initial call plus three 401 refreshes). The CAS write `.eq('oauth', source.oauth)` has its result discarded (`void data`), so when it matches 0 rows (a concurrent rotation or reconnect already changed the column) the newly issued pair is returned but never stored.
plausible.failureScenario: Oura invalidates an access token early (revocation/clock skew) while expires_at still looks valid: all three requests 401, the refresh callback returns the same token, the pull throws 'Oura daily_activity failed with 401' every day and the cron marks the source as failed/retry forever. Separately, after a rotation lost the CAS race the DB still holds a consumed refresh token, and the next pull fails exchange_failed until the user reconnects.
plausible.evidence: oura.ts:104-117 (`.update({oauth: sealOauth(rotated)}).eq('id', source.id).eq('oauth', source.oauth); ... void data;` and the early return at 98-100), oura.ts:130-133 (`Promise.all([ouraGet(...)x3])` with `refresh: async () => accessTokenFor(admin, source, ...)`), lib/oura/client.ts:28-31 (single refresh-then-retry on 401).
plausible.fix: Give accessTokenFor a `force` flag used by the 401 callback, share one in-flight refresh promise per source within a pull, serialize the three reads (or refresh once up front), and check that the CAS update matched one row (re-read the winner's tokens when it did not).
votes: uncertain: The code facts hold, but the impact is overstated and the main scenarios depend on rare conditions. Confirmed: `refresh` in `pullTwoDays` (lib/server/oura.ts:130-133) calls `accessTokenFor` with the original `source` snapshot. That returns the same access token whenever `expires_at` is outside the 5-minute skew, so a 401 on a still-valid-looking token retries with the same token and throws. The CAS write also discards its result (`void data`), so a 0-row match would lose a rotated pair. Not confirmed, for these reasons. (1) "Fails every day forever" is wrong. The initial `accessTokenFor` call at line 128 already refreshes any token that is near expiry, and it hands the fresh token to all three calls. So the "up to four concurrent exchanges" case needs a 401 on a freshly rotated token. A token that was revoked early but still looks valid heals itself once `expires_at` passes and the next pull exchanges normally. (2) Concurrent rotation is serialised. The cron route (app/api/jobs/oura-pull/route.ts:70) takes a per-(job, user, date) `claimLock` before `pullTwoDays`, so two cron pulls for the same account cannot race. The only other caller is the OAuth callback (app/api/health/oura/callback/route.ts:56), which pulls right after connect with brand-new tokens. A lost CAS therefore needs a callback pull overlapping a cron pull on the same account, or a reconnect mid-pull. (3) No owner ruling or earlier audit in docs/ covers this. Net result: a real but low-impact robustness gap, a no-op 401 refresh plus an unchecked CAS on a narrow race window. It is not a medium correctness bug.

confirmed: I confirmed this by tracing the code in lib/server/oura.ts and lib/oura/client.ts. I did not run a repro snippet.

1. The 401 refresh does not refresh. pullTwoDays passes `refresh: () => accessTokenFor(admin, source)` (oura.ts:133), and `source` is the original snapshot. accessTokenFor (oura.ts:105-107) returns `current.access_token` unchanged whenever the snapshot's expires_at is outside the skew window. Nothing forces an exchange. So if Oura rejects a token early, ouraGet retries with the same token (client.ts:33-37) and gets a second 401. The code then throws `Oura <path> failed with 401`, because 401 is not retryable (client.ts:39-42). This repeats on every pull until the stored expiry passes.

2. The near-expiry case also fails. The first accessTokenFor call in pullTwoDays (line 130) may rotate the tokens and write them to the DB. The `source` object is never updated. If a request then 401s, the callback re-opens the stale snapshot. That snapshot is still within the skew, so it exchanges the old, already-consumed refresh token, which fails. The three parallel ouraGet calls can each trigger this, so up to three extra exchanges can reuse one single-use refresh token.

3. A lost CAS write is not detected. The update at oura.ts:112-116 has no `.select()`, so it cannot report how many rows matched, and `void data` discards the result. If a concurrent rotation or reconnect changed `oauth`, 0 rows match. The new token pair is still returned and used for this run but never stored. The DB then holds a consumed refresh token, and the next pull fails on exchange until the user reconnects.

Severity is lowered to low. The 401 case needs Oura to invalidate a token before its stated expiry. The CAS race needs two writers on the same source at once, which is rare, and other code (not checked) may serialize pulls per source.

plausible.title: Gemini provider error detail (300 chars) is persisted and logged
plausible.defect: geminiHttpError appends detail.trim().slice(0,300) from the SDK error message to the ProviderHttpError. That message becomes ai_calls.error (call.ts:297, recorded verbatim) and is logged in plan-inspire, plan-document and pantry-photo. Gemini 400/INVALID_ARGUMENT messages can describe or quote the offending request part. The calls carry health context, food photos and documents. The OpenRouter transport was changed to status-only for exactly this reason.
plausible.failureScenario: A Gemini 400 for a coach, document or photo call includes a fragment of the user's text or filename. The first 300 chars of it land in ai_calls.error and in server logs.
plausible.evidence: adapter.ts:103-106: const suffix = ...`: ${detail.trim().slice(0, 300)}`; return new ProviderHttpError(status, `gemini ${status}${suffix}`); call.ts:297: const message = lastError.message; record(..., message, ...). openrouter.ts:127-132 documents why the body is never read.
plausible.fix: Keep the status and the provider's error code only, or redact. If provider detail is needed for debugging, store a short allowlisted reason.
votes: uncertain: The code is as described. lib/ai/adapter.ts:102-106 appends up to 300 chars of the SDK error message, and lib/ai/call.ts:297 records that message into ai_calls.error. The OpenRouter transport (openrouter.ts:126-131) was deliberately changed to status only because a 4xx body can echo the prompt. Two things weaken the finding. (1) There is no ruling or audit that accepts the Gemini behaviour, and I found no test or doc claiming Gemini detail is safe. (2) The detail is used on purpose. adapter.ts:101 says it keeps the provider's words so a 503 that is really a schema complaint stays diagnosable. failures.ts:isPermissionDeniedFailure matches /permission denied|denied access/ against e.message, so dropping the body outright would break the circuit breaker and fallback logic. The leak itself is speculative. Gemini INVALID_ARGUMENT text is usually generic: field paths, schema or MIME complaints, token limits. I did not find evidence that it quotes user content. Net: a real inconsistency and a cheap hardening item (keep a status-plus-allowlisted-code summary, such as the permission-denied marker), but low severity and not demonstrated as a leak.

confirmed: I confirmed the code path by reading it. I did not run it live, and I could not show that Gemini actually quotes user content. `geminiHttpError` (lib/ai/adapter.ts:101-106) appends `detail.trim().slice(0,300)` from the SDK error message to the `ProviderHttpError`. `callModel` (lib/ai/call.ts:297) passes `lastError.message` unchanged to `record(...)`, so it reaches `ai_calls.error`. The same message is printed to server logs: plan-document.ts:109-111 logs `e.message.slice(0,300)`, and plan-inspire.ts:135 has a similar `console.error`. The OpenRouter transport (openrouter.ts:127-132) deliberately sends only the status, and its comment gives the reason: a 4xx body can echo the rejected request, which may carry health data. Gemini calls carry the same kind of data, so the two transports are inconsistent. The comment on `geminiHttpError` says it keeps the provider's own words on purpose. The 403 `PERMISSION_DENIED` detection in failures.ts:58-62 depends on that text. No owner ruling accepts logging the Gemini body. Impact is limited: the 300-character cap, Gemini 400 messages usually name fields or schema problems rather than quote content, and the storage is a server-side table and logs. The exposure is realistic, but I did not observe a message that quotes user content.

plausible.title: Deployment-wide HEALTH_TZ is applied as a day/week zone to accounts with no stored time_zone
plausible.defect: weekStartOf, todayIso and accountZones resolve a null user_settings.time_zone to process.env.HEALTH_TZ before UTC. timeZoneFor in lib/server/expenditure.ts (line 54) and the HAE ingest in lib/server/health-ingest.ts (line 77) do the same. The account-day contract (lib/server/account-day.ts header, t24b) forbids this: HEALTH_TZ is one account's personal zone applied to every other account. The estimate and weekly-proposal jobs were moved to resolveAccountDay, but the weekly-review due test and week boundary, the weekly-proposal week boundary and the ingest bucketing still read it. docs/features.md F-160 describes the HEALTH_TZ fallback, so this may be accepted legacy behaviour.
plausible.failureScenario: With HEALTH_TZ=America/New_York in production, an account in Tokyo whose time_zone is still null (never opened online) gets its Sunday 18:00 review at New York's Sunday evening. Its weekly_proposal week_start is computed in New York time while the same job's asOf and estimate use UTC (weekly-proposal/route.ts lines 130-133). Health Auto Export samples for that account are bucketed to New York days.
plausible.evidence: jobs.ts:151 and :167 `healthTimeZone(null, userTimeZone, process.env.HEALTH_TZ ?? DEFAULT_TZ)`; jobs.ts:184 same in accountZones; expenditure.ts:54 `process.env.HEALTH_TZ`; health-ingest.ts:77; app/api/jobs/weekly-proposal/route.ts:130-133 (asOf from resolveAccountDay, weekZone from timeZoneFor).
plausible.fix: Drop HEALTH_TZ from these chains and use the same stored zone, request zone, then logged-UTC order as resolveAccountDay. Use one resolved zone for both weekStart and asOf in weekly-proposal.
plausible.knownBefore: docs/features.md F-160 (documented HEALTH_TZ fallback); account-day.ts t24b scopes the HEALTH_TZ ban to target revisions
votes: refuted: The code does what the finding says. weekStartOf, todayIso, accountZones, timeZoneFor and the HAE ingest all fall back from a null stored zone to HEALTH_TZ, then UTC. I don't treat that as a bug, for three reasons. (1) docs/features.md F-160 documents this fallback ("user_settings.time_zone, else HEALTH_TZ, else UTC") as the intended behaviour for the weekly-review due test and week boundary, and the HEALTH_TZ env var is a documented deployment setting (docs/decisions/2026-09-12-wave4-rulings.md, docs/readiness/2026-09-19/03-env.md). (2) The "no HEALTH_TZ" rule in lib/server/account-day.ts is scoped to the server's "today" for target revisions (t24b). Its header does not extend to the health, ingest or review jobs. (3) Reach is narrow: only accounts whose time_zone was never saved. The HAE ingest also prefers the per-source zone and the user's zone before HEALTH_TZ. The finding names no ruling that forbids the fallback. The remaining difference (weekly-proposal week_start in HEALTH_TZ while asOf uses UTC) is a minor inconsistency inside a documented fallback. It is a cleanup candidate at most, not a defect.

confirmed: The code does what the finding says. lib/server/jobs.ts lines 151, 167 and 184 (weekStartOf, todayIso, accountZones), lib/server/expenditure.ts timeZoneFor (line 54) and lib/server/health-ingest.ts line 77 all pass process.env.HEALTH_TZ into healthTimeZone as the fallback for a null user_settings.time_zone. I confirmed this by reading the code only. I did not write a repro, because the call chain is plain. weekly-proposal/route.ts lines 130-137 shows the mismatch: asOf comes from resolveAccountDay, which ignores HEALTH_TZ and falls to UTC, while weekZone comes from timeZoneFor, which uses HEALTH_TZ. Both are computed for the same account in the same job. The header of lib/server/account-day.ts says no deployment-wide HEALTH_TZ is consulted because it would apply one account's zone to every other account, but that header scopes itself to the server's "today" for target revisions. docs/features.md F-160 explicitly documents the fallback chain (time_zone, then HEALTH_TZ, then UTC) for the weekly review. A comment in weekly-proposal/route.ts keeps the cron zone chain on purpose so the proposal week_start matches the weekly-review job. So the review and week-boundary behaviour is documented legacy behaviour, and it is only partly accepted by the docs. Health Auto Export ingest is not covered by F-160.
