plausible.title: Coach role save sends a stale whole-row pref and can revert an Avoid mark (or recreate a removed food)
plausible.defect: persistStoredRole builds a whole-row user_food_prefs update from the IndexedDB mirror row: status, no_cook and note are copied from it, with base_rev set to the mirror's rev. The mirror is not refreshed when another device marks the food. set_food_membership writes user_food_prefs but inserts no change_log row, so other devices' mirrors keep the old status. The server's user_food_prefs upsert replaces status from the payload. On the resulting conflict, mergeEntity does newer-client_ts-wins per field, so the stale status wins.
plausible.failureScenario: Device A's mirror holds pref {status:'eats', rev:3} for a food. On device B the user marks it Avoid at 10:00; set_food_membership bumps the server pref to rev 4 with status 'avoid'. At 10:05 the user confirms a role on A through the coach. The op carries status:'eats' with base_rev 3, so it conflicts. local = {...mirror, ...payload} has client_ts 10:05, newer than the server's updated_at of 10:00, so 'eats' wins. The rebased op overwrites the pref and the food is eligible again although food_membership_revisions says avoid. If B instead set the food to neutral, set_food_membership deleted the pref row. A's op then gets 'gone', and onGone re-queues it as a create with base_rev null, so the deleted pref comes back with the stale status.
plausible.evidence: lib/coach/role-advice.ts:128-146 (payload {food_ref_id, status: row.status, role, no_cook, note} from getRow mirror, base_rev rev). supabase/migrations/20261205090000_food_membership_result.sql: set_food_membership has no change_log insert, and its upsert does rev = pref.rev + 1. lib/sync/outbox.ts:180-187 (merge with op.client_ts vs serverTimestampOf), outbox.ts:332-336 (onGone). The role-only SQL fast path in 20261210090100 only matches the server-side confirmFoodRole payload {role}, not this client op.
plausible.fix: Send the role-only payload {role} (the server already special-cases it with rev = p_rev - 1 and food_role_conflict), or re-read the pref from the server before enqueueing. Do not carry status in a role write.
votes:
confirmed: The mechanism holds in code, but the reachable window is narrower than the finding says.

What holds:
- `persistStoredRole` (`lib/coach/role-advice.ts:128-146`) sends a whole-row payload. `status`, `no_cook` and `note` come from the IndexedDB mirror, with `base_rev` set to the mirror's `rev`.
- `set_food_membership` (`20261205090000`) writes `user_food_prefs` and inserts no `change_log` row. `lib/foods/prefs-client.ts:752` says only `apply_sync_op` emits a pullable change_log entry, and `food-refs.ts` says "Direct Foods writes do not enter change_log".
- The mirror is filled only from change_log pulls (`lib/sync/client.ts:289`) and from `applyFoodRow`. `loadAccountFoodSnapshot` reads rows over REST for the store projection and does not write the mirror. A membership op never writes the pref mirror (`applyFoodMembershipResult` only deletes the op). So the mirror row's `status` stays stale after any membership mark, on the same device or another.
- The role-only SQL fast path (`20261210090100`) needs the payload to equal `{role}` exactly, so this client op takes the full upsert and replaces `status`.
- On the resulting conflict, `onConflict` builds `local = {...mirror, ...payload}` with a fresh `client_ts`. `mergeEntity` then lets the stale `status` win. For a neutral food, `onGone` re-queues the op as a create.

What is narrower than the finding describes:
- The only caller is `applyFoodListMark` (`lib/coach/apply-prefs.ts:97-102`). It runs `confirmMealComponentRole` right after the device's own `setFoodMembership`. Confirm-required advice goes through the server route instead. So the finding's literal story (a user confirming a role on A minutes after B marked Avoid) is not a separate path. The sub-second cross-device race is negligible.
- The same-device variant is real. `roleRowIsReady` checks only that the mirror status is eats or avoid, not that it matches the new mark. Take a food whose mirror pref row exists with the old status, which needs an earlier `apply_sync_op` write, and whose role is still null. If the user then tells the coach `add_to_avoid`, or `add_to_eats` after an Avoid, the op sends the old status with the old `base_rev`. That conflicts with the bumped server rev, and the old status wins on merge. The pref row then contradicts `food_membership_revisions`, and an Avoid mark can be reverted.
- Mirror rows exist only for prefs written through `apply_sync_op`, so exposure is limited. No owner ruling or prior audit covers it, and no upstream guard prevents it.

I did not run a test.

refuted: The only caller of persistStoredRole is confirmMealComponentRole, and applyFoodListMark in lib/coach/apply-prefs.ts calls that immediately after this device applied its own food-membership mark. The status in the role payload is therefore the mark this device just made, not a mirror row left over from earlier. The finding's scenario, a role confirmed 5 minutes later from a stale mirror, does not match the call path. If another device's Avoid mark lands first, this device's own mark is the later user action. That mark also writes through set_food_membership, and food_membership_revisions orders it as the winner. The role op reasserts the same status with client_ts close to the mark time, so it is never later than the other device's mark unless this device acted later. In the offline case (A marks at T1, B marks Avoid at T2 > T1), the role op's client_ts is about T1. The server's updated_at is T2. mergeEntity's newer-wins rule keeps the server's avoid status, so the stale value does not override it. The 'gone' path re-creating a deleted pref has the same limit: the neutral write by B would have to come after A's mark and be dropped by A's reasserted 'eats'. The role op also never reaches the server before this device's own membership op. I did not run a snippet; this rests on tracing the code (lib/coach/role-advice.ts, lib/coach/apply-prefs.ts, lib/sync/outbox.ts onConflict and onGone) and the set_food_membership migration. I did confirm that set_food_membership inserts no change_log row, but that gap does not produce the failure described.

plausible.title: coach_messages and coach_threads are client-writable although record_coach_undo and taste_chips_confirm treat message tool_calls as server proof
plausible.defect: coach_messages carries pattern-1 owner `for all` DML (with a thread-owner check only). record_coach_undo (the `tool_calls.actions` and `tool_calls.composed` match) and taste_chips_confirm (the `tool_calls->'tasteChips'` proposal check) treat a stored assistant message as proof that the coach issued an action or card. A user can insert their own assistant message with any tool_calls, model_id, ai_call_id or provenance.
plausible.failureScenario: A user inserts an assistant coach_messages row with tool_calls {actions:[{actionId:'forged-1',kind:'log_water',...}]}. record_coach_undo then passes the unknown_action gate and reaches the target comparison (local run returned target_mismatch instead of unknown_action). With a fully consistent forged action, a coach Undo record can be created for any action, and taste_chips_confirm accepts any coach proposal. The server-recorded Undo and the chip-proposal checks therefore prove nothing against a hostile client. The impact stays within the caller's own data.
plausible.evidence: 20260911000500_rls.sql:46-50 (coach_messages_rw `for all`). 20261210090300_coach_action_undos.sql:~175-200 reads m.tool_calls->'actions'. 20261220090000_taste_chip_receipts.sql:~345 reads m.tool_calls->'tasteChips'. The server writes assistant messages with the admin client, yet the table grants INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to authenticated.
plausible.fix: Restrict authenticated to select, plus insert of role='user' only (WITH CHECK role='user' and tool_calls is null). Write assistant rows through the service role.
votes: refuted: The premise is true. The coach_messages_rw policy in supabase/migrations/20261103090100_same_owner_references.sql (lines 394-401) lets a user insert, update or delete their own rows, so a user can forge an assistant message with any tool_calls. This is not a defect, because the forgery gains the user nothing. The finding's own impact line concedes this: it stays within the caller's own data. record_coach_undo only creates an Undo record that inverts the caller's own log, water, slot or list-mark rows. The inverse is applied through the same sync RPC that the user can already call directly with their own session. taste_chips_confirm only adds taste chips and cuisines to the caller's own user_settings row. The user can already write that row through the sync RPC and /api/profile/prefs. So a forged coach message crosses no trust boundary: no other user's data, no privileged writer and no money or model spend is reachable. The "server proof" role of tool_calls is a consistency check for honest clients, not a defence against the account owner, so a hostile client gains nothing it could not do directly. This is a hardening nit at most, not a vulnerability. I found no owner ruling that accepts it explicitly, and I did not run a local proof.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the migrations. I did not run a repro. The RLS policy `coach_messages_rw` (re-created in 20261103090100_same_owner_references.sql:394) is `for all to authenticated`. It checks only that `user_id` equals the caller and that the caller owns the thread. The `_coach_chat_insert_guard` trigger sits on `coach_threads` only. No later migration revokes INSERT or UPDATE on `coach_messages` or adds a role or `tool_calls` guard. So an owner can insert or update an assistant message with any `tool_calls` (`actions`, `composed`, `tasteChips`). `record_coach_undo` and `taste_chips_confirm` read those fields as proof that the coach issued the action or card. Earlier spec audits (phase-12 r4 and r9) flagged the same client-writable-`tool_calls` problem. I found no owner ruling that accepts it for these two functions. The impact stays within the caller's own data, so low severity is right.

plausible.title: health_sources is owner-writable, so ingest tokens can be minted, un-revoked or retargeted outside the issuance route
plausible.defect: health_sources (token_hash, revoked_at, kind, oauth, time_zone) has the pattern-1 owner policy with full DML for authenticated. Tokens are meant to be issued only by POST /api/health/tokens (20 per hour, server-side hash). That row is the bearer credential that resolveSourceByToken checks.
plausible.failureScenario: With a stolen browser session JWT, an attacker can `update health_sources set revoked_at=null` on the user's own revoked source, or insert a source with a token_hash they chose. The route's issuance limit, kind allow-list and one-time reveal are then bypassed. The oauth column can be overwritten with junk sealed values, making the oura-pull job error for that source. Local test: `insert into health_sources(user_id,kind,token_hash) values (A,'manual','\x0102')` returned an id as authenticated.
plausible.evidence: 20260911000500_rls.sql:12-21 lists health_sources; no later migration revokes it (20260925000000 revokes only health_samples and ingest_events). lib/server/health-tokens.ts:22-34 authenticates solely by `token_hash = hash AND revoked_at is null`.
plausible.fix: `revoke insert, update, delete on health_sources from authenticated`, and keep a select policy. The app already uses adminClient for every write.
votes:
refuted: The grant is real, but it is documented, owner-scoped, and gives no new capability. Migration 20260925000000_phase5_health_ingest.sql:26 states that health_sources keeps its Phase 0 _rw policy because the owner manages her own sources. That migration revokes writes only on health_samples and ingest_events. All of that is deliberate.

A browser session with RLS can only touch rows where user_id equals auth.uid(). It cannot reach another tenant's sources. The 20261103090100 same-owner trigger also pins user_id.

Someone holding the owner's session JWT can already mint ingest tokens by calling POST /api/health/tokens, and can revoke them via the [id] route. Direct DML adds only these things:
- bypassing the 20-per-hour limit;
- choosing their own token hash;
- un-revoking a source.

All of these act only on the owner's own health data, which the JWT holder can already write through the app. Overwriting the oauth column only breaks the owner's own Oura pull. No cross-user or privilege boundary is crossed.

This is a defense-in-depth hardening idea (revoke DML and route writes through the service role). It is not a vulnerability, and no owner ruling or audit treats it as one. At most it is an informational note, not a low-severity bug.

confirmed: The grant exists as described. 20260911000500_rls.sql:12-21 gives `authenticated` select/insert/update/delete on health_sources under the `_rw` owner policy. No later migration revokes it, and 20260925000000_phase5_health_ingest.sql revokes writes only on health_samples and ingest_events. resolveSourceByToken (lib/server/health-tokens.ts) authenticates solely on `token_hash = hash AND revoked_at is null`. So a session JWT can insert a row with a chosen token_hash, clear revoked_at, or overwrite `oauth` through PostgREST. This bypasses the route's rate limit, kind allow-list and one-time reveal. I read the migrations and app code only and did not run the insert. Impact is small. It is a hardening gap, not an authorization break. The credential only reaches the same user's own data (user_id is pinned by RLS), and an attacker holding the JWT can already mint tokens through POST /api/health/tokens. Junk in `oauth` only breaks the user's own oura-pull. The Phase 5 migration comment at line 26 says the owner policy was kept on purpose ("she manages her own sources"). That is a design note, not an owner ruling that accepts the behaviour. A suitable fix is to revoke insert, update and delete on health_sources from authenticated and, if needed, allow a column-limited update (device_label).

plausible.title: Out-of-scope coach actions are dropped silently, so the claim check ends the turn with a wrong 'tell me the amounts once more' reply
plausible.defect: actionsInScope drops every action the ask box's scope does not allow, and adds no clarification. The prose still claims the write, so verify flags a claim with no action (final-step.ts:174-182). The turn spends a correction round asking the model to resend the action (final-step.ts:186-191). The resent action is dropped by the same filter, so claimWithoutAction is set (final-step.ts:193). modelReply then replaces the reply with 'I have not logged that yet. Tell me the amounts once more and I will.' (reply.ts:37). That text is wrong for every action kind except log_meal, and resending can never succeed from that scope.
plausible.failureScenario: On the Foods tab ask box (scope page:foods), the user types 'log two eggs for breakfast'. The model returns log_meal with 'Logged 2 eggs.' log_meal is not in PAGE_KINDS.foods (scope.ts:28-29), so it is dropped. Verify flags the claim, and a second billed model round produces the same action, which is dropped again. The user reads 'Tell me the amounts once more and I will.' They repeat the amounts and get the same answer every time. The same happens on a meal card when the user names another slot or date, or asks for water or weight.
plausible.evidence: final-step.ts:57 `if (req.scope && finalStep.actions) finalStep.actions = actionsInScope(finalStep.actions, req.scope);` (no clarification pushed); scope.ts:46-61 filter; final-step.ts:178-193 claim correction then `state.claimWithoutAction = true`; reply.ts:36-37 fixed log copy.
plausible.fix: When actionsInScope removes actions, record a scope clarification (e.g. 'That has to be done from Today' or the global coach) in state.actionClarifications. That stops the claim-correction loop and tells the user where the action can be done. Also word the claimWithoutAction copy per action kind rather than always about logging amounts.
votes:
uncertain: I did not run a repro. The code chain is real, but it only runs when the model ignores explicit scope instructions, so the finding's "medium" overstates it. Evidence from reading the code:

- final-step.ts:57 drops out-of-scope actions with `actionsInScope` and pushes no clarification.
- Verify can then flag the prose claim, which triggers one correction round. If the resent action is dropped again, `claimWithoutAction` is set and reply.ts:36-37 shows "Tell me the amounts once more and I will."

What weakens the finding:
1. The scenario assumes the model emits a `log_meal` action and "Logged 2 eggs." from the Foods ask box. `scopeGuidance` (lib/coach/scope.ts, added to the transcript at model-context.ts:84) tells the model the allowed kinds and says "answer in words and emit no action" for anything else. A compliant model never produces the dropped action, so the path is a model-misbehaviour fallback, not the normal flow.
2. The fast path also declines out-of-scope actions on purpose (fast-path.ts:87-88: "the model turn explains where it belongs"), so the design expects the model to explain, not to emit.
3. The fallback sentence is the app's generic "I have not logged that yet" reply. It is true, since nothing was logged. Only the "tell me the amounts once more" advice is misleading for out-of-scope kinds.
4. I found no owner ruling that accepts this behaviour.
5. I did not check whether tests/coach/scope.test.ts covers the claim-fallback path.

The real flaw is a missing out-of-scope clarification. It would cost an unnecessary billed correction round and give poor copy, but only on rare model non-compliance. No data is written wrongly and no safety path is affected.

confirmed: I traced the path in the code but did not run it. The defect is real, though the scope guidance should make it uncommon.

1. final-step.ts:57 filters the actions with `actionsInScope` and pushes no clarification when it drops one. Nothing else in lib/ or app/ handles a scope drop.
2. `log_meal` is not in `PAGE_KINDS.foods` (scope.ts:28-29), so on the Foods page the action is dropped. `state.actions` ends up empty and `actionClarifications` stays empty.
3. `verify` runs because `actions.length === 0`. If the prose claims a write ("Logged 2 eggs."), `claimFlagged` is true. In round 1 that sets `claimCorrectionRequested` and pushes "reply again ... with the action in `actions`", then returns "retry". This costs a second model round.
4. The model is told to resend the action and may do so. The same filter drops it again. On the second pass `claimCorrectionRequested` is already true, so `claimWithoutAction = (clarifications empty && claimFlagged)` becomes true.
5. reply.ts:37 then replaces the text with the fixed "I have not logged that yet. Tell me the amounts once more and I will." That copy is wrong here, because the action is out of scope and repeating the amounts cannot succeed from that ask box. It is also wrong for non-log kinds such as water and weight.

What limits the impact: `scopeGuidance` (scope.ts) adds a transcript-tail line telling the model to emit no action outside scope and to say it belongs in the main coach. A model that follows it writes no write-claim prose, so verify does not flag it. The bad loop only happens when the model ignores that line and both claims and emits an out-of-scope action. I therefore lowered the severity from medium to low.

plausible.title: /api/coach/transcribe has no per-user limit; only a 120/min per-IP brake bounds a signed-in user's paid transcriptions
plausible.defect: The route rate-limits only `coach:transcribe:pre:ip:<ip>` before identity. Once requireUser passes it never applies a per-user key. Each call downloads the user's audio and runs up to three paid model attempts: Gemini primary, Gemini backup and OpenRouter (coach-transcribe.ts:119-154). Capture and coach turns have per-user budgets, but transcription has none apart from the daily spend cap.
plausible.failureScenario: One account, or a client looping on a failing upload, calls transcribe from several IPs (mobile network changes, or a script with the session JWT). Each IP allows 120 calls a minute. The account can use its whole $2 daily spend in minutes. After that every other AI feature (capture, coach, Plan sheet) answers 429 spend_cap for the rest of the day.
plausible.evidence: transcribe/route.ts:27-30: `enforceRateLimit(`coach:transcribe:pre:ip:${requestIp(req)}`, 120, 60)` then requireUser and transcribeAudio, with no user-keyed limiter; coach-transcribe.ts:125-153 primary, backup and OpenRouter attempts.
plausible.fix: After requireUser, add `await enforceRateLimit(`coach:transcribe:user:${userId}`, N, 60)` with a small N, e.g. 10/min, plus a daily cap like capture's.
votes:
refuted: The facts are right but they do not make a real defect. app/api/coach/transcribe/route.ts only applies the per-IP key `coach:transcribe:pre:ip:<ip>` (120 per 60 s) before requireUser, with no per-user key. The attempt chain in lib/server/coach-transcribe.ts is also as described: Gemini, then the backup or OpenRouter. The claimed impact does not hold, for four reasons.

1. The spend cap is the intended per-user bound. `callModel` reserves each call's maximum cost against the per-user daily cap (default $2) and the global cap, and fails closed. Transcription goes through `generateStructured` and `generateOpenRouter`, so it is already metered.

2. The only account that can be hurt is the caller's own. The cap is per user, so a client looping on a failing upload exhausts its own $2 and gets 429 `spend_cap` on its own other features. It cannot affect other users or the global ceiling, and that is a self-inflicted denial of service.

3. The cost is small. Each call needs a real object under the caller's own storage path (`fetchOwnedObject` returns 403 otherwise). The clip must also pass audio validation: non-audio is 415 and anything over 30 s is 422. Output is capped at 1,024 tokens. Each call is a tiny audio transcription, which costs far less than the attempt ceilings.

4. This matches the established pattern on the main /api/coach route, which also uses only `coach:pre:ip:<ip>` (120/60) with no per-user key (app/api/coach/route.ts:68-69). The rate-limit inventory test (tests/server/ratelimit-call-sites.test.ts) requires only a fail-closed limiter call on every model-reaching route, and this route has one.

At most this is a defence-in-depth gap against a hypothetical JWT-holder rotating IPs, with low impact and no cross-user effect.

confirmed: I confirmed this by reading the code. I did not run a repro. app/api/coach/transcribe/route.ts:27 calls only `enforceRateLimit(`coach:transcribe:pre:ip:${requestIp(req)}`, 120, 60)`. It then runs requireUser, readJson and transcribeAudio, and no user-keyed limiter appears anywhere in that path. Nothing in lib/server/coach-transcribe.ts or in `lib/ai` limits it either. A grep for `enforceRateLimit` in `lib/ai/*.ts` and `lib/server/coach-transcribe.ts` found nothing. The sibling route app/api/log/propose/route.ts does add a per-user key, `log:propose:user:${userId}`, at 30 per minute, so the gap is specific to this route. transcribeAudio can make up to three paid attempts per call: Gemini primary, the Gemini backup, and OpenRouter. The only remaining bound is the daily spend cap (default $2, per the AGENTS.md rate-limit notes). The IP brake gives 120 calls a minute per IP, so a signed-in account calling from several IPs or looping on a failing upload can reach that cap. The cap is shared per user, so the account's other AI features would then answer 429 spend_cap for the rest of the day. The tests in tests/server/ratelimit-call-sites.test.ts only require that a limiter call exists, so they do not catch this. Severity stays low. The account's own spend cap limits the damage, only that account is hurt, and the attack needs multiple IPs or a client loop.

plausible.title: Marking one back-dated day as 'fully logged' moves day_marks_started_on to that date and stops every unmarked day since then from counting
plausible.defect: The trigger sets user_settings.day_marks_started_on to the MARKED day's local_date, and moves it earlier whenever an older day is marked. It does not record when marking began. isQualifiedDay (lib/expenditure.ts:144) then refuses every unmarked day on or after that date. DayCompleteControl offers the mark on any past day that has food logged (showsDayComplete: date <= today). So one tap that vouches for an old day stops all the coverage-complete days between that date and today from counting. Before the tap the user had not started marking, so those days were never suspect under R3, whose stated purpose is 'the date marking began'.
plausible.failureScenario: An account has logged complete days for 70 days and has never marked one. Its estimate is adaptive at 2000 kcal and eligible for a proposal. The user scrolls back 45 days and taps 'I logged everything I ate that day'. The trigger sets day_marks_started_on to that date. Every unmarked day of the last 44 is now disqualified. The next nightly estimate drops to status 'held' at the seed (1700), proposalEligible false, reason 'Holding the starting estimate — 0 of 10 counted days in the last 14'. Clearing the mark cannot undo this. The same happens to an account already marking daily that later vouches for an older day: the coverage days before its real first mark stop counting, which lowers lifetime counts and the data weight.
plausible.evidence: Migration lines 55-57: `update public.user_settings set day_marks_started_on = new.local_date where ... (day_marks_started_on is null or day_marks_started_on > new.local_date)`. lib/expenditure.ts:144: `const beforeMarks = marksStartedOn === null || toDayNumber(day.date) < toDayNumber(marksStartedOn)`. components/today/DayCompleteControl.tsx:42-43 shows the control for any date <= today that has food. Reproduced with scratchpad/repro/backdated-mark.ts: never marked -> {status:'estimating', phase:'adaptive', tdee:2000, eligible:true}; with marksStartedOn 45 days back and one marked day -> {status:'held', tdee:1700, eligible:false}. Ruling R3 says 'The first-ever mark date ... never moves later' and that before 'that date' coverage days count. It does not accept a back-dated vouch retroactively disqualifying days logged before the user ever marked.
plausible.fix: Record when marking began, not the earliest marked date. Use the server's account-local date at the first mark (for example, least of current account day and existing value, never a back-dated local_date), or require the marked date to be today or yesterday when it would start the rule. If the owner wants the current semantics, the control must warn before a back-dated first mark.
votes: refuted: The behaviour is the documented design, not an accidental defect. The migration comment (supabase/migrations/20261209090100_plan_days_day_complete.sql) says the column "is set from the earliest marked local date and never moves later". The trigger implements that, and AGENTS.md says the same: the trigger "stores the first-ever marked date ... which only moves earlier". Ruling R3 (docs/decisions/2026-10-04-adaptive-handoff-rulings.md) says: "Before that date, coverage-qualified days count; on and after it, only marked days count." The finding's own scenario matches that rule: a marked date 45 days back means unmarked days from that date on stop counting. Its complaint is that "marking began" should mean when the user first tapped, not the earliest date vouched for. That is a different policy from the one the ruling and migration chose, so I did not find an owner ruling accepting it, and I also did not find one rejecting it. The UI text "From your first mark on, only marked days teach your burn estimate" is consistent with it. A back-dated mark has a real side effect, and the owner could choose to change the rule to the date of the first tap. That would be a design change, not a bug fix against the current spec. I read the migration, isQualifiedDay, DayCompleteControl and R3. I did not run the repro script.

confirmed: The mechanism holds in the code. The trigger plan_days_record_first_mark (migration lines 55-57) sets user_settings.day_marks_started_on to the marked day's local_date. It moves that date earlier whenever an older day is marked. isQualifiedDay (lib/expenditure.ts:144) counts an unmarked day only if its date is before marksStartedOn, so every unmarked day from the back-dated mark onward stops counting. The scratchpad repro (backdated-mark.ts) was not re-run. I read the code and it matches the finding's numbers (adaptive at 2000 kcal, eligible, versus held at the 1700 seed, not eligible).

No ruling accepts this case. R3 (docs/decisions/2026-10-04-adaptive-handoff-rulings.md) says the first-ever mark date "never moves later". It never discusses a back-dated mark, and I found no text on back-dating in the ruling or in docs/specs/phase-16-adaptive-handoff.md. The migration comment ("earliest marked local date") shows the earlier-only movement was written on purpose, so the code follows R3's literal wording. R3's stated purpose, "once marking starts", and its carve-out that an account which never marked keeps coverage days, suggest the intended anchor is when marking began. Under that reading, a single back-dated vouch retroactively disqualifies days logged before the user ever marked.

Severity stays medium. The trigger needs a user to mark an old day, and the result is advisory, not destructive. It cannot be undone by clearing the mark, because the date never moves later.
